speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given the very extensive set of fiscal measures that were introduced in quick succession over the last eight months, it is most timely that Deputy Prime Minister Heng updated the House again on the Government’s continued response to the on-going pandemic and outlined the next bound of support.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While COVID-19 continues to be a threat to our lives and livelihoods, we are today in much different position than we were in, in March.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We now know a lot more about this virus and better able to mitigate the risk than six months ago.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have weathered the sharp spike in cases with our concerted response and has help kept the fatality rate at a very low level.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There is now much higher public awareness on the virus and Singaporeans have largely adapted to the new normal of wearing masks, distancing, safe-entries and many other precautionary measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is therefore timely that the Government signal that we are entering into a new phase of our battle with the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And importantly, to also set our sights on how we will eventually emerge from the crisis and press on with our longer term strategic priorities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As we have just entered into the new term of Government and in its first year, the Finance Ministry would not have any accumulated surpluses at their disposal to pay for the further spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We know that the COVID-19 support measures continued to be necessary; although we can now be more targeted in the next phase.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In his reply to my Parliamentary Question and also in the Ministerial Statement, Deputy Prime Minister Heng has shared that the additional expenditures will be funded by reallocating monies from other areas where projected spendings have either been delayed or reduced due to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I noted from the Third Supplementary Estimates that the main reallocations are from the development items such as: MOT $3.6 billion, which is the highest of the reallocated amount; MTI $745 million; MND $615 million; MSE and MOH, I supposed it is related to hospitals and polyclinics, each about $500 million; and the other Ministries like MINDEF, MCCY, MinLaw for their projects, each a couple hundred million dollars.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These are developmental expenditures set aside but unutilised at the moment; and this amounted to $6.8 billion.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Also, in the Supplementary Main Estimates, we saw that despite having downward adjustments by some Ministries, there is a net increase of $1.7 billion due to increase in spending estimates by the other Ministries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Taken together, it provided MOF with a net freed-up funding of $5.1 billion to pay for the continuation of the COVID-19 support measures (which costs $8 billion).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If there are no new revenue sources to offset, there would be a potential deficit contribution of about $2.9 billion; just a few months into this new term of Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the revenue front, the pictures look daunting as well; with latest estimates projecting a drop in operating revenue of $12.3 billion or a 16.1% projected decrease.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Where would the Government find the funding for this outlay if the revenue situation continues to be weak?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, some of these projects are actually capability investments for the future, which will enable us to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the immediate aftermath of the pandemic crisis, the economic knock-on effects impacted all sectors of the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government’s swift and broad base support to businesses, helped in averting the situation of massive job losses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With gradual opening up, we have seen some of the demand and businesses recovered.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Companies have adjusted to the different operating environment and many pivoted into different business models and products.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, there are sectors and businesses where the pandemic has significantly altered the business propositions or changed the operating landscape permanently.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Demand that businesses used to enjoy before COVID-19 may never return.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses live and thrive on demand for their goods and services; where they generated revenue to stay profitable, to stay as a going concern.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We know that no amount of Government stimulus or support can possibly make up for the lost demand and revenue in a sustained way; or bring back the business viability of the past.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the Government taper down the support and assistances, we can expect the companies to start releasing more workers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some companies may not survive even with the best of efforts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is the phase of the crisis where we may see deeper structural adjustments, changes happening to the business eco-system and also inevitably, we will see harsh adjustments to the labour market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, in our next bound of response to the crises, we need to now intensify our efforts to help Singaporeans who are retrenched and unemployed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In particular, greater effort must be channelled to help mid-career PMET jobseekers; as they face the greatest difficulties to find new employment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Making mid-career switches is an uphill task; especially under current circumstances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Job seekers are also often under tremendous pressure to find a new job quickly so that they can continue to support their families.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are also many inherent frictions to content with; such as skills and expectation mismatches, employers’ biasness, individuals’ psychological barriers and many others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must avoid the situation of structural unemployment from creeping up and taking roots.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are high expectations for our National Jobs Council chaired by Senior Minister Tharman; not only to implement the Jobs and Skills Package but also bringing to bear the resources of the various stakeholders to produce tangible results.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am very thankful to MOM and WSG for setting up a SGUnited Jobs and Skills Centre at Bukit Panjang Club.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are, at the grassroots level, stepping up publicity and awareness; including exploring roving centres at different parts of the town or neighbourhood locations just to help as many of our residents as possible.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In other words, it makes a great deal of difference to the job seeker, if there is someone to talk to and to hand hold the job seeker through the journey.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I remember when I was studying in Australia, I used to visit neighbourhood job centres to look for vacation jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Earlier, I spoke on the huge deficit expected for this FY and possibly next; due to higher spending and reduced revenue projections.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Cutting cost to balance the Budget would be a painful option.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We do not want austerity budgets as it will actually aggravate the situation; both economically and socially.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We cannot keep tapping on our reserves in an unlimited way; as that will undermine our long-term viability; including possibly weakening our international credit ratings and weakening our Singapore dollar.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, the sound and sustainable path ahead is really to grow the economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We grow our economy; so that we could, firstly, generate the revenue to pay for the expenditures and, secondly, to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Without new economic growth, not only are our well-being at risk, our survival as a Nation is at stake.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am heartened that our economic Ministries and agencies are going all out to drive new growth and attract new investments; even as we battle the pandemic crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are pressing on with economic transformation, developing capabilities in our companies to digitalise, innovate, internationalise and raise productivity; sector by sector, thanks to the stewardship by the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This crisis actually presents an opportunity for us to seize new growth opportunities if we can quickly respond to the new realities and develop new competitive edges.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister mentioned in his speech about the works by the Emerging Stronger Task Force, the various progress made through the Alliances for Action and remaking Singapore as a global-Asia node by enhancing both physical and digital connectivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am glad that he has also raised the bar by highlighting that we are not going for growth just for growth's sake but actually focusing on inclusive and resilient growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: What it means is that the economic growth that we pursue must bring about opportunities for fellow Singaporeans, including continued wage progression and supporting the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Here, I would like to suggest that another area of resilience that we should look into is the sources of our foreign labour, especially in the low-wage sector.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: How we can we reduce this dependence and reliance over the medium to long term?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government still has to do what is right and what is in the long-term good for the country and for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a small and open island state, we have to remain open and competitive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fostering social harmony continues to be an important nation-building imperative and a necessary condition for sustained growth.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We continue to need a capable political leadership and stability to steer us through the storm that will come time and again, and to chart an exciting future ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But we should also capitalise on this crisis to write another exceptional chapter of the Singapore story.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Looking ahead, we must focus on our medium to long-term strategy to boost our economy, help Singaporeans find jobs and signal a positive vision for our post-COVID-19 economy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will address the following topics in my speech: first, on unemployment; second, on debt repayments; and third, on boosting infrastructure for economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have been and must continue to address these issues, enhancing or changing our strategies, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Times are changing, so our policies and infrastructure must move with the times.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must heed the changing landscape of employment and the demand for new infrastructure to support growth sectors and changing work habits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is heartening that amidst depressing news of mass retrenchments and job losses, there are still many job openings to be filled.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note that MOM and WSG are roping in employment agencies as placement partners to assist with job placements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a good initiative and idea to tap on the expertise of the recruiters with a good understanding of the sectoral human capital trends and expertise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps MOM can share more about the top hiring sectors and the specific job roles in these sectors that are being created.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the targets set for successful job matches and how will the various agencies measure effectiveness of outreach efforts?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be good if the Ministry can share how it determines the number of job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it based on the number of job listings submitted to SGUnited platforms or are there other factors?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A young resident shared that she had spoken to a career consultant who said some employers are still cautious about hiring but posted their job listings to test waters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In case business picks up, they would have a ready pool of applicants to pick from.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, they are not advertising for jobs that are currently available but plausibly in the near future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my view, such practices would distort the statistics on current job vacancies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The current measures made available by the Government are timely and excellent but clearly focused on keeping Singaporeans gainfully employed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet, if someone loses their job and their company does not offer retrenchment benefits, they would receive a smaller amount over a period under the COVID-19 support grant as well as potentially, financial assistance from various organisations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A direct comparison may not be very appropriate as not every employee who benefits under the JSS draws a salary of $4,600 and above but the disparity is apparent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, having a job is the best insurance to preserve livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But despite best efforts, some are struggling to find stable employment.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The gap between someone who is gainfully employed with income for months and someone who is unemployed will simply keep widening if the economy continues to see scarring in some sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And I am not just referring to the atypical scarred sectors such as aviation, travel and retail but even sectors in manufacturing and services with local SMEs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I recently met a 60-plus year old resident who was laid off with no retrenchment benefits after working for the company for more than three decades as the company closed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And his was a narrow expertise in the production line.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He said that non-performing loans and bankruptcies probably would rise through the start of 2021.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is certainly a cause for concern over the next 12 months.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The intent of the measure is to support people or sole proprietors who are adversely financially affected by COVID-19 and need help to meet expenses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They do have stringent eligibility criteria but accessibility to these funds was created nonetheless.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore, currently at age 55, the CPF account holder can withdraw up to $5,000 from his or her Special and Ordinary Accounts or your CPF savings after having set aside the Full Retirement Sum in your Retirement Account, whichever is higher.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Those who are younger than 55 may utilise this sum from their CPF early but there can be an option, if they so wish later, where the funds used can be put back eventually if they withdraw before age 55.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are difficult times and we should exercise creativity and flexibility to ensure everyone gets help in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: At this juncture, it could help meet the needs of some Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This brings me to my next focus area on financial solvency of households and individuals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the unemployed individuals and struggling businesses, mortgages and debt are crippling.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am grateful that the Government will extend loan repayment relief measures into 2021.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can we have more perspectives on the segment of the population who require these deferments?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The volume of personal credit deferments has also increased.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope there will be further enhancements by the MAS and the Government to monitor the situation to ensure that businesses and individuals have a feasible strategy to make these loan repayments when it comes in 2021.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we need to anticipate and take steps to get ready for mitigation now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: COVID-19 has changed society in many ways and it is unlikely that we will ever return to pre-COVID-19 normalcy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must plan our infrastructure to align it with our post-COVID-19 vision, especially in shaping Singapore into a global-Asia node of technology and innovation as mentioned by the Deputy Prime Minister in his Statement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the past months, global tech giants have moved or expanded their operations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is thanks to the excellent foundation the Government has laid in terms of political stability, ease and cost of doing businesses, openness to global talent and a diligent and reliable workforce.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our infrastructure must be capable of supporting these companies' operations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister share plans on building up our data infrastructure, such as how can our fibre and satellite networks be enhanced to be future-proof, go faster and be more reliable?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the past, there have been a number of major Internet outages in Singapore domestically, with one of them even lasting more than a day.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Geographic diversification is critical to our economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Work-from-home arrangements will become a possible norm so we have to consider decentralising the CBD and creating more business hubs in satellite towns around the country with the necessary amenities and data connectivity to support large-scale remote work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the course of the circuit breaker, we have also heard from workers and students across different demographics and different sectors facing challenges working at home due to distractions from their family members and neighbours, not having the necessary equipment and so on.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, among some of these amenities could include more shared and private work and meeting spaces for rent or access at the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many residents asked me why the grant only applies to babies born from 1 October.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many would consider 2020 a year of misery but every baby born is a bundle of miracle and this one-off support records our appreciation, encouragement and shared happiness with the family in this difficult year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We could do with more tailored help for the retrenched, unemployed and viable companies that are struggling.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Moving ahead, policies – particularly those concerning employment and infrastructure – must be enhanced to help us move with the post-COVID-19 times to put us in better stead for the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the COVID-19 situation in Singapore appears to have stabilised, the same cannot be said for many other countries and our trading partners around the world.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must remain vigilant and reopen safely to prevent a resurgence of COVID-19 cases in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, on the economic front, we too must take proactive steps to support our businesses and fellow Singaporeans to ensure a sustained economic recovery.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On this note, I would like to present four points that I would like to cover with regard to the on-going efforts and plans for Singapore going forward.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is the continued need for an accommodative fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore, like many other countries, has responded to the negative economic impacts via expansionary fiscal and monetary policies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I also note Minister Ong Ye Kung’s Statement last week that this is not the time to talk about an environmental tax.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I believe this same logic can and should be applied to the lives of all Singaporeans, in the sense that any increase in taxation, especially regressive taxes, such as an eventual GST hike after 2021, could worsen the already precarious financial position that many Singaporeans are in right now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With the depth and duration of the current global economic crisis still to be ascertained, we must caution against being overzealous in strengthening our revenue position through a GST hike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Here, I would like to be clear that I am not for the squandering of resources built up by the blood, sweat and tears of the generations that came before us.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, just as Deputy Prime Minister Heng has mentioned, I believe in the need to exercise prudence when planning for the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, we need to acknowledge that the current weak economic environment requires sufficiently accommodative fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of contractionary fiscal policies, such as raising taxes on consumption, which might, in turn, lower consumer spending, we should be focusing on policies that aim to stimulate and boost domestic demand and keep our economy going.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In a similar vein, I agree with Deputy Prime Minister Heng’s position to maintain a disciplined and judicious use of borrowing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is perhaps scope to rethink our position on debt, however.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In May this year, the UK sold negative yielding Government bonds, similar to Germany in 2019, meaning the UK government is being paid by investors to borrow from them.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore’s long bond yields are currently at less than 1%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Temasek, a private company, albeit owned by MOF, has issued 50-year bonds at 2.5% – 50 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In this lower for longer interest rate environment, we should, as a Government, be open to exploring such possibilities, instead of funding our expenditures with higher cost equity funding or funding from our reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially if the funds are being used for quality investment projects that will benefit current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we, as a country, have the ability to help Singaporeans get back up on their feet in their time of need, then we must do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second point I would like to cover is on the Jobs Support Scheme or JSS.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The JSS has, indeed, been an important policy measure to support our businesses and save jobs, amidst these trying times.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The conversation in my view, however, should move towards considering how we can help SMEs more and how we can more directly support Singaporeans who have lost their jobs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the heart of the policy, JSS aims to save as many jobs as possible during this period.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It would, therefore, be more effective to direct a higher proportion of JSS payouts from the scheme towards SMEs, who make up a bigger proportion of jobs saved in comparison to larger MNCs, which tend to have more resources on hand to tide them through the crisis.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Administratively, I note that we already provide differentiated rental support for SMEs where, under the rental relief framework, eligible SMEs which have experienced a 35% or more drop in revenue qualify for additional rental relief.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a further example, the Australian Jobkeeper Payment scheme separates the eligibility of the scheme based on business size.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This actually helps the Australian government to direct more help to smaller businesses that require more assistance, rather than larger ones with more resources to stay afloat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A refinement, such as this, should not be expected to have significantly higher administrative burden and would definitely be a more efficient allocation of resources to those who need it more.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, we may need to think of implementing automatic stabilisers instead of discretionary ad-hoc schemes, as I have mentioned in my maiden speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Direct assistance to companies, such as the Jobs Support Scheme, could arguably provide indirect support to employment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, many have still lost their jobs, even as the companies they work for receive JSS subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure many Members in this House can attest to the frustrations that unemployed residents face, particularly for those who are victims of disguised retrenchments and are unable to receive financial support from the COVID-19 support grant as a result.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather than providing blanket wage subsidies across companies, it is perhaps the workers themselves that are most in need of direct support and financial buffers in the event of unemployment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have used a generation’s worth of savings to combat a crisis of a generation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand that the NIRC estimates are based on expected long-term real rates of return and not based on short-term returns which tend to be volatile.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I would like to ask: if the draw on reserves is that sizable, that is, a generation's worth of savings, would it not cause a rather large decrease in our reserves and, therefore, reduce the NIRC, based on the simple mathematical formulation of returns multiplied by assets?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the spirit of prudence, is it still relevant and an accurate representation to keep the forecasts unchanged?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As the paper notes, a majority of the lower revised estimates are due to COVID-19-induced construction delays.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would, therefore, like to seek clarification on what the nature of these big-ticket project items are, how much of a delay is estimated in these projects and how much of these can be deferred indefinitely or even cancelled.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, Changi Airport Terminal 5 has already been delayed for at least two years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would also like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister if we can consider re-assessing the need for some of this projected spending, in the hope that we might be able to direct more of these resources towards investing in Singaporeans, particularly in the more vulnerable groups in society instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, I would like to seek clarification on the expected NIRC forecasts in the spirit of prudence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And, finally, I would also like to seek clarification on the development expenditure adjustments, in the hope that we might be able to reassess the necessity of these deferred projects and direct investments into the more vulnerable in society instead.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since the Deputy Prime Minister first presented the latest set of relief measures on 17 August, Singapore’s employment landscape has experienced another sharp contraction.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the figures from MOM’s labour market report are concerning, the reality is that retrenchments could have been a lot worse, if not for the swift and decisive measures put in place by the Government.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many companies have told me that initiatives, such JSS, have been instrumental in helping them to retain their workers while they work on adjusting to the new normal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I am, therefore, heartened that the Government will continue to provide tiered wage support to sectors that are hardest hit by this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In his recent address to the World Health Organisation, Prime Minister Lee acknowledged the impact that COVID-19 has had on the mental health of our population and that protecting mental health takes a collective effort.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Multi-Ministry Taskforce recently announced that more employees will be allowed to return to the workplace and that the Government is working on a roadmap towards Phase 3 of the safe reopening of our economy.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Working from home will, however, continue to remain as the default.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In recent Parliamentary sittings, I have repeatedly highlighted the challenges faced by our workers who telecommute.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They must juggle multiple responsibilities, such as looking after children, taking care of elderly parents and trying to remain productive at work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To make matters worse, because they work from home, their bosses think that it is easier for them to answer work-related calls and emails at any time of the day, even after office hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Workplace burnout has become an issue, as many employees are not well-rested.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Since then, Singaporeans have written to me to share their thoughts and personal experiences, support as well as criticism.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The three most common criticisms against having a Right to Disconnect in Singapore are: One, it would be too rigid to legislate work hours, as every sector is different, and doing so would not be feasible for those working in essential services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Two, productivity would drop if workers are not allowed to work outside of their specified hours and it would erode Singapore’s competitiveness as a global hub.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Three, colleagues who work longer hours would obtain better appraisals from their supervisors because this is, after all, a “dog-eat-dog” world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is simply about ensuring that our workers have protected time to rest.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But I can see why some have this misconception about rigid working hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In France, where this was pioneered, their labour laws were modified in the year 2000 to specify that the length of their work week was 35 hours, exceeding which, overtime had to be paid.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When the country implemented its Right to Disconnect legislation in 2017, that is, 17 years later, people got confused between the scope of these two separate pieces of legislation and mistakenly thought that it was forbidden to send work emails outside of 6.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But the reality is that many French workers still choose to work beyond their official work hours and get paid overtime.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The difference is that they now have to respect their colleagues’ personal time and cannot expect them to work past official hours for non-urgent, non-critical tasks that can be completed the next working day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For those worrying about the delivery of our essential services, our frontline officers have actually been practising protected time for years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When I was with the Police Force, my officers and I would be on call 24/7.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We would receive phone alerts on incidents happening throughout the day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But between the “silent hours” of midnight to around 7 am, these alerts were restricted only to a specific list of critical, sensitive cases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This was to ensure that we were sufficiently well rested, even while we are always on standby.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: On the criticism that a Right to Disconnect would erode our competitiveness and productivity, research provides evidence to the contrary.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: He also observed that overwork led to increased workplace accidents and injuries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The professor's findings are not unique, and other researchers have also found that well-rested employees are more productive, more careful and are better able to contribute creatively at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There were also some who were concerned that a Right to Disconnect would disadvantage them as they felt that bosses tended to favour those who worked longer hours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is fundamentally an issue of presenteeism at the workplace, which a growing body of research has found to be detrimental to a company’s performance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Staff’s performance should be measured by the outcomes achieved against clear goals set, not by the extended hours spent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Disconnecting is all about creating protected time to rest and recharge – not unlike what MOE does for its teachers during the school holidays.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Even the Germans – who according to a survey, work on average five hours more than their contractual hours each week – they too understand the need for clearly defined periods of rest so that they can be more productive the next day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Germans have a concept called “Feierabend”, which describes the time after their work day ends and when their rest time begins.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our German friends understand that they need to have dedicated time outside of work to rest properly in order to have the energy to work hard and be productive again the next day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For those who remain unconvinced, let me share the experience of Rebecca Wong, a Singaporean currently working in France, who wrote to me last month.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: She shared that when emails are sent outside of office hours in France, it is usually accompanied with a disclaimer to state that no immediate response is expected.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Alternatively, they can use technology to schedule their non-critical emails to be sent out only at 8 am the next working day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This will allow us to track how well our workers are faring mentally, what are the best practices among our companies and guide our collective efforts to provide better workplace mental health support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that tackling workplace burnout will be a key priority in the newly announced COVID-19 Mental Wellness Taskforce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: After all, a mentally resilient workforce leads to a safer work environment for all.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The latest Workplace Safety and Health or WSH report published by MOM found that workplace accidents and injuries fell for the first half of this year.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is not unexpected in view of the suspension of most work activities due to the circuit breaker measures.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The number of workplace fatalities had, however, remained similar to the first half of 2019.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As more workers return to their workplaces, there is a need to ease them back gradually into their jobs, as many have not returned to their worksites for months.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is imperative that companies implement a structured re-orientation programme for workers returning to work, especially in high-risk worksites.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Companies should also conduct refresher WSH courses for all returning workers so that safety remains at the top of everyone's minds.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Experiences from other countries have shown that workplaces have the potential to become super-spreader events.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: A factory in Sri Lanka where over 1,000 workers caught COVID-19, a five-star hotel in Hong Kong and even the White House are just some of the recent high profile cases of the coronavirus spreading unabated at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We need to ensure that Safe Management Measures are adhered to strictly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We need to avoid complacency and prevent virus clusters re-emerging from the workplace.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To conclude, I would like to commend every Singaporean and resident who have been involved in this tireless fight against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: From our healthcare workers fighting hard at the frontline, to every individual who practises Safe Management Measures	every single day – wearing a mask, using SafeEntry, carrying the TraceTogether token and simply keeping a safe distance where possible.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It is not easy and we still have a long way to overcome COVID-19, both as a public health crisis and as an economic crisis.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Let us continue to stay united, keeping each other safe and sane as we transit together to a new normal.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just two weeks ago, in my Secondary school alumni chat group, one of my alumni mates posed a question to the ladies in the chat group.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She asked for our opinions as females progressing in our careers and workplaces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now, in that chat group, we have women born in the1970s, 1980s and even 1990s.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many are executives in MNCs, SMEs, some are business owners, recruiters, community leaders and we even have Members of Parliament in there – not just me, but also the hon Ms Carrie Tan.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the answers came in, I saw the most fulfilled and happiest of us, are women who are able to adapt well because they have the opportunity of choice.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Due to these choices, they are able to move freely in and out of different work arrangements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, we all know of sisters, mothers, daughters in our lives who have made changes to their work and lives due to changing family responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are women who have heeded the call of motherhood, taken on the role of being sole care-givers, stepped up to take on extra work in the face of job and wage cuts.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I recently met with Ms L, who used to work 9 am to 6p m in the office as a manager, but now works full time as an interior designer at home to take care of her home-bound adult special needs brother.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She intends to continue to make adjustments to her work and her life as her brother and her grow old together.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women need choices in their work arrangements and I believe that micro-jobbing would be something very welcomed in our communities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In my constituency work, I have come to recognise that more women are coming back to the workforce as part of their efforts to supplement their household incomes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in reconnecting with work, the issues that took women away from the workplace still remain.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Their children and elderly loved ones still need caring for and women need to be able to be in full control of when they work, where they work and how they work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She was contracted to look after an elderly for three hours while his family members went out for the afternoon.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After four hours, the family had not returned, and Mdm H had to leave to pick up her granddaughter from school.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The elderly she was caring for told her to come back another day for payment, as his family member had left him with no money to pay Mdm H.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Till today, Mdm H has yet to be paid for her services, but she has kindly deemed it to be an act of community service, even though she needed the money for her own family.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps all micro-jobs below a certain amount needs to be cash upfront payments as an informal industry standard.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such informal practices are set by strong first movers and I look forward to the leadership by the CDCs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Micro-jobs run into the danger of work agreements that are contracted with no overriding legal agreements set into place.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is especially so should the work be contracted with individuals as service buyers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We perhaps can take a page from the Public Transport Council that penalises and fines fare evaders through the Public Transport Council Act.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hassle-free escalation pathways need to be created to protect both micro-jobbers and their service buyers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Mdm H’s case, she had no recourse other than herself to recover her service fees.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She is not covered by the employment act, and TADM would be too large a blade to weld in her representation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could we perhaps have a mediation hotline set up for a small fee for such cases?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Micro-jobs and other non-traditional career pathways can be viable livelihood choices for women seeking to balance work with home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These choices should not be seen to be second-best options.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through implementing strong protective safety nets, we can remodel these choices into strong first choices that merely look different.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to ensure that no one falls through the cracks, so that we can build for our women to reach for the stars.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there are some concerns and clarifications that need to be voiced and addressed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this unusual time, it is crucial that our population has unshakable faith in the Government to lead them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Government does not inspire confidence by hastily increasing taxes and fees while at the same time pledging COVID-19 support measures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, the new actuarial assumptions behind the projected future liabilities have not been disclosed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such information is fundamental in determining the fiscal health of the scheme and justifying any increase in premiums.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The increase in coverage which accompanies this premium hike is scant comfort to Singaporeans who are still struggling with the financial woes of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In any case, there is also no information on how much this increased coverage would have cost the MediShield Life scheme if it had been implemented in earlier years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is already approved by the Energy Market Authority.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Here is a power-grid monopolist which does not generate electricity but makes billions of dollars since the liberalisation of the electricity market in 2012, sparing no time in raising prices at the first available opportunity even as Singaporeans struggle under the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the increase is for paying a higher price for the power generating companies, the gencos, the SP Group could have easily absorbed the increase from the past profits it has earned instead of passing the increased cost on to consumers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While ERP charges at some gantries along the CTE have been reintroduced in July and August following the end of the circuit breaker, it is hard to imagine that congestion has already built up to the pre-COVID-19 level.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These untimely announcements were made consecutively in a short period of two weeks, adding hundreds of dollars more to household expenditures during these austere times when every cent counts to the average Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These policies only act as a catalyst to heighten the already increasing public apprehension of more tax and fee hikes coming their way, giving rise to concerns, such as whether the GST will be increased soon, after 2021, for example, given that $6 billion is still parked under the GST Voucher Fund although the Government needs to draw down from the Reserves – when, in fact, announcing the shelving of the GST increase indefinitely could be a much-needed boost to the ailing consumer sector and remove another potential uncertainty on Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We could also then make better use of the $6 billion parked under the GST Voucher Fund.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This begs the question of the timing of these tax and fee hikes when the support measures are being phased out slowly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can these hikes not be shelved till later?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the SP Group not absorb the tariff increases with their past profits?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can premium increases not be deferred for a period of one to two years as the current insurance claims are still way below the collected premiums after all?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The man on the street must be baffled by the seemingly contradictory actions of the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the one hand, it is purported that the Government is putting up $100 billion to help with COVID-19 support measures.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, on the other hand, the implementation of the tax and fee hikes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is the country so overstretched financially that we have to replenish our coffers with those hikes in such haste?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This leads to the three key questions often asked by Singaporeans regarding the $100 billion of COVID-19 support measures: how is the $100 billion spent?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How much reserves are left after paying the $100 billion?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Although the Government has given most of the relevant information in answers to Parliamentary Questions, Ministerial Statements and published financial statements, these questions need to be answered in a more precise and simplified manner so that the layperson can comprehend.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have attempted to do this below and I would welcome the Deputy Prime Minister to correct me if I am inaccurate in my humble attempt to address those queries.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Seven billion dollars are paid directly to Singaporeans in the Care and Support Package, Solidarity Payment, Self-Employed Income Relief, SingaporeRediscovers Vouchers and so on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of the $12 billion of tax and public fee rebates, $2.5 billion is in the form of rental relief for SMEs and $0.9 billion for worker levy waivers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The drop in GST and betting taxes accounted for about $4 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, this is not an immediate expenditure as the loans are provided for by the banks.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, while the Government does not want to disclose the National Reserves for security reasons, it has nonetheless published detailed annual financial information on our national assets and liabilities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the same time, according to the latest revised fiscal position for FY2020, the Net Investment Return Contribution (NIRC) remains at $18.6 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given that the NIRC is 50% of the Net Investment Return (NIR), the NIR for 2020 is $37.2 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Accordingly, the net decrease of the total financial assets for FY2020 will be the $52 billion drawdown minus the $37.2 billion NIR, which gives us $14.8 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it is not $52 billion or $100 billion.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This $14.8 billion represents only a 1.1% decrease in our total financial assets.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We commend the Government for its shrewd financial management skills and, at the same time, Singaporeans can rest assured that our national finances remain intact and we are far from squandering away our past savings.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it appears that there is no need for the tax and fee hikes to take place so soon.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should let Singaporean households recover from the aftershocks of the pandemic and find their footing before we take further action.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The finances of many Singaporeans have been severely affected by COVID-19 and the Government must support Singaporeans as they work to recoup their financial losses.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is the most opportune time to focus on grooming the resilient Singaporean and not just economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Economic resilience belongs to the Government-led economic development model, which has become ineffective in these technologically disruptive and pandemic-prone times.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, we want each resilient Singaporean to become an independent decision-making unit which, collectively, will make Singapore a stronger economy and society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first step to grooming the resilient Singaporean is to re-examine our overall safety net policies, like the CPF, MediShield Life, CareShield, HDB lease and so on which will go a long way to increase the confidence of Singaporeans and re-boost their energy to rise to the challenge to build our economy and society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The crucial economic inputs in this new era are creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship, and not land, capital and cheap labour anymore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also have to understand that civil servants are not the best persons to decide which entrepreneur to help or which industry to promote.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need the resilient Singaporeans to make those crucial decisions on their own.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's role should be restricted to being a facilitator and custodian of our funds but the actual work of building our future economy should be left to entrepreneurs and experts in different fields from the private sector.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Intrinsic motivation with a buy-in by our citizens will go much further and last longer than extrinsic instruction from the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recently, both the Prime Minister and the Leader of Opposition have commented on inter-generational equity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My humble opinion is that before we talk about equity, we must not forget that the next generation can do well only if this generation continues to do well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If we do badly, the next generation will not be able to hold on to whatever financial assets we leave behind for them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And now, there is a grave danger that this generation may not do as well as the previous one, if we leave things the way they are.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to move away from the "one-size-fits-all" attitude and adopt a more dynamic mindset that moves with the times.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is my belief that they will not be ready to participate in any governmental endeavours wholeheartedly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to strengthen our social safety net before we can convince and attract Singaporeans to take up the entrepreneurial challenge.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is an opportune time to rethink and to re-calibrate as we move forward post-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the information and ideas I have shared can help Singaporeans understand our current situation better and in turn help the Government to achieve a better outcome from the strategies announced by the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Progress Singapore Party intends to continually bring up ideas for discussion in this Parliament.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Government has tapped into our precious reserves, to give out billions of dollars to help businesses, workers and individuals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We are nearly a year into the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many Singaporeans are appreciative of the various COVID-19 support measures.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, it may be timely for us to calibrate the manner in which funding is given out.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It is apparent that COVID-19 has a very different impact on different industries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Some, like aviation, tourism and the events industries, are badly hit.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Some, like supermarket chains, IT companies, logistics companies and medical companies are doing better than previous years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, all companies receive JSS, including companies that thrive due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I suppose the accumulated returned JSS payouts by now would be worth a few hundred million dollars.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I hope Deputy Prime Minister Heng can provide us an update and give recognition to these companies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: MOF has stated they "do not intend to instruct firms that report profits to return their JSS payouts, whether in whole or in part".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Rather, firms are encouraged to use the JSS payouts to hire more Singaporean workers or to accelerate their transformation efforts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To this note, one good example of a business that has utilised its JSS funds in a meaningful way is Shell.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Taking its own initiative, it is providing $10 million it received from JSS, to run courses for its staff in demand areas like data analytics and data mining.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: PSA International has also informed the union that it will use the JSS payouts to not only accelerate the digital transformation in PSA, but the entire marine logistics industry as well as financing some of Singapore's COVID-19 activities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We hope more firms will follow the lead of these companies.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, I would like to offer another avenue for firms that are profitable to put JSS payouts for good use.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: From my interactions with many Social Service Agencies or SSAs, I understand that most SSAs are struggling to raise fund especially this year when the economic recession is very bad.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, Singapore Hospice Council has only been able to meet 10% of its fundraising goals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: It does not help that some may have even more beneficiaries to care for during these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Thus, I would like to urge profitable companies that receive JSS payouts to donate part of the payouts to charities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: When these charitable organisations receive the donations, the Government will also match dollar-for-dollar and the companies that donate will enjoy 2.5 times tax deductions.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The donation would greatly benefit the vulnerable, the disadvantaged and the disabled.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In contrast, almost 2,200 employers were under review for suspected abuse of JSS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In addition, we understand some of these cases came to light due to whistleblowers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: At the same time, would MOF consider charging some of the more blatant culprits in Court?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: JSS funds are our money, our reserve and our lifeline.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We do not want JSS to be abused or enriched greedy individual shareholders.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For example, many staying in property with an annual value of more than $21,000 but do not own a property and yet need some help, could not qualify for many of the COVID-19 support grants.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, some of the support schemes pertaining to individuals will expire soon.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For instance, the Self-Employed Person Income Relief Scheme or SIRS, will disburse its last payout in October, this month.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Going forward, I would like to ask if the Government would consider continuing the SIRS schemes as many Singaporeans still need help, but calibrating it so that it is more targeted.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For instance, SIRS could be fine-tuned if MOF were to extend for another six months.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Rather than a binary approval of yes or no to a fixed payout of $3,000 for three months, the SIRS amount disbursed could differ according to the criteria like past income or type of housing.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: This might allow those who are currently not eligible for SIRS, like those who stay in private property with an annual value of more than $21,000, to receive a smaller SIRS payout.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In addition, part of the payout could be in the form of vouchers so that the recipients will have to spend them rather than save for some of them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: And this will help to further pump prime the economy.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To reiterate, I would like to appeal to Deputy Prime Minister Heng to extend the SIRS and widen the criteria to benefit more Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But the quantum could taper off gradually, to allow the self-employed persons who may have grown dependent on the payouts to wean themselves off.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I urge the Government to give out another round of Community Development Council (CDC) vouchers to low-income families to buy food and necessities from neighbourhood shops and hawker stalls.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Many residents and neighbourhood shops in Nanyang and West Coast feel that the vouchers are timely and useful.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Hence, I hope the Government will take more care of the neighbourhood shops.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I hope these schemes will be fine-tuned and tweaked to better suit Singapore's needs, especially now as we have a clearer picture of the impact of COVID-19 on different segments of the society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Of late, in my weekly house visits, I hear more residents who have been displaced from jobs, unable to restart their work as freelancers in different industries and more company are undergoing restructuring.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It will lead to social and economic problems if not addressed for the short to the mid term.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is only the beginning for us as a country and people in gingerly threading the path as we look towards emerging from COVID-19.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We must now put extra focus in our efforts on re-opening our borders safely, rebuilding our economy and prepare for the future unpredictability.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There are three areas I would like to touch on, with respect to soldiering on for our future, specifically the future of our industries and our workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This was not simply a sign of how securing necessities like masks, food products, and so on was critical.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It strongly reiterates the pressing importance for Singapore to invest in economic resilience and sustainability as a source of competitive advantage.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There is a need to relook at the overall business continuity planning of supply chains, both in the public and private sectors.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned about the need to transform our economy and be ready for a post-COVID-19 world, it is thus timely that we look at strengthening our local start-ups, our SMEs and even the large enterprises to boost our foundation and economic resilience as the world becomes increasingly volatile and uncertain.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, contrary to what Member Mr Leong Mun Wai has said that he thinks our economic strategy has been a failure, I would like to put it this way.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While Singapore’s economy has been diversified with a strong focus towards the tertiary industry of services, take for example financial, intellectual property or healthcare and biotechnology hubs, I think we need to move beyond this as we cope with all the global changes.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How can we foster greater resilience in our economy by looking further and developing some things around our primary and secondary industries. for example, our energy or agri-food supply chains?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: To spur our economic growth, we need more than just innovative business ideas and funding.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: We must create business niche as well as aggregate our capabilities in some core parts of the market segments, in order to have an eco-system that well supports the design, production and associated services of different verticals.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Some initiatives have been earmarked to support this goal like the NParks Community in Bloom gardens where planting edibles and urban farming are being allowed at rooftops of HDB multi-storey car parks.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Additionally, with the mix of efficient use of technology, agriculture in Singapore has also evolved to agri-tech with areas such as aquaculture and stacked farming.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As the UNDP Global Centre for Technology, Innovation and Sustainable Development noted, gaps in the scalability and feasibility could impact the sustainability of agri-tech.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How does the Ministry have oversight on greater integration of technology throughout the entire value chain, from production to consumption; and sufficiency of players within the value chain itself?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, I would like to say I disagree with what Member Mr Leong Mun Wai has said.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: He thinks the Government should not be picking the players or the winners, and leave it purely to the private sector.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Well, I think the Government has really not quite been doing this and did not pick any of the players.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: But I would like to say if we want to move forward and have an active participation, I would think the Government needs to play the role of being an active business catalyst, a facilitator and a binder.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And why is it important as we move forward to do this?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Because without this sort of role in the Government being that player, I think it is probably very difficult for us to create a more comprehensive eco-system, an eco-system where you have a multitude of different players, not only from the private sector, the smaller businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is difficult for them among themselves to decide how exactly to participate within the value chain.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, I would like to say, in contrary, I hope the Government can take a more active role on this aspect.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: On the next thing about nurturing the green economy, I think the topic of green economy is no longer one about carrying buzzwords or even a feel-good factor to be a part of.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: It is one of existential needs and one which has both social and political implications.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Over the past few years, there has been growing focus on building a sustainable economy for Singapore.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The capitalisation on the creation of a green economy for our next generation was also identified.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While the vision has been explained on the National Roadmap and some high level plans have been outlined on how to achieve this vision, there remains a need for greater clarity and communication between the Ministry and its citizens to better understand what this green blueprint means, in terms of implication on the economy and the country.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: By so doing, it would better allow citizens to identify the opportunities, the role each can play and how we can move towards the same goals that is set for the green economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One of the immediate questions we have would be how do we equip our citizens with the relevant skills in order to capitalise on and that are required for this future green economy?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I believe this begins in building the knowledge and pipeline for the future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Looking at the education front, Institutes of Higher Learning have identified that the future economy would be one that requires inter-disciplinary thinking.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: One example is that of National University of Singapore making a step in that direction with its preliminary consultation on the proposed College of Humanities and Sciences.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This is a step in the right direction as we review issues of the likes of climate change.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Tackling climate change cannot be addressed by just having a narrow understanding of environmental sciences, but rather an appreciation of economics, anthropology and public policy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As individual and society, we have to better understand the balance and trade-offs involved on how the economics work for public and private sectors, how do societies evolve across time and space and the impact of different aspects of public policies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This would ultimately bring about a different rhythm in our conversations of where and how to spend public funds, understanding the complexity of issues that require addressing at phases or using multi-prong resolutions and recognising interdependencies across many areas of society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This will facilitate more participation and result in more active and balanced discussions that are helpful to tackling increasing multi-faceted issues.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Meanwhile, for those currently in the workforce, how can we better prepare them for this green economy?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Take for example in the construction industry, there are some bright spots such as green specialists, green building architects and designers, green energy project management, and others that individuals can be trained and certified in.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Similarly in agriculture, urban farming would be an avenue for those whose interests lies in food and research.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: New jobs will be created and even new work scopes that do not exist today can be ready and be available in future markets.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Thus, to capture this future growth and ensure we have local talents to meet the job requirements, we have to begin now to adjust and adapt mindsets to changing times.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Jobs should not be judged by today’s lenses and how glamorous it may be.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With a heavy reliance on technology and science, even mundane roles in traditional farming will excite those that are keen to move beyond laborious work.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Moving towards a green economy may take many dimensions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While we may find that we could see a lack of gumption and probably open attitude to try new things, not so much the lack of opportunities nor the imposition of relevance of tomorrow.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And, lastly, Sir, I would like to highlight fostering of inclusive growth in our workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In my past speeches, I have spoken on the need to extend holistic aid and uplift the low-wage workers, seniors and special needs community.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This pandemic has once again showed us that they are indeed the most vulnerable groups as many of them hold jobs as essential and front-line workers in our economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Much has been mentioned on seizing opportunities in this challenging time through upskilling to upkeep one’s competitiveness in the workforce.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, the fundamental question is how successful has the upskilling profile been in ensuring Singapore’s workforce remains competitive?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While “what skills” has been an often-talked subject, “who gets access to training” is another pertinent question.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: So, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister what can we do to bring different skills and development to them with very specific curriculum that is embedded through funding their employers for in-house upskilling?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: At the same time, I would ask that we rethink about the need and the impact of these workers in service industries when the economy at any point of time has to shut for a period, for example, like our recent circuit breaker.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The larger impact they face goes beyond income, as a daily routine has already become disrupted and this sort of abrupt disruption has a huge impact on their mental state, especially for those with special needs – they can be inevitably scarred.
