speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: With wider acceptance of remote working, this model seems to be the work for the future that we are shifting to.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Can we better adapt to support the special needs community?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There is no better time than now for us to work together and create the future workspace and economy that will put Singapore on a better footing as we charge forward.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The area that I am keen to speak on today is mental health.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I would first like to disclose my involvement as a founder of an organisation that works on social issues including mental health.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Mental health is increasingly an issue that Singaporeans face.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: However, mental health issues continue to be stigmatised, as respondents in this survey cited.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Many residents have approached me to seek advice for how they can receive help to improve their mental health.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: They have also shared their experiences accessing mental health services.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: One resident shared on the long waiting times to access psychotherapy at IMH.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The earliest appointment she could get was in February of next year.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As Minister for Health Gan Kim Yong noted, stigma and the lack of mental health literacy may be contributory factors to the delay.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Even as we are more aware, there are some misconceptions of mental health.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: This stigmatisation might only have hurt us as we deal with the mental damage that the COVID-19 pandemic has wrought.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I remember reading the concerns of mental health practitioners during the initial circuit breaker measures which categorise them as non-essential.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: An IPSO online survey done during the circuit breaker indicated that one in four respondents were not in good mental health.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: The vulnerability to stress exists across a population regardless of their work situation.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: To be clear, this is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: A recent WHO survey has noted that COVID-19 is disrupting mental health services in most countries.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: As this pandemic continues, we must guard against the long tail effect on mental health, as experts are predicting.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: An editorial on the Lancet Infectious Diseases publication noted that "to minimise the impact of the pandemic, we must also address the substantial unmet mental health needs of whole societies with a focus on the most vulnerable".

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: A High Court judge in a recent sentencing also drew attention to mental health access.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: She said, and I quote, "As a society, it is critical to continue with efforts to improve and enhance access to mental health services".

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I could no agree more with the sentiments expressed.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: But there has been innovation in this time of crisis.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I welcome these developments but I believe we can go further to make a huge step in destigmatising mental health issues, and improving and expanding on current services.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: In fact, this period may be a good launching pad for Singapore to make a society-wide effort to destigmatise mental health issues.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: It is important that we bank on the expertise and experiences of our fellow citizens who can help shape and lead the change that we need.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Finding suitable treatment requires time and effort from an individual.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, improving the quantity and quality of information about mental health resources may encourage more people to seek help.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Cognitively, many may be unable to find the appropriate mental health service as it can seem like an overwhelming experience.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Having helpful guides for people to navigate the many options may be more helpful to those who wish to take that first step.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, ensuring that mental health remains affordable especially for youths, especially as mental health prevalence has been largely on young people.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: However, they may hesitate to resolve their issues as mental health treatments are long term in nature and the cost of treatments can stack up quickly, especially for those who need weekly treatments.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Can there be reviews on treatments and coverage?

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: If we truly want to take mental health in this country seriously, we should not draw distinctions between psychiatric and physical treatment.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, consider adding social, emotional learning to our education curriculum and mental health campaigns.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Preventive work needs to be done alongside destigmatisation efforts.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: And that includes learning the appropriate language to use when speaking to a family member or a friend who has a mental health condition and what actions to take when they are in severe distress.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: An effort to improve mental health is not only good for the self but good for our country.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: Psychological defence is an underlying key pillar of our Total Defence and it will serve Singapore well when any Singaporean, even at their most mentally vulnerable, can trust that society at large will also have their back.

speaker: Ms Raeesah Khan (Sengkang)
text: I hope the authorities will take this opportunity to reset the conversations on mental health for the betterment of society.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister spoke extensively about the economic plans to address the post-COVID-19 situation in Singapore, but not enough on how to prepare our people for the future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Upskilling and re-skilling our workforce is part of the solution but it is a reactive approach.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If upskilling and re-skilling were our only recourse, Singaporeans will always find ourselves one step behind.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of focusing only on giving working adults new skills to survive the new economy, we should also look into preparing our youths to thrive in the future.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead of preparing for jobs that we cannot foresee, we need to focus on building resilient growth mindsets in our young people today.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why are Singaporeans losing out in the job market in our own country?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Employers repeatedly cite the lack of creativity and risk-taking, not to mention poor communication skills as reasons for this.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our grade-centric education system was also cited as a contributory factor.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition to facing competition for jobs from foreigners, we are increasingly facing competition from machines as well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, standardised written examinations often reward behaviours like memorising and regurgitating facts and standard answers but encouraging such behaviours make our people most vulnerable to being replaced by machines.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is not easily replaced by a machine, however, is the ability to think creatively, take risk and communicating and social skills.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are the same skills that employers find Singaporeans lack.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, with digitalisation accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, there is even greater urgency to hasten the pace of education reform as old methods of teaching and learning become obsolete.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We had been facing growing uncertainty even before the pandemic struck.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The key to thriving in uncertain environments is adaptability.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To help build the ability to adapt to different or changing circumstances, we need to provide a learning environment that is non-standardised and non-prescriptive, one that constantly contains elements of unfamiliarity.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Diversity is also an important factor in the fostering of creativity and innovation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The modern innovations of today have always required inter-disciplinary approaches to reach fruition, a point also brought up by the hon Member Cheryl Chan earlier.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, similarly, I believe that our educational system not only needs to be diverse in terms of curriculum, but in student mix as well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to offer a wider range of subjects to students and greater flexibility in choices and combinations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In other words, an a la carte approach rather than set menus.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Here, I would like to quote the American psychologist Abraham Harold Maslow, who said, "It is no more necessary to study animals before one can study men than it is to study mathematics before one can study geology or psychology or biology." Take the range of Primary school subjects, for example.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In UK, their primary schools have 11 core subjects including design and technology, history, geography and computing, plus three optionals.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Finland, they have 13 core subjects including environmental studies, religion, history, social studies and guidance counselling, plus optionals in art and skill subjects.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This unequal treatment skews time and effort towards the four subjects, effectively further narrowing the range.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The practice of streaming students with similar abilities and aptitudes into groups reduces opportunities for our students to interact with others who are different.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This has already been highlighted in a CNA documentary "Regardless of Race".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Students with different skill sets and interest will have few opportunities to share and discuss diverse thoughts and ideas.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It also stymies broader social interaction and the development of people management skills.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, additional pathways have been created for older students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At the Primary school level, children are still on a single track with all Primary students taking the PSLE route.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But as any parent knows, the PSLE is a stressful exam for students and parents alike because the outcome has very important implications on a child's future education and development.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With so much depending on the results of examinations like the PSLE, it is not surprising that Singapore students have a high fear of failure compared to students in other countries.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe high-stakes examinations contribute to the building of such fears by making the price of failing too high to pay.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such fears can inhibit risk-taking entrepreneurship and the willingness to venture into the unfamiliar.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A single failure should not mark you for life.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in the UK, national examinations like GCSE are conducted twice in May and November.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope MOE can give our students similar chances.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To introduce greater diversity and differentiated learning into our education system, we need smaller class sizes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With Singapore's total fertility rate dropping, the number of school-going children is decreasing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would have been a good opportunity to decrease class sizes, but MOE has instead closed schools and reduced teacher recruitment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not only is this a missed opportunity to reduce class sizes, it also reduces meaningful job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In our local Universities, the tuition grants given to foreign students are already a recurring bugbear for many Singaporeans, and is a popular theme in media reports.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans are perplexed at why foreigners are given Government subsidies and question this use of taxpayers' money.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Australia and UK, full fee-paying foreign students are an important source of revenue.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Foreign student enrolment, however, should not be at the expense of the enrolment of local students.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we personalise education, we will be able to look at everything we do in life as an education in itself.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No longer bound to a classroom, children will be free to learn from life, learning to think creatively, take risk and adapt quickly in youth.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Children will become more resilient in adulthood and better able to handle any crisis that comes their way.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These are generating companies or gencos – whatever that is procured is passed on to the gencos.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And then, the gencos charge consumers at the same price.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is known as the entire regulated tariff.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: SP does not benefit from the increase in tariffs directly.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This fuel cost increases are incurred by many of these power gencos.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The additional amount of electricity tariffs that SP can collect or collected from the consumers in Q4 of 2020 will then be passed on to these power gencos to offset their fuel cost increases.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I have also alluded to earlier on that we have provided Singaporean households very targeted support – very, very targeted support – for their utilities bills.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: A second tranche will be sent out and dispersed in January 2021.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If I break it down, the 1 to 2-room HDB flats get up to six to eight months of support.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The 3- to 4-room HDB flats get four to six months of support for their utility bills.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, quite a vast majority of this 48% is on fixed price plans.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, they are not affected by the change in electricity tariffs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we are talking about the balance and of this balance, the Government has stepped out in a huge way to support them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Now, I guess I am a bit disappointed in a sense that I am past my 50-year mark and in all my 50-odd years, this is the first time I have seen the Government spending so much to support all of us here in this country.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We understand the concerns that many of our fellow Singaporeans have in terms of tariff pricing increase.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Perhaps for the hon Member Leong's consumption, fuel costs actually do constitute a huge part of the tariff.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, in terms of the entire continuum of the gencos, the fuel costs actually come up to anything from a third to up to 50%.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have had a period of time when we have benefited from low costs of importing of this fuel from overseas but we are seeing some upswing in terms of pricing coming back up.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government is also doing everything it can to move into some other forward thinking measures to ensure that we can manage the volatility and also the price fluctuations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Manpower and Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I hope that I am able to clear this point of clarification with everyone.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In fact, just now, the Minister had already touched on the electricity tariffs, so, there is some understanding on that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My point in the speech is that we are generally advocating that we should be paying more attention to grooming Singaporeans to be more resilient.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: As a result, the pricing of all these public services is a part of it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am just expressing an opinion that perhaps the SP Group could have waited a little bit longer.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The whole pricing mechanism of the electricity market and all that – that is another topic we can deal with.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For example, we know that SP has made a lot of profit when the electricity wholesale market collapsed from 2012 to 2018.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: They did not actually pass on the benefits to the consumer at that time because the retail market was still in the process of being liberalised.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, they had made some profits – in fact, a lot of profits – during those years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Why can they not just wait a little bit longer?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is just a general policy attitude and things that we are trying to express here – that we hope, going forward, if we want to develop a different model, we need the Singaporean to be more resilient.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Of course, there are many facets to that and we can discuss more and more of that going forward.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think that how we have worked together as a nation, Mr Speaker, Sir, in terms of making sure that our support is very surgical, very precise, very targeted to the group of people who needs it most, perhaps not because of the fact that they lack resilience – I think, in fact, many of them are very resilient.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, from many of my Meet-the-People Sessions – people from the 1-room, 2-room flats, the 3-room, 4-room flats.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope Mr Leong is not saying that they are not resilient because we want to support them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, I think that many of them are in circumstances are beyond their control.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Where we think that support is needed and where it is targeted, we will not hesitate to make sure that we are able to not just care for them but to also carry for them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To the point about fluctuations and volatility in energy markets – we are a very small country and 95% of our power supply comes from fossil fuels, which we are also trying to see how we can move out to reduce our carbon footprint, so that we can go on to more renewable energies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you talk about this 95%, we are subject to fluctuations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have said it many a time that the gencos do need to have some form of returns because they have also invested significantly in the infrastructure here in our country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, in terms of pricing the electricity tariff, one question I want to ask is: did SP make a lot of profit from 2012 to 2018 when the electricity prices market collapsed but they have not passed on the benefits to the consumer?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I cannot help but notice that Mr Leong Mun Wai has made a wrong attribution to the SP Group – their commercial model and their business model.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: He mentioned the wholesale price has gone down and why is it that the SP Group did not pass on the savings?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They provide the infrastructure to transmit and distribute the electrons that are being produced by the generation companies – as Minister Tan See Leng mentioned, the gencos.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: After the electricity is produced, the SP Group's transmission and distribution system, the grid, then transmits the electrons from the power generation companies to the users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: As Minister Tan was saying earlier, that is what the gencos are charging for producing the electricity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I think it is important for us to be clear on what is the business model of the various entities before we make comments like: why are they making so much money and they are not passing it on?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Why are they making so much profit and they are not passing through some of these to consumers?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Leong needs to understand what the facts are so that we can have a meaningful discussion based on accurate facts.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.42 pm until 4.05 pm. ﻿Sitting resumed at 4.05 pm.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we must protect lives, we must also continue to grow in order to secure livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is critical if we want inclusive growth and Singaporeans to be ready and able to seize the opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Third, the important role of the Government needs to continue to play in building and strengthening Singapore as a Smart Nation through the right investments in infrastructure and, more importantly, policies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The strategy to be a magnet to attract leading companies, including technology companies and building strong local companies, is an important one.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore's success in attracting top technology companies and start-ups to locate their operations in Singapore and providing an eco-system to nurture local companies and start-ups is strategic for growth.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In this new normal, we have seen that digital is, indeed, a game-changer.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: COVID-19 has disrupted many aspects of life and forced people to think about new ways of doing business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digital technology has accelerated the disruptions and has played a crucial role in enabling connectivity and operations to continue when physical borders and interactions are restricted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But ultimately, technology is about addressing needs and solving problems.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Digital technologies enable agility and new business models to respond to these needs and to capture new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The shifts driven by the digital transformation and, now COVID, have taught us, however, that the disruptions businesses are facing are not coming from traditional players but non-traditional competitors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, a non-banking player like WeChat handles an array of payment transactions for more than a billion users in China without the need for a bank account.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, the new opportunities that are being created from the adjacencies between industries and partnerships across sectors are also equally important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we drive the ITMs, how are such disruptions being addressed with the work that we doing with the ITMs and the opportunities that present themselves?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But to that point, as these opportunities present themselves, I would like to touch on the second point that Singaporeans must also be ready for them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And today, as we have discussed quite a bit in this House, many Singaporeans have had their jobs impacted or at risk of having their jobs impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we are saying is, many times, that match is not quite there.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I want to touch on this point that we must also look at how we ready Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And this is not something that we can leave to chance.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We must be deliberate in preparing Singaporeans for these new opportunities and we must be able to do it at scale.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: If there are too few people with the appropriate skills for the jobs created, this not only has a gap but increases the cost of talent and will drive business cost up and, therefore, again, create other disamenities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, more importantly, while there are good jobs available, Singaporeans must be ready for them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Training at scale – I spent a lot of time thinking about this point about training at scale because it is not easy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, with technological disruptions, many in the workforce are finding that they need new skills to stay relevant and to take on new opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, the training actually needs to happen for those who are in the workforce and not just for those who are entering the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, training must be demand-led and, therefore, a very key competent of this must be the companies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They must be key participants in the development process and the programmes to provide context.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Understanding what industry and employers need will allow us to appreciate the skills and competencies needed to do these new jobs and the appropriate training and development programmes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Precisely because we are preparing people for the digital world which is fast moving and dynamic, agility is an important criterion embedded in these programmes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In today's context, to achieve relevant training at scale and to do it in a timely manner are difficult.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because while training and development are available and we have lots of it, it is disparate.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, we have got to recognise the adjacencies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What does not happen enough today is the understanding of competencies that individuals already have in the workforce, because what individuals have is knowledge of businesses and that is a very, very precious knowledge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What we need to then equip them is today's skills to accentuate that knowledge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And that part, I think, we also have not done very much in profiling what we have in the workforce today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And being able to then say to individuals, "What is the experiences, competencies that we must preserve, and then accentuate?" We talk about data analytics, for example.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Data analytics only make sense if you understand the business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You do not see the pattern at all, unless you know the business.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And then, suddenly, illumination happens, but how do you marry the two?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You have got to preserve what is in the workforce; where is the experience?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And many of our mid-career people have these.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But they are at a loss because they lack that little piece to join the puzzle.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And we need to do this and scale that – I repeat that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will then allow us to leverage all the adjacencies – the adjacencies of what educational institutions themselves are doing, but also the competencies we have in the workforce and the experiences as well as what the companies need; and bringing that knowledge together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how do we create these right platforms to get people in the workforce and those whose jobs have been impacted to participate?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because until your job is impacted, you tend to just keep working.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You forget about upgrading yourself and picking up the skills when you do not need them.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because it is too late sometimes when you need it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How do get people to go for the appropriate training.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is a very bad analogy but I just could not find another example.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I asked myself, "What have we done in Singapore that we brought people altogether really fast and really quickly?" And actually, the mask distribution was amazing, because there was a need!

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And because there was a need, we pulled people together, we brought the resources together, and people came together.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, same thing – we then use the same mechanism to do the next round and the next round.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And so I think we need to think about training in that aspect; not training for a skill but really to equip people with the pieces that they need to then function effectively and be able to take the opportunities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The last point I want to talk about is the Government's role in Smart Nation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To foster a culture of innovation to support growth and quality of life for Singaporeans, I firmly believe that as much as we want society and businesses to participate, the Government now has a very important role to play in making the Smart Nation's efforts really scale and be really forward-thinking.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And no one else will be able to do that.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Not businesses because businesses have a PNL to run.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They are never going to be that much ahead, unless they are doing R&D.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Otherwise, you need the Government to play that role.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I must say the Government has been doing a good job in this, and I am glad that we started this early because otherwise, we would not have been able to respond the way we did so far.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not about digitalising the economy as much as I have talked about digital, let me be very clear.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not about digitalising the economy, but it is about connecting Singapore to the world and in understanding the opportunities such that Singapore can be relevant, so that our people and our businesses continue to have opportunities and better lives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the journey will not be easy, I am confident that if we do it together, truly together, we will emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This crisis also marked the second and third times in history that the Government drew on its past reserves to fund a recovery package.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister now clarify if the Government intends to return all of the $52 billion drawn and if it will include interest?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am concerned that a commitment to restore $52 billion within a short time frame may subject our people to unnecessarily high levels of austerity and constrain the Government's fiscal space.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Austerity can have a contractionary effect on the economy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It could slow economic growth and cause some painful cuts to public services, which might impact the poor.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister assure Singaporeans that they will not have to go through a period of austerity after the economic crisis is over, in order to restore the reserves?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the Government's commitment remains to restore the full amount of the reserves, then will the Deputy Prime Minister share the broad timelines for this restoration?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that he responded to similar questions from Members back in June, but he did not give any indication as to how long it will take.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He only said that it would depend on Singapore's economy emerging stronger so that we would be in a better position to build our resources.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This will translate to vastly different levels of tax hikes and spending cuts required to meet these provisions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is more than the combined FY2020 Budget for the Prime Minister's Office and MFA.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: During this 30-year period, we could also face multiple economic crises where more deficit funding may be necessary.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There might be even a need for a further drawn past reserves in order to battle another crisis, which would set the timeline back even further.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the Budget impact of potential provisions to restore this extraordinarily large amount to the reserves, I feel it is important for the Government to provide more clarity about its broad timelines to do so.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The $52 billion draw on past reserves during this crisis was necessary to prevent excessive job losses, make up for a decline in investments, boost consumer spending and stabilise aggregate demand.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The reserves have served their purpose in this crisis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As we plan beyond this current crisis, let us consider carefully how much we want to burden the next generation of Singaporeans with the committed repayment of this draw on past reserves.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I rise in support of the Ministerial Statement made by Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, though the pandemic has brought challenges for us to overcome, we must also leverage on the opportunities it brings while preparing for the upcoming challenges facing our workforce to remain competitive in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am in support to rebuild and grow our physical and digital connectivity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our position as an airhub is not only important to those working in airlines such as SIA.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our position as an airhub is a strategic economic asset as it serves as a conduit for other industries and it is the source of livelihoods for many of our fellow Singaporeans in dependent industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Take for example, the following residents in Pasir Ris.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Faizal Sains, father of seven, a licensed aircraft engineer who works in the maintenance, repair and overhaul industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Ahmad Khalili, father of two, who works for a major airframer and ensures aircrafts for airlines from across the world, not just SIA, are dispatched safely and reliably.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Foo, who sells prepaid telephone card supporting his 80-year-old mother and his income has since significantly dropped because there is no demand for prepaid cards by local Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And many similar Singaporeans families whose livelihoods are dependent on Singapore's status as an airhub.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While Minister Ong, shared the plans for us to safely, and in a controlled way, open up our borders to protect our livelihoods, it is also important that as a community, we come to the realisation that it is our collective social responsibility to ensure that the safe management measures are adhered to, in order to protect each other.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we look beyond our shores, we see countries such as Australia, South Korea and Japan hit by the second wave of infections.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we open up, we must work together in order to minimise the risk of that happening in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must not let our guard down and slip into complacency.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must be psychologically prepared to overcome the challenges that still loom ahead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses such as restaurants, cafés, shops and workplaces must ensure that safe management measures such as sufficiently-distanced tables and chairs, are adhered to.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must continuously remind each other, to keep a social distance, wear a mask, practice SafeEntry and Tracetogether, because together, we can minimise the risk of infection and we can swiftly contain the episode in the event a transmission occurs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we work towards rebuilding our physical connectivity, we need to remain vigilant and protect both our lives and livelihood.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we aspire towards an inclusive and resilient society with a dynamic and growing economy, we need to incorporate the lessons learnt from this pandemic and integrate these lessons into the Industry Transformation Map.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must take actions now that will allow us to not just get through COVID-19, but more crucially, transform and prepare us for our next lap of inclusive economic growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of us have not been back to office, yet we remain productive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To cite an example, one of the Pasir Ris residents, Mr Ismail, is in his late 30s, smart and gets around in a wheelchair as he lost his foot to diabetes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Working from home, behind a computer, he is equally, if not more capable of performing an office-based job just like everyone else.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The past six months have taught us that for some jobs, it also did not matter that you start working remotely at 8 am at home or work every single minute including extended hours.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We found a way to remain equally productive in this new flexible environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can this provide an opportunity for care-givers, who need to have more flexible work schedule to take care of their young and the seniors?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could this also be the solution for mothers or fathers, who gave up their career and now want to rejoin the workforce while still taking care of their loved ones?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must incorporate these lessons learnt, to provide more equal employment opportunities for the seniors, less-abled as well as care-givers seeking employment such that Singaporeans will benefit from the inclusiveness of employment opportunities and there is a place for these each and every Singaporeans in our industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is an opportunity to relook at how we work closer with help-groups such as SGEnable and Agency of Integrated Care or AIC to ensure that there is a place for all Singaporeans in our inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through the Industry Transformation Map, the Tripartite Working Group can chart out opportunities and create stepping stones for the vulnerable groups to upskill and go up the ladder so that they have a lower risk of being redundant in the future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One example could be for the pump attendants who tend to comprise our senior workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I had a very interesting conversation with my 12-year-old daughter earlier this week.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My daughter asked, “Dad, what will happen to the Uncle at the pump station when all cars are electric?” That got me thinking.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More importantly, these initiatives help to provide the stepping stones to train and increase the skillset of these lower wage workers to prepare for the changes to their respective industries that lay just beyond the horizon.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When the majority of us are working from home, we took a while, but we managed to reach the a new norm.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many found that the savings from commuting time can be productively used as exercising time or time for the family.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This new norm on the way of working could improve our worklife balance and quality of life as we are able to use the time more productively.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the past six months, while we have enjoyed working from our our homes in Pasir Ris, Punggol or Jurong, it also means that our jobs can be done anywhere else in the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Whether it is in Pasir Ris or a cafe in India, for example, PMET job competition is no longer confined within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The challenges our PMETs face is no longer a question of quota to protect our jobs but rather how do we ensure the Singaporean workforce is competitive in the global market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Global companies will be looking at how the Singaporean workforce create additional value.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is no longer a question of lowest cost but one of creating best value to maintain the competitive edge and remain relevant in the global workforce market.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic has shown that digital capabilities represent the game changer to open markets and opportunities for businesses which then creates jobs and ensures that jobs are preserved.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Companies that leverage on these digital capabilities and evolve their business model have been able to survive and unlock growth during this downturn.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As much as it is about increasing the workers digital skillset, it is also important for us to look at the mindset, and the ability to leverage on these opportunities that are available.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to equip our workforce with the softer skills of change management in driving changes to the workplace.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To quote Charles Darwin, “It is not the strongest or most intelligent who will survive, but those who can best manage change.” This is especially true in at this juncture, as we, in Singapore, will have to transform to not only just get through COVID-19, but more crucially, gain strategic advantages that prepare us for the next stage of economic growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the right skillset and mindset, we need to leverage on these opportunities to drive the change.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we look at assessing the training providers and courses, the effectiveness of SkillsFuture courses should not only be based on attendance or the number of courses taught but rather it should also be assessed on its ability to drive real changes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must structure and integrate training with business solutioning to support business performance and industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This same concept can be applied for digital courses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An example would be for a company to receive full subsidy if the attendee to the course can show proof that they have led the change and contributed in some form to the digital transformation for the company These are just some examples of how we can integrate training with business solutioning so that our investment in resource, both time and money, is able to generate change.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the right skillset, the right mindset and working together to leverage on the opportunity the Singapore eco-system brings, we need to drive this change, this game changing transformation to develop the competitive edge for economy and our workforce.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   As we rebuild and re-establish our physical connectivity, we need to be cognisant of the importance of doing so in a safe and controlled manner.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses and the general public must continue to maintain our psychological resilience and not be complacent about the safe management measures that should be implemented.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Among others, businesses such as restaurants, cafes and shops, as well as workplaces must ensure safe management measures are adhered to.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In our efforts to rebuild physical connectivity, we need to protect both our lives and our livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to use the lessons learnt from this pandemic and apply it to the Industry Transformation Maps.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to provide equal job opportunities for the elderly, the disabled as well as caregivers who are seeking employment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is to ensure that there is a place for these Singaporeans in our Industry planning and they can also reap the benefits of this inclusive job opportunity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While working from home has created many opportunities, it is also accompanied by several additional challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To quote Charles Darwin: "The one who survives is not the strongest or the most intelligent, but it is the one who can best manage change".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, in summary, as we rebuild and grow our physical connectivity, it is our collective social responsibility to ensure that we protect our lives and our livelihood.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we aspire towards an inclusive and resilient society with a dynamic and growing economy, we need to incorporate the lessons learnt from this pandemic towards creating inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, many have also called this, an opportunity-of-a-generation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the right skillset, right mindset and leveraging on opportunities that are available, we can transform, our future, and together, we will emerge from this stronger.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On that note, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Motion by Deputy Prime Minister Heng.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng said in his Unity Budget speech in February this year that we must address climate change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He said that we will be updating our commitment to the Paris Agreement and take a further step to chart our vision for low carbon sustainable future Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even as the Government tackle the effects of COVID on our economy and attempt to mitigate its effect and work on the recovery of our economy, we must concurrently work on our efforts to address the climate emergency.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our COVID recovery efforts and policies must also be sustainable and be planned with sustainability in mind.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The importance of sustainability at the forefront of economic recovery should not be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The World Economic Forum has, in fact, called on all countries to pursue and I quote, "a great reset, a commitment to build a fairer, more sustainable and more resilient future following the COVID crisis".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I next move on to certain issues relating to helping those affected by COVID.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Last month, I had asked in a Parliamentary Question whether there will be further assistance for the self-employed beyond the Self-employed Relief Scheme or SIRS.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Minister Josephine Teo said that MOM would study the possibility of extending SIRS.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Meanwhile, I would like to urge the Government to some more of the self-employed Singaporeans who still need help and who have hitherto not receive any assistance at all.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Applicants may not have declared trade income in 2019 primarily because they have just started business in that year and have sunk start-up costs into their venture.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Income may not become immediately upon starting up a business.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In some of these cases, they were hoping for business to take off and trade income to come this year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Unfortunately, the COVID crisis took place this year instead and had serious effects on their business.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That is why they need help from the Government.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For many of these people, they have endured much of this year and face the year-end closing with dwindled savings, and worst, and mounting business and household debts or expenses and worse still, little prospect of their bleak business outlook coming to an end soon.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I urge the Government to provide some support to some of these Singaporeans who may have narrowly fallen short the current criteria under SIRS but who may still need help.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is especially if they can show that despite their best efforts in sustaining or restoring the fortunes of their businesses, they are still not out of the woods, or if they can show that they are also actively looking for a job or are undergoing courses to retrain or upgrade themselves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Government can consider giving them a lower level of grant as compared to the full payout under the scheme to give allowance to the fact that they had originally not complied with the original criteria of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Unless the Government explicitly expects some of these affected to sell their properties to raise funds, the challenges that many such Singaporeans face cannot be underestimated nor disregarded.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Moreover, many in this category have shared that in better times, they have been contributing by paying a higher level of taxes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In their hour of need, surely, some consideration must be given to that.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Separately, a resident of mine who owns a discotheque expresses deep concerns about the continuing closure or restrictions on businesses like his.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Businesses like his, including clubs and bars, see no end in sight in the restrictions imposed on them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the same time, they have to continue to pay rent and salaries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This crisis has also exposed some shortfalls of how our current eco-system may not assist some who have got into trouble because of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, a constituent of mine is trying to come back from abroad with her two children due to the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Job prospects here for her are not good, to say the least, and she does not expect to find a job immediately.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: She did not have a relatively high income in the past years but her earnings rendered her ineligible for subsidised HDB rental.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: She was told to buy a BTO but we all know from present BTO waiting times that she is not likely to get a new BTO at once.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Buying a resale flat may pose a difficult financial hurdle.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What should a person in her position do?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A resident wrote to me over the weekend.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They had thought that the grant was meant to provide support to new parents during the pandemic period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is important as we face rising unemployment now.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But I wish to raise some concerns related to helping Singaporeans to get new jobs, especially for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I was struck by Prof David Chan's comments at a recent forum by the National Library Board on "Living with the Pandemic" and in his recent book "Combating a Crisis".

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am sure they resonate with Members as you meet many Singaporeans at your Meet-the-People Sessions and during your house visits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Prof Chan described how the pandemic has uncovered new vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He also discussed how we need to better understand the reality from these groups' perspectives.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is so that we can work effectively with them to navigate post-pandemic challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This group was earning a comfortable salary for many years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But they are now retrenched or had to close down their businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, they are often left on their own to deal with their unemployment and its many associated adverse effects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is unlike those in lower paying jobs who have benefited from the many Government schemes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Specifically, many in this age group have high mortgages to pay, schooling children and elderly to look after.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The challenge for them is not just to get any job but one that gives them a minimal sustenance income.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The common advice given is to adjust expectations, be less choosy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yes, luxuries can be cut out to reduce the financial burden.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But if they are forced to take up a new job just to meet their basic needs, the individual ends up not having the time and capacity to retrain or to seek out a more relevant job.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not optimal for him nor for the economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Take for example, Mr Tan, a 50-year-old father who stays in a terrace house in Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He told me he has gone for numerous job fairs and sent out many resumes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I still remember his parting words to me at the Meet-the-People Session: "I have been paying taxes all my life before this.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Why is the Government not helping me now?" Some may continue to hold out for as long as they can.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is not because they are choosy with unreasonable expectations but because they need a job that can pay their minimum bills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For seniors, especially those supporting dependents who are in schools or universities, the stakes are even higher.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is well and good to say, "Go for training, upgrade your skills", but realistically, when you are in your 50s, 60s, with mounting bills and financial commitments, you do not have the luxury of time and resources to pursue a new career.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They may even be mistaken for a disconnection with ground realities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To create real job opportunities that result in appropriate placements, we must do more to match the job nature with the jobseeker's knowledge, skills and other work-related characteristics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yes, we now have many job vacancies in cybersecurity, data analytics, AI and so on.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, these are usually jobs that require deep technical skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These skills cannot be acquired in a short time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so for those in their 40s and above, lacking the prerequisite technical skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I agree that employers have to be patient as their new employees get up to speed with the necessary knowledge and skill set.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can say it is short-term pain and long-term gain for the companies to embrace IT and to move on to the new post-COVID-19 era.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But the reality is companies have practical finances and many other post-pandemic realities to deal with too.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can Government provide more targeted financial help to companies?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What other effective drivers can we employ to change the situation quickly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this way, we can take a more proactive and structured approach to speed up transformation of growth sectors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can jobs be redesigned to allocate wider scope, higher responsibilities, so that it can better fit someone who has some seniority in his previous career?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, we need more tailored support as an extension from the Seniors Go Digital movement to help jobseekers improve their digital skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It can even be something basic like enhancing their online job search and communication skills.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This can be done, for example, via community classes to learn Excel skills or how to use Zoom effectively for team meetings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need more focused and specific solutions to better address the challenges of workers in different sectors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially important for older workers, many of whom may not be as educated but willing to work.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Jobs Support Scheme or JSS has clearly helped to save good jobs and kept many Singaporeans employed through this year.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It does that by providing wage support to the employers, giving them the resources to retain their local employees when revenue has taken a severe beating this year.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many companies are only beginning to see sustainable revenue returning.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For other companies, they may need the cash flow support for their industry's uneven recovery.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such an intermediate payment will not increase any cost to the Government.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It spreads out the payouts and instead increase the relevancy of the JSS in this next phase.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Otherwise, the risk to these jobs will increase, which runs contrary to the goal of the JSS.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope MOF will consider my suggestion to help enterprises during such economic uncertainty while focusing on the long-term growth of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Asia as a region will continue to grow even as COVID-19 has thrown a massive curveball.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From North Asia to Southeast Asia and the Oceania region, the entire region is in the midst of a global re-orientation as it takes its cue from uncertainties from the US-China tensions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: New supply chains are being reimagined as fast as new markets are emerging following the rapid uptake in digital transactions from the variety of circuit breakers or movement control orders employed by governments to contain the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is the time to prepare our industries to include the region in our bid for continued competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is already inking digital agreements, and new travel bubbles are on the cards.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ITMs 2.0 should include components where the region is integral.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One obvious area would be to ensure that the Continuing Education and Training or CET as well as SkillsFuture components for each ITM include understanding the industry models of our neighbours, the supply chains in these countries, the ways of doing business and the cultural context of how things are done.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even language courses could be included as we need to be more connected at the people-to-people level for economic and social win-win outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another area would be for the new ITMs to focus on our regional opportunities even more within the internationalisation component of the blueprints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Encouraging more cross-country business chamber collaborations or joint ventures in the co-creation of new products and services that can serve two or more cities could provide a larger market, even at the prototyping stage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Making the region a core context of our ITMs rather than the "next step" would accelerate how our companies are thinking in this new decade.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This crisis is the right moment to pivot our local enterprises away from a local mindset.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An added area under ITMs would be the welfare of our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While the ITMs are being reviewed to ensure its relevancy in the ever-changing environment, each ITM should also focus on the low-wage workers in their own industries.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They should dovetail upskilling of these workers, thereby leading to higher wages with higher productivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, higher productivity should also lead to business sustainability.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Businesses need to remain competitive and avoid passing on the cost to consumers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must ensure both upskilling of our workers and business sustainability to avoid a case where a low-wage job becomes no job.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially so with the growing trends of automation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the role of cashiers at supermarkets is needed lesser with auto check-out machines and cashless payments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These cashiers need to be upskilled and their jobs redesigned to take on higher value-added jobs so that they can continue to be employed, enjoying good wages with better skills and productivity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, ITM 2.0 needs to ensure that as we push industries towards innovation, it has to be coupled with upskilling and job re-design to ensure our workers are not displaced.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My final area of focus would be to draw the all-important interconnection of technologies with design.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While we encourage innovation driven by technology, we should also encourage innovation driven by design.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We only have to look at countries, such as South Korea, Japan and Denmark, to appreciate how they have embraced both technological advancements with deep design capabilities resulting in innovation that has provided economic and societal returns for their citizens.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Design is the economic equivalent of creation with the user and customer at the core.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is about designing for specific needs of markets and segments so that real value can be unlocked.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Design is also the skill to bring about integration and synthesis – how different technologies or platforms could be organised into appropriate economic units that are scale-able.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Design capabilities are even more essential today when we look at how technologies have evolved.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, we are now seeing how social and live commerce has cut into omni-channel sales because buyers are now showing signs that they prefer to purchase through existing well-designed social messaging platforms rather than another app.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe that we need to match our investments in technology with a renewed focus on design – a 21st century duet of design and technology where we draw the value out of these interconnected twin engines of growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just like how we do not isolate one specific technology from another, we must go beyond looking at design simply as vertical industries, such as publishing or furniture, but, rather, cross-sectional skillsets, such as interaction design and experience design.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must also go past buzzwords like "design thinking" to better appreciate the deeper substance of design, which is a serious academic discipline of creation that focuses on divergent and convergent problem-solving with the user and customer at the core.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of our Autonomous Universities and Polytechnics have already included design as a core curriculum.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to deepen this capability inside companies and across industries so that new technologies can be even more successful.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Design leaders and design departments need to be created to work with the strategy and digital functions of the business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A good example of a local company that has brought design into its core business is DBS.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: DBS strives to be the "Apple in banking".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: DBS uses design methods and approaches to focus on serving customers better both in their digital services as well as in their branches.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure all of us have heard of ATMs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I recently found and learned about BTMs – the Branch Teller Machine!

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has shortened waiting times for seniors while continuing to provide the all-important psychological and emotional comfort for this segment of seniors who still want to use their passbooks.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This BTM example shows the user-empathy element in interaction design when adopting technology.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is possible when technology solutions are designed and implemented with the customer at the core.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thus, DBS is able to be socially inclusive while still using technology to enable productivity of their business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe design is a critical partner for technology and this will further enhance our country's competitiveness in the economic sphere.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Design 2025 would require new thinking, especially in the spheres of economic inter-connections and societal value creation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need a dynamic and growing economy to deliver our priorities as a society.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a nutshell, we need to, one, ensure that our enterprises survive and grow to save jobs and livelihoods of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two, we must ensure that our next phase of ITMs is focused on cross-industry and border collaborations with a deeper cultural understanding of the growing Asia region.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, we must augment innovation driven by two-fold engines – technology and design.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This has been much welcomed by the WIS recipients.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is an effort to be applauded, but we must continue to see how the scheme can better benefit our citizens and uplift the workers who need it the most.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I previously called for the Government to consider providing a higher WIS payout to workers in the essential services to acknowledge their actual social value and the hardship faced in their line of work.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This has been even more prevalent in the last few months, where many of our essential service workers have stepped up to become our "everyday heroes", continuing to keep Singapore clean, green and safe.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps, the Government can reconsider this suggestion with a view of giving these workers greater recognition.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Under the current structure, the WIS payout is dependent on the age and income of the worker.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In general, this means that older workers and those with lower incomes will receive higher payouts.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This differentiation assumes that younger workers have greater potential to move up the career ladder and, with that, move up the wage ladder.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While I do not discount that we should support our older workers, it does stand to reason that our younger workers may have dependants, such as elderly parents or young children, which can be a strain not only financially but also mentally.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Any extra income that these workers receive from the WIS can make a difference to many families and workers with young children.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
