text: This is a step in the right direction in recognising that all of us, be it workers, employers, the Government and the greater community, have a part to play in creating an environment conducive to improve their work prospects.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The creation and implementation of the PWM Mark should involve unions, employers and the Government to ensure that the PWM Mark will take into consideration the specific circumstances of each occupation and industry.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: More importantly, each stakeholder should lead by example to be the first movers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Only then can we see PWM Mark gaining traction on the ground.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   Another way to keep supporting our workers is for the Government to consider extending the Jobs Support Scheme or JSS.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The JSS has helped businesses and companies to retain local workers during this economic downturn and its impact should not be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As mentioned previously, more than half of the jobs that were saved are due to the JSS alone.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: A large number of these industries are industries with a large proportion of low-wage workers such as the retail sector, or the food and beverage sector.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This measure can help us save jobs for our local workers, while we are slowly and cautiously rebuilding the economy.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As I mentioned earlier, the WIS has supported many low-wage workers by providing additional income to them.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I urge the Government to continue looking at how the scheme can benefit more workers, such as through higher WIS payouts to workers in essential services, as an acknowledgement of the hardship faced in their line of work, especially during this COVID-19 period.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Government may also wish to reconsider the assumption that younger workers should get lower WIS payouts as they are more likely to get wage increments.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In addition, I am very much encouraged by the PWM Mark so that companies that pay progressive and fair wages to their workers will be recognised.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Workers, employers, Government and the community are all playing a part in creating a better environment for our vulnerable workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): In conclusion, as Deputy Prime Minister Heng mentioned, we are currently in the “test of a generation”.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I echo his sentiments that there is light at the end of the tunnel for us as a country to emerge not only stronger and more united, but also emerge as a society with more empathy who believe in creating a fair society for future generations.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: But we are not out of the woods as yet and we must remember not to leave behind those who are most vulnerable in our society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This has been a difficult journey for all of us and, because of all of our collective sacrifices and effort, we have managed to flatten the COVID-19 infections curve and have kept the number of community infections low.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But we are coming from a low base.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Notwithstanding the improved performance in the third quarter, the recovery path ahead is expected to be slow and uneven across sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As the COVID-19 situation here in Singapore stabilises, we have the opportunity to reopen our economy safely, in a careful and calibrated manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And the importance of reopening in a careful and calibrated manner cannot be overly emphasised, as the hon Members Mr Louis Chua and Mr Sharael Taha had mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But since we exited the Circuit Breaker on 2 June, we have been resuming more activities in a safe and progressive manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are currently in Phase Two and have reopened most of our economy, subject to safe management measures in place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: About two weeks ago, we took another significant step towards restoring economic activity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We allowed more employees who have been working from home to return to their workplaces for up to half their working time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have also allowed work-related events at the workplace to resume.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But as we strive to maintain Singapore’s position as a business and transport hub, we are progressively reopening our borders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are establishing reciprocal green lanes to conduct essential travel with other countries and regions and with the necessary safeguards in place to ensure the safety of Singaporeans and our international visitors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are piloting new concepts to support our businesses in this new operating environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These efforts will allow us to play a role in setting the global standards required to resume activities safely.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Some cruise lines will soon start to operate cruises, under stringent hygiene and safety measures, for safe cruising.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To ensure the highest hygiene and safety standards, Singapore is one of the first countries in the world to develop and implement a mandatory audit and certification programme for cruise lines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: A CruiseSafe certification is required before a cruise can commence sailing, and cruise lines which have been allowed to operate have since reported an overwhelming number of bookings received.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have also begun pilots of events and activities with a larger number of attendees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For instance, we are piloting the resumption of MICE events of up to 250 attendees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Under STB’s Safe Business Events Framework, event organisers are required to demonstrate their ability to meet specified health and safety outcomes before they are allowed to pilot events.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We will continue to adapt and adjust our protocols and assess how we can allow more large-scale events to proceed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Critically, we have also ramped up our testing capability and capacity and we are evaluating alternative tests and sampling methods as they become available, to ensure they can be deployed safely and effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In the immediate term, countries that manage the COVID-19 situation best can reap economic dividends, as they will be able to minimise any further disruptions to lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To do so, our business and community must continue to stay vigilant and exercise social responsibility as we resume more activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As announced earlier this week, we are further extending and calibrating the loan schemes to ensure enterprises can continue to access financing for their cash flow, trade activities and project needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: At the same time, there is a pressing need to help businesses build new capabilities, as Members have shared earlier, and adapt to new realities because there is no going back to a pre-COVID world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, we are encouraged that many businesses have taken the opportunity to strengthen their capabilities and capture growth opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For those that need it, they can get support available through grants, such as Productivity Solutions Grant, Enterprise Development Grant and Market Readiness Assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have also announced enhancements to these schemes, as we continue to support companies to tap new sources of growth and adjust to the new operating environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For instance, we are expanding the scope of the Market Readiness Assistance grant to include support for participation in virtual trade fairs, so that companies can find new business opportunities overseas without any physical travel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But as I have said earlier, our economic recovery will be uneven.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, some sectors will progressively recover, while others will have to pivot or restructure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must, therefore, also ensure, as Members have suggested, that our assistance is more nuanced and targeted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: MTI looks at the firms in three broad areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Earlier on, the hon Member Mr Dennis Tan had mentioned about discotheques.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But moving forward, we need to reposition our economy to capture these new opportunities and support our enterprises as they transform and restructure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must also set our sights on capturing new growth trends brought to the fore by COVID-19 and by positioning Singapore as a global-Asia node for technology, innovation and enterprise – the points raised by Members Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Jessica Tan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But in an increasingly complex global economy, we will not compromise on our hard-won reputation as a safe, trusted and well-connected business hub for companies and workers to pursue growth.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have a good foundation; we have worked hard to create the right macro-conditions for cross-border trade and investments and innovation – even at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: What is critical is that we have kept our supply chains going, our businesses open and ensured that goods and services continued to flow freely and efficiently through Singapore and we will continue to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In MTI's discussions with foreign chambers and businesses, they have recognised these efforts and deeply appreciate our commitment to a free and open trading system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Earlier, Member Ms Jessica Tan had mentioned about the new economic space in an increasingly digital world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is very important as our interactions with the global marketplace of digital ideas are critical for new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will share about how we will help businesses tap onto these new growth opportunities beyond our region.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: First, we have been working on the Digital Economy Agreement which complements our network of Free Trade Agreements by establishing international rules, setting benchmarks and aligning standards in areas of digital trade.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As we will do so with more partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This supports the interoperability of Singapore’s digital platforms and systems, such as e-payments or e-invoicing on digital identities, with those in other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It is very important that we smooth this out with different countries and we have mutual recognition and standards of interoperability.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This will allow our companies, especially SMEs, to internationalise and do business overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We will continue to encourage innovation and support companies in the journey to develop new products and solutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This will enable us to capture new opportunities, especially those led by changing preferences and needs, for example, consumer needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I think somebody mentioned earlier about purchasing online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For instance, the growing concerns about supply chain disruptions and climate change have led, for example, to the demand for sustainability-related products.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The hon Member Ms Cheryl Chan spoke of the agri-food industry earlier on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Last week, I had an overseas trip to St John's Island where I visited the Singapore Food Agency’s Marine Aquaculture Centre.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Marine Aquaculture Centre houses a cluster of companies set up to innovate sustainable aquaculture solutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, they are feeding shrimps, sea bass and others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It is a sustainable recirculating aquaculture system or RAS, as they call it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: One of the companies was Adisseo, which announced the set-up of its first-in-the-world Global Aquaculture Research station in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This research station will focus on innovative nutrition, health and technologies to develop optimised aquaculture feed solutions for the region and beyond.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Another example is homegrown start-up TurtleTree Labs, which uses biotech to recreate the full composition, functionality and taste of milk in a lab environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This method of producing milk is 95% less resource consumptive, as compared to regular milk production practices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It is an example of a novel solution towards sustainable dairy production globally and could potentially strengthen Singapore's long-term food diversification efforts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, we will continue to build on our public investment in research and innovation through the Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2025 plan.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We will take into account shifts in the COVID-19 situation, as we guide public sector R&D to identify critical technologies for Singapore and drive solutions that will meet the changing needs of Singapore and our global partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For workers, as we restructure our economy and seek new growth opportunities, some jobs and livelihoods will be affected but the Government will continue to work closely with our workers, businesses and industry partners to help them seize the new opportunities available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On their end, our workers must also keep an open mind and be nimble to capture opportunities, including entering sectors which are new to them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But at the same time, our businesses must also do all they can to retrain workers, retain and treat them fairly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And we will support them as we do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have been working industry partners, including Trade Associations and Chambers or TACs, and unions, to provide valuable support in this journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For instance, the extensive network and industry knowledge enable these TACs to reach out to companies and workers to facilitate job matching and training.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: An example is the Singapore Semiconductor Industry Association or SSIA, who I spoke to a couple of weeks ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SSIA has been working with WSG on a Professional Conversion Programme to attract jobseekers who are new to the electronics industry, and this is a growing industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SSIA also partnered training institutes like Singapore Polytechnic and the NUS School of Continuing and Lifelong Education to train and re-skill the workers as they make a career switch.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And we will continue to help our businesses and workers to adjust and transform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our journey is fraught with challenges, as businesses and workers will need to make painful but necessary adjustments to adapt and to transform.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But as I mentioned in my maiden speech, Singaporeans are no strangers to difficulties and challenges since our nation's founding.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have been through many ups and downs over the years, but we have always risen above the challenges and bounced back from adversity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We will continue to press on with resilience and will overcome this challenge together.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: COVID continues to cause massive disruptions to many industries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As we hope for normalcy and eventual recovery, we must expect that recovery will not be uniform.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For some, the impact of COVID will have permanence.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Some countries will recover faster and with less disruptions.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We can already observe shifts that will affect us with permanence: the changes in the nature of retail, the realignment of supply chains with reshoring of capabilities, how educational services are being delivered, and the rise of teleworking – just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There are a few things to think about.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The world has become more global, more digitally connected, sophisticated and culturally attuned to global competition.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And at the same time, the world has also become more localised where circumstances have forced corporations and governments to rethink their strategies to build local economic resilience.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: With such a backdrop, how do we build up our local SMEs to become regional and global champions?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For us to do well, we must be able to stack the competencies of different industries to build services and products.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We have much unrealised potential in Singapore that has the legs for expansion.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: When it first started in 1963, it was a small hardware company selling electrical products.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I wanted to suggest to them that they should start printing the Singapore flag on their product.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: BH is continuing with this strategy of stacking different competencies, for example, cybersecurity for ships, advanced materials for marine sustainability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The true productivity gains of our Singapore companies must be their ability to develop cross industry solutions, to be able to stack different competencies and develop high value products and services to compete regionally and globally.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, we have strong and diverse competencies within a small geographical area.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are better poised to collaborate and leverage on one another's strength.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As the African proverb states: "If you want to go fast, go alone.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: If you want to go far, go together." We must move away from focusing on being faster, cheaper and better.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must develop an eco-system to enable Singapore companies to move into high value, differentiated markets.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Closely related to our survival is sustainable infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We are now increasingly aware of the dire impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This includes food shortages, large-scale human migration, threat to our coral reefs and extreme weather events.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: An area of growing interest is the concept of a circular economy: resources are being recycled in a loop to maximise their value.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must be strive to look into more sustainable methods of construction, such as the use of steel structures.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They are usually stronger, lighter and easier to recycle.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The rails, frames and cladding can be melted to make new steel, and this takes three times less energy than making new ones.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The concrete floors for steel structures can be much thinner than regular concrete floors, and the salvage rate for such buildings is around 94%.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It enables manpower savings of up to 20%, allows flexibility in design with less columns and load-bearing walls, less dust and smoke at construction sites and is environmentally sustainable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Another sustainable action is to be deliberate in building new infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This means not demolishing existing structures unless we really need to.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We should look into the conservation or to design future buildings to enable modular upgrades, lifespan extension and to be retrofitted for other purposes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: South Beach Tower and our National Gallery Singapore are noteworthy projects.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Repurposing and integrating conservation buildings can be environmentally sustainable and modern.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: For example, in London, one of the world's most prestigious art galleries, the Tate Modern, is located at a former power station on the banks of the River Thames.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: By deploying modern technology, it uses 54% less energy and generate 44% less carbon today with natural air circulation and advanced temperature controls.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The recent proposal to conserve Golden Mile is also noteworthy.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Another consideration is conserving and repurposing the “zhap tze yit lau” Diamond Blocks located in Jurong.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Both Golden Mile and the Diamond Blocks have the potential to become the hallmark of conservation and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: I recall vividly a number of Singaporeans had expressed a sense of loss over the demolition of existing structures over the years.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Demolition for progress and development is crucial to land-scare Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But as we grapple with ways to feel connected with our heritage and in our aspiration to protect the environment, we should explore with increasing urgency the alternatives.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Like recycled steel, we constantly recast ourselves for the future but deeply aware of our history that made us who we are.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is hard to imagine that when this year started, COVID-19 was still a little known virus in China and it seemed to be largely contained at that time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I looked back at my Facebook page and still saw happy gatherings and get-togethers at the beginning of the year.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Barely 10 months later, the world is a different place.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many have lost and continue to lose loved ones to the virus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Global travel has frozen and all across the world, economic contraction is the reality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those who have not been directly impacted by the virus, livelihoods remain a key concern.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Much has been mentioned in this debate about the uneven impact of the virus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And one of the most stark example of this is perhaps the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The US is the country with the largest number of cases and the largest number of deaths from the virus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, at the same time, US stock market indices continue to make new highs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What this really shows is that there are many companies that continue to thrive even as others in this virus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is what the Austrian economist Joseph Schumpeter would have called creative destruction.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are new businesses coming up, they innovate and break the mould even as old ones suffered and get destroyed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The gains in the US markets are largely driven by tech stocks that were not only unaffected by COVID-19, but in fact have thrived in that environment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, Singapore has done remarkably well in its fight against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: From early on, a Ministerial Committee was formed which met regularly and coordinated decision making with a focus to contain the virus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Coordinated efforts were taken as the need arose.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And if we look back, the developments in this was really quite significant.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It started with guidance, eventually, restrictions became more serious as the spread of the virus grew in Singapore, culminating in a two-months circuit breaker where many of us remained at home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, the economic impact of COVID-19 has been significantly cushioned by the Government.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is important because if businesses shutter, then when the economy recovers, there may be significant gaps and recovery may be stalled.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Life is slowly becoming more normal, and while wearing masks has now become part of our lives, most Singaporeans are otherwise returning to work and more and more businesses are opening doors and resuming.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some sectors remain under significant pressure, including travel and tourism, as well as those related to oil and gas.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singaporean businesses also continue to be under pressure and as Government support is taken away, things may get more difficult, which is why it is important to continue to provide some buffer for them to stay in business.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, I believe these latest Budget measures provide a well-thought through suite of measures focused on economic continuity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it rightly recognises that performance across sectors is uneven and provides tailored support as needed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, in sectors such as aviation, retail and tourism, support packages, which include the Enhanced Aviation Support Package, which is a temporary redeployment scheme for affected employees so that they can still get jobs at the moment while at the same time, they get to return to the industry if it recovers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The wage support packages for hiring new employees are helpful, particularly for companies in the start-up sector, as it helps share the risk of hiring new workers.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That greater support is given for hiring workers above 40 or workers with disabilities is also a good incentive to help groups that may otherwise have a harder time finding jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The lifeline of businesses is of course credit and the bridging loan programme supported by MAS continues to provide businesses with credit lines even as the outlook remains uncertain.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Given that we do not know when hard hit sectors will recover and given the current warnings that the economic scarring is likely to take full effect in the coming months om the MAS, I think it is important for us to continue to create new opportunities so that displaced workers can find new jobs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While “creative destruction” is a necessary component of development and progress, as a Government, I think we can help our people to continue with their lives even if the businesses they are working in get disrupted and they are forced to change.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to express my support for the Supplementary Supply Bill and thank Deputy Prime Minister Heng for his Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am very much encouraged by the plans to prepare our nation for the next phase as we emerge from the uncertainty of the past few months.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are not out of the woods yet but we must stay positive, do our best, and work hard for our future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am inspired and moved by the many Singaporeans who are taking brave steps to learn new skills, take on new jobs, and adapt to a very different world.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am grateful for the unity and cooperation of Singaporeans and residents during this difficult time.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Unlike some parts of the world which are polarised over measures to contain the virus, we are working together to overcome this pandemic based on scientific advice, logic and common sense.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: People from all walks of life are putting up with inconveniences and making sacrifices for the greater good.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All these qualities put us in good stead for the future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am confident that we can achieve the goal of remaking Singapore as a Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In view of the difficulties we face, this is an ambitious, perhaps even audacious, vision.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This vision requires a huge investment in our human capital, especially as we want to achieve it together with the objective of inclusive growth.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We are deep in the midst of the Fourth Industrial Revolution.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must seize the opportunities presented by new technologies, particularly in the digital domains of the Internet of Things, robotics, artificial intelligence and cloud computing, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we fail to do so, we will become irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Being a small nation state with no natural resources, our survival will be at stake.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In a knowledge-intensive future, these children will not stand a chance if they live in overcrowded flats with access to borrowed equipment, limited or slow connectivity and minimal adult supervision and guidance.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We may need to tighten our collaboration with the volunteer groups and private companies which are willing to sponsor and mentor these children as well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will be a worthwhile investment to help them break out of a vicious poverty cycle.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Allow me to quote from the 28 September article, "The Equality Issue” of the Bloomberg Businessweek.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Harvard economist Raj Chetty's research suggested that, and I quote, "Improving education for poor kids wouldn't just help them personally...it should also boost the economy overall.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Within 10 to 20 years, we will be able to see the fruits of our efforts in these children.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In less than a generation’s time, we can boost literacy and education levels, reduce crime and recidivism rates, and improve health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But we must be prepared to intervene more, and the earlier the better.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As the saying goes, "A stitch in time saves nine".

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under our laws, children already have rights for living necessities, education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What we need is effective oversight for children in low-income families to ensure that they are receiving these essentials.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, if the adults in the families pass away or are imprisoned, the state must step in to protect and provide for these kids.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Schools should alert relevant agencies when children do not seem to cope well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Protecting them, helping them, lifting them up will prevent a future group of potential permanent underclass.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should watch over our children as zealously as we would over our reserves.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The children must have guaranteed access to basics, regardless of their families’ situation – accommodation, food, water, electricity, mentoring, healthcare, transportation and so on.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The agency should also provide and manage the eco-system of support, such as supervision, mentoring and fostering, so that these vulnerable kids will have better chances of growing up healthy and well-adjusted, enjoying school and be capable of learning well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Increasingly, underprivileged kids who will find it harder to catch up with their peers in a knowledge- and skills-intensive economy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the kids from these underprivileged families fulfill the specialised roles required by the Foreign Direct Investments brought in painstakingly by the Economic Development Board?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister mentioned that the best way to protect the welfare of our workers is a good job.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, we need to ensure that these underprivileged kids can level up and have a good education now so that they can take on the specialised roles and uplift their families in 10 to 20 years’ time.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am heartened by recent announcement about the Government’s commitment to this.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the transition period, we may face some difficulties recruiting Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, I am optimistic that the pressure from the demand for the services will drive productivity and result in better work conditions for these jobs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Building a strong Singaporean Core in these various sectors will boost our resilience.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On this note, allow me to conclude with my support for the Statement.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: During this difficult time, I would like to appeal for more help for the sandwiched class, especially our young families.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The young parents are just starting out in their new careers and new family lives when this crisis struck.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have spoken to many young families in my constituency and I share their worries.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the Government will consider providing higher subsidies for their children’s medical and insurance expenses, including some support for expenditure for the third child onwards.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will be in addition to the current Baby Bonus cash gift of up to $10,000.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I have received a lot of feedback from parents whose babies were born after the onset of the pandemic this year but before 1 October 2020.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that all policies have to have a specific start date.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I also understand how difficult it has been for parents who were expecting or who just gave birth during or after the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They shared with me how they had trouble getting a confinement nanny, grappled with the challenge of obtaining supplies when shops were closed and how they fretted over getting necessities for their newborns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   I have received a lot of feedback from parents whose babies were born after the onset of the pandemic this year, but before 1 October 2020.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand that all policies must have a specific start date.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I also understand how difficult it has been for parents who were expecting or who just gave birth during or after the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They shared with me how they had trouble getting a confinement nanny, grappled with the challenge of obtaining supplies when shops were closed and how they fretted over getting necessities for their newborns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many couples also could not have their parents visit and help out due to safety measures during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I appeal to the Government to consider extending the $3,000 Baby Support Grant to all Singaporean babies born in 2020 so that we can better support our young families in these trying times.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope babies born to single mothers can be included too to help reduce stress for the mother in an already challenging situation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): For vulnerable families, they need more support and guidance during this very difficult time.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Government be channeling more resources into counselling services for them?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How about setting up mutual support networks, supported by experienced professionals and other community partners, where they can learn helpful tips from one another and provide mutual encouragement?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important for them to know that they are not alone and to realise that they do not need to walk this journey alone.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to express my concern and slight alarm over the increasing discomfort in some parts of our society towards the idea of a cosmopolitan Singapore.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to be very vigilant and take proactive steps to ensure that this will not worsen as it may lead to fault lines widening in our society.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am worried that part of this problem may be along racial lines, which may cause discomfort among members of our minority groups.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think that the acknowledgement of this problem is important in order for us to start the process in managing this issue.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: National education for our young and public education for the rest of us will continue to be essential.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All of us must understand that a Singapore that closes its doors to the outside world is bad for all of us.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am keenly aware that some of these questions and comments arose because there is an impression that foreigners are here competing with Singaporeans for jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to strike a balance between meeting our economic needs and maintaining our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to keep a careful balance so that we do not feel overwhelmed while trying to maintain our economic competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, we do need to look beyond COVID and to do that, we have to look before COVID.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There were many deep economic trends already gathering pace before COVID, including rising geo-political tensions, nativism and economic nationalism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The rise of Industry 4.0 or disruptive industries more broadly has been much talked about around the world, among economists, experts, business persons, unions, activists and politicians.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Industry 4.0 refers to the Fourth Industrial Revolution where data from the Internet of Things and other sources revolutionises economic activity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Industry disruption more broadly refers to the recent wave of new technologies and business models that threaten or, should I say, promise to disrupt existing industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Simply put, these refer to new industries like drones which may displace conventional last-mile delivery, including food service delivery, artificial intelligence or AI which may displace clerical jobs or functions like para-legal work or even radiology, autonomous vehicles which may displace jobs like taxi and private hire car driving and quantum computing which is possibly the mother of all disruptions and may drive machine learning, pattern recognition and other activities traditionally associated with AI beyond the bounds of what is conventionally recognised as AI today, in turn potentially displacing many skilled white-collar jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What does the advent of all these disruptive industries mean for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some may argue that these are alarmist projections.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But it is possible that COVID-19 has, in fact, delayed the advance of these disruptive industries by delaying timelines for R&D and new business investment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As COVID recedes, the threat and opportunity from these disruptive trends may return to the old trajectory, which means that many jobs in Singapore will be jeopardised not from COVID but from long-term industry disruption.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It argues that the threat of industry disruption hollowing out middle market, skilled jobs as chillingly imminent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Among the examples he cited was that of a person who was exchanging emails with another person whom he thought was the secretary of a business associate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He later discovered that the person he was emailing with whom he had exchanged pleasantries and had a fruitful conversation over email was, in fact, an AI-driven bot.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lest anyone misunderstand my reference to Andrew Yang, let me make clear that I am not arguing for universal basic income or UBI here, as I think the jury is still out on the topic and addressing UBI now would be premature – though it is something we should keep an open mind about.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat in his COVID-19 Statement in Parliament last week spoke about providing holistic support for vulnerable workers and for ensuring that workers have the skills to stay relevant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: He also spoke of the even greater urgency for middle aged and middle income workers to gain new skills and transition into jobs with good long-term prospects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Schemes such as the PCP, CSP, SGUnited Traineeship, Mid-Career Traineeship and others have been put in place, some for a long time, some recently to address the systemic risk to jobs in certain industries as well as the risk to employability among certain segments such as older PMETs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are various CETs and SkillsFuture programmes for training.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The newly formed National Jobs Council has said that it will work with the Future Economy Council on the overall upgrading of the economy, including addressing the issue of future proofing jobs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The tsunami of industry disruption that is likely to emerge in future argues for more scalable schemes which induce more workers to join the industries of the future, including industries that are not big employers right now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2019, close to 4,500 individuals were placed through PCPs which is comparable to the placement achievement in 2018.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, this is a very, very small percentage of the labour force.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, not all of these placements would be in emergent disruptive industries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is perhaps insufficient attention at the policy level to industries that are doing okay now, like delivery or driving jobs or certain types of clerical and service jobs which are at risk from industry disruption a few years down the road but for whom there is no urgency on the part of employers and employees to prepare for a more uncertain future right now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To raise the example of jobs like driving taxis and private hire cars which are I and others have spoken about in the past, many of these jobs could be wiped out by autonomous vehicles in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many younger entrants to these industries may find themselves on the wrong side of industry disruption when they hit their late 30s, 40s or 50s, at which time reskilling and transitioning to a new industry will be hard.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Should we not give some thought to these challenges and encourage these workers to plan for the same?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We do want to attract and root disruptive industries in Singapore so that they can become engines of our economic growth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Because if we anchor the technical skills, employee qualifications, business know-how and entrepreneurial talent behind these industries of the future in Singapore, that will enable us to export these skills to the region and the world, thus facilitating high-quality, inclusive economic growth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If there is an insufficient supply of workers for these new industries, workers whether through traditional industries including sunset industries, that means these new industry investments may not come to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rather, they may go to Hong Kong or Bangkok or Jakarta or Shanghai or Hyderabad.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Or it could mean that if and when these new industries land in Singapore there would be too few Singaporeans with the will and skills to take jobs there so workers will have to be imported on Employment Passes and special passes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This may mean that it would hard to establish a strong Singapore Core in such industries going forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It may also mean that these investments may be less firmly anchored in Singapore in the future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But I do not think any serious commentator or stakeholder will really argue this nowadays.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a move would doom us to economic irrelevance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, I would not spend any more time addressing that straw man argument.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How then can we attract and anchor disruptive next generation industries in Singapore and, at the same time, and in tandem urge our workers to transition from sunset at-risk industries to these new industries, thus creating a virtual cycle of enhancing employability and protecting jobs on the one hand and attracting and rooting these industries in Singapore, on the other?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are a few chicken and egg conundrums here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The first conundrum is how do we attract employees to join or to train for riskier, less mature disruptive industries like AVs, AI and so on when they may not feel assured that there will be a job there at the end of their training or that the job will be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second conundrum is how do we nurture the growth of such industries in Singapore when there are few workers with the relevant skills in the short term, without relying on an unsustainable importation of skilled foreign workers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many of these industries rely on highly specialised skills that may not be taught in courses available in Singapore or courses that are widely subscribed to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The lead time to create a critical mass of Singaporeans trained in these skills could be years and the challenge faces the chicken and egg problem discussed above.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As in many Singaporeans may not want to invest in such training out of uncertainty about whether it would be worth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, workers with such skills may be available at short notice in other cities in the world to be recruited for work in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Silicon Valley, for example, London or Israel or China.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The term could be five years, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That could be formal academic training or employer-led training, using one of the many existing schemes that we have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When the term ends, there would be enough Singaporeans with the relevant skills to fill that position; and if they are not and that is proven, the pass can be extended a little longer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The presence of the employer in Singapore with fixed term foreign work passes will provide some assurance to prospective Singaporean employees that their efforts to train for a role in this new industry would be likely to lead to a good job.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By adopting an approach like fixed term work passes, we can bring in foreigners with rare but future-ready skillsets while buying time for Singaporeans to be trained in those very same skillsets, in a way that gives some assurance to those Singaporeans that the training would have a decent chance of landing him or her a good job in a future-ready industry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They may also be able to find another employer, perhaps in a different industry before the end of that term.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Otherwise, they could be posted to another city by their employer.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In contrast, some states and cities in the US saw de-industrialisation because they did not have concerted state-sponsored retraining and income support policies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This led, in some cases, to entire communities and regions becoming impoverished and facing social decay, in turn fueling populist politics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Journalist Thomas Gross, in a 2018 article wrote and I quote, "Most Swedish workers who are replaced by machines fairly quickly land another job as good as their old one, thanks to a network of job security councils jointly run by industries and unions, that retrained laid-off workers in skills that are still in demand and out of reach of robots.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Denmark's main skills anticipation activities include: skills forecasting, for example, statistical forecasting of education status and the demand and supply of labour; skills assessments, for example, quantitative sectoral assessments on imbalances in the labour market; skills foresight, for example, sectoral assessments on future needs in the labour market and employer surveys.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The aims and approach, while not similar to the Denmark example I cited, have some points of commonality.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At this point, let me declare my interest as a CEO of an international research consultancy that undertakes research on such issues among other things.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, we currently have various mechanisms and platforms for workers of the receiving end of industry disruption to receive help in respect of job matching and career coaching.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have referred some of my constituents in Serangoon onto such services and they are not without value.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, it is less clear if the providers of such services practise an approach where one career coach sticks with a prospective employee from end-to-end, seeing him or her through to a successful placement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The KPIs for such agencies and data on success versus failure are also not clear.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How does it vary, based on industry vocation, gender, age, race, PwD status or other variables?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would be good for such data to be made public so that success can be measured and debated publicly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In doing so would not mean accepting that the employee has no responsibility for her or his success in finding a new job.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would just mean that some transparency and a proper account management approach may be more effective in enabling us to refine our strategies for finding jobs for displaced workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Work coaches are trained to play a complex role, almost like a social worker – in listening, encouraging, advising and ensuring jobseekers have access to support.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Work coaches seek to understand the barriers faced by each jobseeker and deliver a personalised approach to support them, sometimes coaching them to develop the requisite skills and confidence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is noteworthy that the Baby Bonus Scheme was introduced on 1 April 2001, almost 20 years ago, and has gone through numerous rounds of enhancements, the latest being in 2012.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Parenthood tax rebates and other types of tax incentives are also given in an attempt to boost the birth rate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To make matters worse, we are now anticipating that couples will put off their parenthood plans, which will in turn have knock-on effects on our population's fertility rate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore is not alone in trying to boost our birth rate, as fertility rates around the world have also been falling.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, we should ask ourselves, are there any blind spots in the way we have tackled this issue?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Have we focused too much on the financial aspects of child-rearing, and forgotten to tackle other significant barriers to having children?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The matter needs to be dealt with in a holistic way.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is notable that studies have shown that in developed economies, greater gender equity is correlated with higher birth rates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That is, better support given to women boosts fertility rates.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To address this, one important area would be the role that fathers play in child-rearing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just last weekend, while visiting friends for lunch, our two-year-old announced that he needed to go to the toilet.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My husband stood up to take him, and was immediately met with a chorus of amazement and praise for being such a hands-on father.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the same have occurred if a mother had brought her child to the toilet?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Should we not also think hard about what it says about the roles of mothers and fathers that we are expected to sing high praises for fathers who change nappies or who bring their children out to "give their wives a break"?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To be sure, we should not knock positive changes in fathers becoming more involved in bringing up their children in recent years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, at the same time, it strikes me that we should be making better and more conscious efforts to view parenting as something that both parents have equal stake in, and that domestic and child-rearing work should not be the purview of mothers only.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Looking at this from the other side, I would like my sons to grow up in a world where they have the freedom to decide for what works for their families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If they would like to have children, they should feel completely at ease to choose to stay at home be stay-at-home fathers, and not be seen as a "failure" or "not manly" enough for choosing this path.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Every family should have a right to decide what works best for them and their children's care needs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our current policy of a new father being able to share only up to four weeks from the mother's leave only encourages the sense that it is primarily a mother's job to care for her newborn.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, leave policies are only the tip of the iceberg.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As children grow, they require an incredible amount of care and attention.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The emotional, physical and time demands on carers have been made worse by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And I am not the first to point out that studies from all over the world have shown that parents, particularly mothers of young children, have found lockdowns especially challenging and have seen their share of caring responsibilities multiplied.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that the end of the pandemic and its social and economic effects are probably nowhere in sight, we should pay special attention to the needs of young families to ensure that they are not burning out while trying to cope with what is after all a unique situation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must encourage employers to support greater flexibility and career options and ensure this recalibration of work is accessible to both mother and father.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This will allow families to make childcare arrangements that work for their particular circumstances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This move away from traditional work structures must not be seen as a cost borne by employers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, it is the key to fully unlocking the human capital in their employees.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With a bit of trust on both sides, businesses would benefit from better motivated employees with a resultant increase in productivity.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Businesses should seize on recent disruptions caused by the pandemic and turn it into an opportunity to rethink about how we work and understand why it is important that we allow more flexible working arrangements in our businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For parents and family members who chose to stay at home to care for the next generation, I reiterate the call I made last month for better support and recognition for informal carers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We often hear jokes about maternity leave being a four-month long holiday, and stay-at-home mothers are idle "tai-tais".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Now would be a good time to conduct these to enable us to better understand the strains and pressures that these parents face.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is only when we have better identified these problems that we can start looking at the solutions as a whole, and change the narrative to better support and recognise the invaluable work of these unpaid carers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hear of parents having to volunteer for many hours to get their child a chance at a top Primary school, of the multitude of tuition or enrichment classes that parents send children to, and the stress that parents undergo whenever a key examination looms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must relieve the pressure on parents and build a more forgiving education regime, where children are given fairer opportunities to succeed from kindergarten and up, and where kids and their families are not made to feel like the next examination will determine their life trajectory.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Reducing class sizes, increasing the support and training for teachers to focus on a more inclusive and nurturing system would be a good first step as we start to tackle the stresses caused by our demanding education system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Having said all of this, one can only imagine how much more difficult this year has been for single parents who often have less access to alternative resources and support structures.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is only natural that single parents end up more stressed and burnt out than their married counterparts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This one-time payment must not obscure the importance of doing the hard work of changing the culture around care-giving and what we define as work in the context of family, even if these measures do not have an instantaneous effect like a transfer into a bank account.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The importance of getting this right cannot be understated.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Fertility is inextricably linked with sustainability and of increasing concerns about the Earth's finite resources.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as we work to boost our birth rate, we must take action now to soften the impact and address the concerns of a world where an inverted age pyramid will become the norm with all the economic implications that come with it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must no longer operate within the parameters or assumptions that we can keep our economic strategies along traditional population and economic growth models and ensure that we are not at the same time tackling increase costs of our ageing population, while maintaining inter-generational fairness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our CPF, care systems and even physical spaces must now begin in another shift towards a society where older people will form part of majority.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must also combat ageism, embrace innovation, productivity and entrepreneurship, for a golden age, and the time to do so is now.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister’s Statement was an extensive one.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am heartened by the strong people focus in the Statement, placing front and centre, the interests of our people as the Government pushes forth with its plans for the economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Not only were the strategies outlined broad in nature, it is also clear that the Government is paying special attention towards inclusive growth to ensure that vulnerable groups also keep pace, survive and thrive coming out of this crisis.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that skills prioritisation must begin early – even before commencement of jobs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Here, I am referring here to the Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Relevant courses must be identified and prioritised at the Pre-employment Training stage, whereas courses that are more specialised should be pushed towards the Continuing Education Training stage.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In that way, all our graduates are assured of a solid yet flexible foundation that can be applied in other disciplines.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, an aviation engineering student may be provided with a strong engineering foundation coupled with modules relevant to Industry 4.0.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Similarly, a student doing tourism may be provided with a strong business foundation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will provide them with the much-needed agility in an ever-changing job landscape.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is important for us to close the skills and practice gap so that Singaporeans can quickly apply and put into practice what they have learnt.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This matching of skills to actual practice also creates a synergy between companies and requires skilled manpower and our workers who are equipped with these skills.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our graduates pick up relevant skills to a job which then leads to a transitioning to more long-term employment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, I hope we also give allowance to our workers and grant them flexibility in pursuing new skills.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Looking to the future, leading the digitalisation bandwagon allows us to unlock the growth that comes with it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We have experienced how technology has been critical in navigating us through this crisis.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To be digitally literate means that our people not only know how to use technology meaningfully, but we have laid foundations for them to explore in this area more confidently.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: There have been stories of our children being given laptops by their schools, or community agencies, but not knowing how to effectively use these gadgets towards learning.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our elderly too may need more support in adapting to a digital economy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They may own the right smart-phones, but may still struggle to log in to and out of simple apps.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, as we move into the digital economy, we must ensure that all people are digitally literate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In the schools and the Institutes of Higher Learning, I hope that our curriculums will continue to emphasise digital and data analytics skills so that our future generations are effective at using technology as a tool to solve complex problems.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   	In his Ministerial Statement last week, Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat gave a comprehensive overview of Singapore’s position in dealing with the Covid-19 crisis so far.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government is working hard to secure the economy with a focus on manpower skills and further strengthening Singapore's workforce through technology.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that education in Singapore will emphasise the importance of skills, especially those related to the current industries, as the foundation for all courses in Polytechnics and Universities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In that way, all graduates are assured of a solid yet flexible foundation that will give them the opportunity to try other disciplines.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will ensure that our children are ready to address the current challenges in the industries and provide them with the much-needed agility in an ever-changing job landscape.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As for technology, it is an enabling tool and can unlock opportunities.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, companies using digital payment platforms can develop their businesses in cyberspace.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Embracing technology will enable us to continue progressing with the increasingly vibrant wave of digitalisation and I urge that we reap its benefits.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Being an educator for the past 15 years, having taught from the Primary school to University levels, I have seen how our education system has progressed and evolved over the years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our education system is not perfect, but it also has considerable strengths which we should recognise.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Like how different perspectives may see this elephant, we have to be mindful of the many trade-offs that may come with it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It may become a pure through-train system and this may worsen the pressure in Primary 1 registration, as you all have known by now.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Regardless, I do believe that this is one area that we should continue to explore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Contrary to what some Members of this House may perceive, I believe that this is one clear indication of how our education system has become much more holistic.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their dedication and their ability to adapt is amazing.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our teachers work hard to ensure that we meet the diverse needs of our diverse students.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I believe that there should always be a balance between drills and free exploration, formative and summative assessments, group work as well as individual work, and of course, the mingling and teaching, based on the different and diverse abilities of our students.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our teachers have been amazing in ensuring that.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And I hope as we move forward, we continue to provide them with the best support and work-life balance as it is possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It also begins the important process of repositioning the Budget away from crisis support to crisis recovery.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, I have a few additional thoughts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will share about how I believe the process of de-globalisation is both on-going and persistent, and about how we need to do more to pivot away from our historical focus on being an entrepot for the rest of the world towards fostering internally driven growth focused on raising the productivity of our domestic firms, especially small and medium enterprises or SMEs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Before I proceed, allow me to declare that I am an educator at a business school and that I have occasionally provided economic and strategic views for an investment advisory firm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Minister Heng stressed the importance of enhancing connectivity to ensure that our economy is ready for when the pandemic is behind us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: He reiterated our commitment to reviving our air hub and transshipment capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a student of the international system for the past few decades, nothing would make me happier than to see a revival of such a globalised world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
