text: That said, I believe that it is imperative for us to have a Plan B if this does not occur.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this vein, it is worth pointing out that the breakdown in global integration significantly predates COVID-19.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Global Financial Crisis of 2008 marked the beginning of a dramatic turnaround in global financial flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even in financially open Singapore, capital flows have steadily eroded as a share of our national product and we experienced a surge in outflows in the most recent quarter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The financial crisis did not just usher in a decline in financial flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And closer to home, our historical entrepôt model is challenged as never before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And now COVID-19 has completely devastated the global movement of people, with the international tourism virtually vanishing overnight, and even typically more resilient work-related migratory flows are under threat, as corporations rethink their need for business and conference travel, and upend historical cross-border relationships in favour of reshoring previously outsourced business operation and shortening international supply chains.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The fear, then, is even after a vaccine is discovered and the world is able to return to normal, that new normal and encompasses permanent structural changes in a manner by which the world conducts business and pleasure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If anything, major economies are turning inward, with China's stressing "internal circulation" – a euphemism for a domestic turn – Europe is preoccupied with ensuring the integrity of its own union, and the United States – once the bastion of globalism – eschewing the multilateral system that it once used to champion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If this fracturing into a multipolar world persists, our traditional approach of positioning ourselves as a global intermediary could face unprecedented stress.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thankfully, it is possible for us to prepare more deliberately for a Plan B.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Minister Heng also spoke about the importance of Technology, Innovation and Enterprise – a theme that he has mentioned in speeches at least since 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Clearly, the Government is aware of this alternative model.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What I am suggesting is a willingness to commit to this shift in a more decisive fashion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Although many forms of international exchange are in retreat, there is one channel that has been further advanced by the pandemic – the even greater importance of global information and knowledge flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As borders shut down worldwide and work-from-home arrangements become the norm, the information has become the lifeblood of many organisations and countries trying to stay afloat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Service-based businesses digitised their back ends and sought to bring their front end operations online.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And goods oriented firms were forced to resort to online strategies to keep demand afloat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Many of these digitally transform functions and automation disintermediated jobs will never return to their pre-pandemic states.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is therefore time for our small and medium enterprises to make the bold transition as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has rolled out a host of grants such as the Enterprise Development Grant and Productivity Solutions Grant, aimed at this very purpose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is important because such firms account for 99% of our local companies, but only contribute to half of our national income.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, we have precious little information as to whether these funds have succeeded in raising the productivity and enabling the digital transformation of these firms, as the Government has not released systematic studies of either the coverage nor the efficacy of these programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To know whether we are on track, we have to know how far we have come and how far we have to go.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And as much as financial assistance, especially in the recessionary environment, can help our SMEs eke by, financial support will only go part of the way toward helping our companies realise their full potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Beyond relieving financial constraints, SMEs need to build stronger fundamental business skills and capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such skills in marketing to a diverse regional market, adopting best practices in bookkeeping and budgeting and inventory management are not sexy skills, but essential ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, we have to ensure that those who have undergone SGUnited jobs and Skills Future re-skilling programmes, continue to closely meet business needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This can help avoid mismatches that can lead to disappointment and discouragement and experience that one of my residents, Danny, shared regarding the continued difficulty faced by his colleagues in securing work despite having undergone retraining.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: More generally, what is the return proposition of such training and how is it evaluated?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It strikes me that a dedicated unit within Enterprise SG, tasked with identifying, supporting, disseminating and evaluating skills development can be an important complement to our primarily financed focus efforts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My colleague, the hon Leon Perera has also offered a host of additional considerations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, many public-private venture funds such as Startup SG tends to privilege technologically oriented firms.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While such investments are appealing in that they can lead to the next Carousell or Grab, we cannot leave the vast majority of old economy firms behind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, raising productivity levels in such firms is not limited to deploying the latest technology or adapting AI solutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: They are often derived from much more modest sources such as focusing on improving core management practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such practices in performance evaluation, conflict management, team motivation are skills that could be lacking in smaller family run businesses, inhibiting their ability to grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, our funding and support policies should look beyond just the infotech or biotech space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Growth can arise from what many may dismiss as pedestrian businesses, such as coffee roasting and brewing, automotive repair or elderly care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is required is a willingness to disrupt the existing market regime, but rather than promoting winning firms or championing winning sectors, we should strive to create an environment where every firm, especially SMEs, can potentially succeed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At the aggregate level, what this means is that our regulations could be prepared to be more flexible to ease the wrenching shifts that will accompany structural transformations in our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Some sectors may, despite our best efforts, may be destined to shrink and we should ease the teething pains for those poised for expansion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: SMEs that have traditionally focused on trade in goods must evolve to add value higher up the ladder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And those who provide services must learn to deliver these across borders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may also mean greater regulatory forbearance on the part of Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should also be more aware of the unintended consequences of our policies, even when enacted in good faith, especially in terms of how they affect small businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On a positive front – the number of permissible businesses allowed under existing programmes such as the Home-Based Small Scale Business Scheme can be re-examined and expanded if possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if the world does eventually carve itself out into multiple regional markets, our firms must be ready to compete within our economic sphere – which is southeast Asia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This means recognising that a Singapore firm is essentially an ASEAN firm.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government has understood this for a long time, but we have to make sure that our workforce and our people fully embrace this identity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Doing so has become even more imperative in what is promising to become an increasingly balkanised world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our workers should be prepared to spend time in our ASEAN neighbours, learning specificities and idiosyncrasies of our neighbouring markets and returning to Singapore to disseminate the knowledge they have gained and their experiences, either with their sending firms or by starting new companies of their own.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: After the Allied bombing of Japan in World War II, many major cities there were destroyed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In principle, the architects of post-war Japan could have chosen many other locations to site their new economic hubs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But ultimately rebuilding occurred in those very same cities that experience some of the greatest destruction, a testimony to the incredible resilience of cities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our forefathers have already made Singapore into a globally competitive city and we will rise again after the crisis is over.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To inherit this destiny, we have to be willing to be even more economically nimble, to recognise the limits of further leveraging our trade and transportation infrastructure alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The strength of any modern city is his ability to be a gathering place for innovators to exchange debate and improve their ideas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure that our SMEs fully participate in this knowledge based future economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Undeniably, the germs of many such programmes already exist.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I speak in support of the Supplementary Bill and will be emphasising my speech today on the following two points: one, the efforts to better support our seniors in their transition towards i-banking services as our country steps up on its Smart Nation initiatives digital connectivity; two, the suggestions with regard to building environmental sustainability within our community to fight climate change.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In relation to the first point, pertaining to digital banking for seniors, Mr Speaker, please allow me to speak in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin):   	In the face of COVID-19, many senior citizens, especially those living alone, feel helpless and are at a loss.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Before the outbreak, they often went out with like-minded friends.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They will participate in community activities, they will go to a coffee shop or hawker centre and sometimes, they will order a cup of coffee and spend the whole day chatting with old friends.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, when the circuit breaker came into effect, all of a sudden, they seemed to be at a loss: "I don't know how to use a smartphone.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How can I get online and have a video conversation with my grandson?”, “I am alone at home facing the four walls.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When can I go back to the CC with my friends and do our health dance?”, “The queues at the wet market are too long, I am too weak to stand for such a long time.”, “When I go to the supermarket, I am too slow to compete with others.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Is there a way to improve the situation?" These are the complaints I often hear from them.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fortunately, the Government has worked together with businesses, community organisations and Singaporeans to overcome these challenges.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our local enterprises such as NTUC FairPrice have also set aside a special time for senior citizens and persons with mobility issues to purchase daily necessities in supermarkets with peace of mind.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In addition, their neighbours and Residents' Committees have also demonstrated the kampung spirit by helping them to buy food and essentials items and deliver them to their doorstep.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, one thing that cannot and should not be done by someone else on behalf of the elderly is bank transactions involving money.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In recent years, all the banks have undergone transformation by introducing more artificial intelligence, encouraging customers to use online transactions and making banking more invisible.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These moves have reduced banks' operating costs by a lot, for example, in rentals and manpower.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is also in response to the Government's call for technology transformation and further strengthening Singapore's position as a global Asia node of technology, Innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But my concern is: have our seniors kept up with this technology advancement?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is very tiresome for the elderly and those who have difficulty moving around.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many elderly living in the seniors' Studio Apartments told me that they live off their CPF retirement money and government subsidies every month.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because of this, they will personally go to the bank at least once a month to use the counter services to withdraw money.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some of them are illiterate and some have poor eyesight.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Hence, they are less inclined to use ATM cards to withdraw money.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Most of them do not know how to use Internet banking either; they are fearful that they may transfer their lifetime savings to others if they click wrongly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another advantage of counter services for senior citizens is that they form a line of defence against fraud.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If Singaporeans, especially our senior citizens, are to keep pace with technological changes and accept and use online banking services, the banks should fulfil their social responsibilities by using their resources to work more closely with the Government and the community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am confident that with the guidance and help of dedicated people, our seniors will gradually accept and move towards a more diverse digital life.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): Like many First World countries, Singapore has begun taking steps to address the issue of climate change and environmental sustainability.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While this is a good first step, it is important to ensure that this movement continues to gain momentum amongst our Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: J F Kennedy once said, and I quote, "Ask not what your country can do for you but ask what you can do for your country." Apart from the Government's efforts in transforming our industries to build a sustainable economy and providing opportunities for the green section to be a growth industry in its own right, every individual in Singapore should also play our part to ensure the preservation of the environment we live in.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Semakau Landfill is our only offshore landfill in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To rectify this, we will need to encourage responsible consumption of resources, such as food, water and energy, while advocating for environmentally-friendly means of disposal for non-perishable items such as electrical appliances.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A renewed focus on recycling will go a long way towards slowing down the landfill’s rate of usage.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With these factors at present, how should we step up our 3Rs efforts nationally in order to achieve measurable outcomes and a positive impact for our environment?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Through the feedback which I have gathered from our Woodgrove residents and various community partners, I wish to suggest a few ideas for consideration.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that education can go a long way towards inculcating values that favour the 3Rs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We should therefore endeavour to educate every student and resident on good 3Rs practices through experiential learning.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MOE can also consider incorporating Responsible Resource Consumption Saving Tips as part of the school curriculum.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, various schools in Woodgrove have participated in North West CDC’s Reduce@Northwest, where students would conduct door-to-door house visits to encourage families to reduce energy and water consumption and food wastage in their homes, while also imparting knowledge on fighting climate change.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The schools also adopted another North West CDC’s initiative called WeCare We Recycle @ Northwest, where students are educated on proper recycling practices to counteract the high contamination rate of existing blue recycling bins.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As part of this initiative, active recycling points are set up within the participating schools, enabling our students to put the knowledge that they have learnt into good use by taking the lead in active recycling.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is important to continue to engage schools as partners and educate our children on these recycling and energy saving tips, so that they will in turn educate their parents and influence the people around them to conserve resources and adopt eco-friendly practices at home and in the community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that we should measure the reduction of resources consumed through the use of monitoring systems powered by digital applications.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It can be difficult to understand one’s contribution towards the greater whole while adhering to the 3Rs; if we can show them that tangible change is occurring through their actions, I believe residents will be further encouraged to continue these good habits.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Meanwhile, we can also introduce new initiatives to encourage the use of energy or water saving devices and appliances in every household.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If coupled with the aforementioned monitoring systems, we may see increased adoption islandwide.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To jumpstart these schemes, we can first work with grassroots volunteers and schools to engage residents via a pilot project that "adopts" a pioneer batch of select blocks, which students will visit and share energy saving tips with every household.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These blocks can thereafter be monitored and their outcomes measured to evaluate the results of these measures.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To further incentivise adoption of the energy saving measures, we can grant the block showing the highest drop in energy and water usage with rewards such as grocery shopping vouchers or ActiveSG credits.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that the People's Association or PA, as the foundation of the community, can eb a valuable ally in our mission to encourage ground-up initiatives by the community for adopting of the 3Rs wihtin our community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The BCA Green Mark is the national green building rating system which evaluates a building for its environmental impact and performance.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Not only will this raise awareness of the importance of green living, it also ensures that the CCs islandwide will attempt to reduce their own emissions as a result.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Next, the PA can also help to provide platforms for residents to exercise green living, for example with organising events that encourage residents to pick up the 3Rs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some CCs and RCs in Singapore have already begun doing so, through collaborations with the Northwest CDC, Tzu Chi Foundation and NEA with a monthly "recycling day" where residents can bring out their recyclable waste for sorting and processing, fostering good habits and also presenting an opportunity to bond as part of a community.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another option that we can consider to do is to hold regular flea markets for the exchanging or trading of pre-loved items between residents in the halls of our CCs.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On such flea market days, we can take the opportunity to also welcome community partners or residents to share tips on adhering to the 3Rs.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parents of babies born in October and expectant parents are happy and we are happy for them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: At the same time, however, since the announcement, we have received feedback and appeals asking why 1 October 2020, and whether the commencement date can be brought forward to cover children born prior to 1 October 2020.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members, too, have asked about it in this debate.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Saktiandi, yesterday and Ms He Ting Ru, today.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Ms Tin Pei Ling1 and Miss Cheng Li Hui2 have also filed Parliamentary Questions.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I fully understand that parents who are not eligible to receive the Baby Support Grant are disappointed, especially since this has been a challenging year for everybody.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The questions asked are fair ones and it is only right that I should address them and explain our considerations when designing the scheme and also our approach to the appeals that have come in.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They expressed worries about the global COVID-19 health situation, as well as job and income insecurity.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is understandable as having a child is a major decision and a long-term commitment.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We know couples consider many factors when deciding on when to have a child – whether care-giving support is available, the impact on their career plans, and most fundamentally, whether they are prepared mentally and financially.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The pandemic has affected our lives and livelihoods in a major way.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Employment and financial stability have therefore become even bigger considerations for many couples and made them rethink if they should have a child in the next one to two years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, the fact that couples are considering delaying having children is a cause for concern.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When designing this scheme, we explored several options for the start date.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Indeed, one of the residents wrote in to say that "if the grant was meant to encourage couples to have children, then children born in October 2020 should not qualify, as the child is already conceived prior to the grant announcement".

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But this would mean that all babies born between now and July 2021 will be left out.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We then considered providing this additional support only next year, with effect from 1 January 2021, and then drawing on next year's Budget.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, we felt it was important to get the support out as quickly as we can, to help more Singaporeans with their parenthood aspirations.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Announcing the plans next year could mean that couples may delay attempts to have a child in the meantime.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, we tried hard to see how we could do this earlier.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I know parents of babies who are not eligible to receive the Baby Support Grant are disappointed and I can fully understand why.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They would have experienced inconveniences and challenges in caring for newborns this year, especially during the circuit breaker.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: From coping with new visitation guidelines and restrictions at healthcare facilities, to making quick adaptations when they could not get sufficient help to care for newborns, to juggling care-giving duties while working from home when infant and childcare centres were closed.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, we would like to seek the public's understanding that specific start dates are required for any new measure or enhancement.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Regardless of the effective start date, there will always be some babies who are born before it.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The appeals we have received to change the start date of the Baby Support Grant have come with a wide range of suggestions for the start date.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To give you a sense of this, just let me run through some of them.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some have suggested that the Baby Support Grant should cover babies born in September on the basis that it is so close to October.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But this would mean that all of those in August upwards would not get it.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Others suggested April 2020 as that was the start of the circuit breaker – and obviously, that was when all the hardships really kicked it, but that would mean all those before April do not get it.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui, in her Parliamentary Question has suggested 7 February because that was when DORSCON Orange was declared.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, if we go with those, then all those in January will be left out.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In other words, that the effective date should be 1 October 2019.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We have also received an appeal that the grant should be given to children under the age of seven years.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, you can see, it is not straightforward.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office and Second Minister for Finance and National Development (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Some of these new measures commenced in 2019/2020, which young children born since 2014, including the babies born from January 2020, would benefit from.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is over and above the other support in the Marriage & Parenthood Package, some of which we also enhanced this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There have been suggestions from the public that more help with affordable childcare will go further than a one-off cash grant.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This means that many more households can receive this support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The amount of subsidies provided have also been increased.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: A working couple who earns a combined income of $8,000 a month, pays $524 per month per child for full-day infant care at an Anchor Operator pre-school.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is about one third less than what they would have paid previously.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: When their child turns 18 months, the amount that the couple needs to pay for childcare at an Anchor Operator will further reduce to $280 per month.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, free National Childhood Immunisation Schedule or NCIS vaccinations and developmental screenings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This extension of fully subsidised services at our CHAS GPs will improve affordability and accessibility for parents, who can now enjoy these services islandwide.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, support for households, jobs and salary amidst COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The other source of concern on the part of many parents, like other Singaporeans, are the employment-related challenges and anxieties at this time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Raising children during the COVID-19 pandemic can be more challenging, especially if a member of the family has lost his or her job.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We recognised this earlier in the year and provided more support for households, as well as jobs and salary support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To provide more assurance and support to Singaporeans with their household expenses during this period of economic uncertainty, the Government provided the Solidarity Payment and Care and Support – Cash payout in April and June, to every Singaporean aged 21 years and above.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This amounted to $600 to $1,200 per Singaporean, depending on income.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On top of this, we gave each parent with at least one citizen child aged 20 years and below as of 31 December 2020, an additional Care and Support – Cash payout of $300, that is an additional $600 per couple.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, a Singaporean couple with a child, including those with babies born before 1 October, could already receive up to $3,000 in additional cash support this year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition to these, all households with at least one Singaporean citizen member would have received the Solidarity Utilities Credit of $100.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Eligible HDB households can also receive up to 2.5 times their regular GST Voucher – U-Save and up to 3.5 months of Service and Conservancy Charges (S&CC) Rebate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Such a household living in a 4-room flat with five or more can receive $800 in U-Save and 2.5 months of S&CC Rebate this financial year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the support for jobs and salary, the Government has also provided significant support to ease concerns about employment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This includes employment and salary support through the SG United Jobs and Skills Package and the Jobs Support Scheme.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I have listed the financial support, but we all do know, of course, that it is not just about the money or the finances because there are other things that are factored in when couples are deciding to have a child.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this regard, we have taken many steps to make sure that we provide additional support, from increasing the number of pre-school spaces to also working on flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms He Ting Ru earlier spoke about a holistic approach and I am so glad that she agrees with us because these were exactly the recommendations of the Citizens' Panel on Work-Life Harmony.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Those included recommendations to further encourage and enable companies to provide flexible work arrangements, such as through recognition schemes as well as the nomination of Work-Life Ambassadors.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Panel also called for the shift of societal norms over time, to one where family time and other life priorities are placed above work and workplace practices become more progressive and family-friendly.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we can see that the idea here is that it is not just about money but how to make Singapore a place that is conducive for families as a whole.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms He had a specific question on singles and whether the Baby Support Grant, or BSG, would be applicable or whether they are eligible for it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The BSG is a one-off grant to help reassure couples and minimise delays in their marriage and parenthood plans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The BSG is an add-on to the Baby Bonus Cash Gift which, in itself, was designed to encourage marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These benefits aim to support the child's developmental and care-giving needs, as well as the parents' efforts to provide for the child.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As society continues to evolve, our policies will be updated to keep pace with societal realities.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many groups of fellow Singaporeans need our support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Parents who have children, or are planning to have children, are one such group.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, I am heartened by the efforts of many corporates and community partners which have joined the Government’s efforts in further supporting Singaporeans on their parenthood journey.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I hope that many more will come on board.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This Government remains committed to supporting the marriage and parenthood aspirations of Singaporeans and we will continue to review and enhance the strong suite of measures already in place to help Singaporeans form and grow families.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To Minister Indranee Rajah, thank you so much for that response to some of the questions the Workers' Party Members of Parliament had on the Baby Support Grant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I fully recognise the trouble and the issue about settling on a start date for a grant like this which was unexpected by many members of the public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Having said that, would the Government consider extending the Baby Support Grant to Singaporeans who have received some of these COVID-19-related subsidies, such as SIRS and the COVID-19 Support Grant, because they have already exhibited particular difficulty arising out of their circumstances once COVID-19 started?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, they are already pre-qualified in that sense to be in need and, hence, they have received Government subsidies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are mainly Singaporeans at the lower to lower middle income group.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the extension is not really about a date that will reach back for all Singaporean parents, but specifically for lower to middle income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would that be something the Government could consider?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, for those who are already low income, proceeding with parenthood plans would add to some of the responsibilities that they have.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think Mr Singh's question is: can we extend the Baby Support Grant to those born before 1 October who are low income.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For those, what we will do is we will utilise the existing schemes that we have for the low-income to make sure that they are taken care of and their needs are taken care of, because we do actually have a very strong social support system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does not necessarily have to be in the form of the Baby Support Grant, but we will still help you.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would just want to make further points for the single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think this Government has said that single unwed parents are no less a mother or a father just because the child is born outside of marriage.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, irrespective of whether they have the Baby Support Grant, if they are, indeed, struggling and if they are in need, please do approach the SSO.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are other schemes available and in place and we will look to see how we can support them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Speaker, Sir, I support the plans of action, as detailed in the Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: I am confident that this suite of measures will facilitate our progress and ensure that we emerge from this crisis stronger.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We will be a competitive yet inclusive economy, a dynamic yet sustainable one.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In order to stay relevant and be an active participant on the world stage, we have to remain open to the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We need to attract more quality investments and accept investors, entrepreneurs, specialists and professionals who can work with us in order to prosper as an economy and society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Bringing in investments and attracting organisational set-ups here will create jobs and other opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We need these regional and international collaborations to stay ahead of the competition, increase our value and usefulness to the world, thereby ensuring our survival and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The better approach is not to stay away and shield us from competition in this rapid technologically advancing world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We should rather face the competition and equip Singaporeans with leading skills and tools to make us stay ahead of competition.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Even as we welcome foreigners to share their knowledge and skills with Singaporeans, we need to be mindful of the risk of being over-reliant on a particular country, source or nationality.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We should also take note of social costs and other implications that might outweigh the benefits in the longer run.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Hence, we should be open but selective, monitor the employment market closely and take proactive steps to maintain the right balance.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: It provides another revenue source for the country as the Government continues to invest in Singapore holistically.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: While cost is one of the major concerns for investors, Singapore has many other attractive advantages which more than make up for the higher costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: These include a conducive business environment, security, stability, excellent infrastructure and telecommunications, updated facilities and amenities, transparency and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: These are all prime determining factors for businesses and workers too.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: While other countries are grappling with COVID-19, we must continue to invest in both our infrastructure and human capital and provide incentives to pull in companies and individuals to place their investments in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The good cycle of investments, jobs and opportunities will bring many benefits to our island and our people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Hence, we need to continue with our major infrastructure investments that will support our economic growth for the benefit of Singaporeans in the face of the slowdown.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In addition, would MOM look into a hybrid of WIS, CSG and SIRS to form a new scheme to incentivise employment, reduce the pain from income reduction and narrow the job/income mismatch?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Notwithstanding, I do agree that all these have to be done with proportionally increase in productivity through job redesign, use of technology, automation so on and so forth, so that our workers are better skilled, productive and equipped, as compared with peers in other countries for the same job with better output.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: This would help mitigate avoidance of cost inflationary.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We need to expedite the industry transformation, for example, more use of machinery in town cleaning jobs and higher productive method in construction industry to reduce reliance of foreign workers and higher income for our Singapore workers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We all need to be very clear that we cannot afford to be complacent in an environment which is advancing rapidly technologically.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What is the norm today can easily be disrupted.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: To ensure that Singaporeans can remain in a leading position in the fast-changing and competitive world, we must continue to invest and equip all Singaporeans with the best skills, knowledge and tools.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Singaporeans must be the assets which attract investors.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We can further incentivise the investors and businesses to equip and train Singaporeans with leading and competitive skills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The Government should continue with the overseas training and study internship initiative for our citizens so that they will gain wider exposure and market knowledge and deepen their problem solving skills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: With that, I would like to conclude with my support again.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But if there is something positive, it has reminded us about the important things in our life, the things that we may have taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I realised that I missed out on so much of my children's childhood over the last couple of years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While working from home, I was able to spend so much time with my little ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Together – Ella, Katie, Poppy and I cooked, ate, played, enjoyed bedtime stories and even managed to set up a tent in our living room.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Before this pandemic, I was never able to spend so much time with them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was often out on the ground at work, like most of us, and by the time I got home at night, the kids would be fast asleep.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reality is that work from home is something that us, as Members of Parliament will not be able to completely do as our work is often on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But many fellow Singaporeans can benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Working from home will benefit all employees, whether you're married or single.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Employees will have better work-life balance, more freedom, spend less time commuting and it promotes employee well-being.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond this, there are four other main reasons why we should give people the right to work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first reason that it will be better for fathers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This pandemic has hurt many Singaporean families but it has also provided opportunities for parents, especially fathers to bond with their children like never before.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A recent media article spotlighted the stories of several fathers during the circuit breaker and how COVID-19 has given fathers a chance to bond with their kids.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Marketing manager Imran talk about how his wife and him are so glad that he has now more time to play and eat together with his two toddler children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Imran talked lovingly about how his kids now miss him even when he stepped out of the house briefly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Shahid Nizami, a managing director, spoke about how he had to strike a balance between working from home and supervising his son, Kain's home-based learning and how he jammed with his son for a virtual talent competition, with his son on drums and the dad on a guitar.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said, "This has been really special for both of us." It is clear that many fathers now want to reconsider their work-life arrangement and we should not waste this opportunity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The right to work from home will give fathers more flexibility and more time to spend with their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the reason this working from home would help benefit mothers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One mother, Sheena, wrote to me, expressing her joy at seeing more fathers picking up their kids from schools these days as a result from our work from home policy which she says used to be a rare sight previously.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Fathers picking up their children from school is part of a bigger solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A study conducted this year by the US National Bureau of Economics found that a pandemic would likely cause fathers to become more interested and experienced in childcare, reducing the childcare responsibilities on mothers and increasing gender equality at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: An IPS study found that fathers who had more time to be with their children at home were able to better develop effective childcare skills.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When fathers become more adept with handling childcare responsibilities, their families rely less on the mothers for childcare.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This not only improves delegation of home responsibilities more equally between fathers and mothers but allow working mothers to focus better at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In short, when fathers buck up at home, mothers get to lean in at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The third reason is that it would be good for businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A 2011 guide by the tripartite committee on work-life strategy says that working from home enhances business performance and competitiveness for employers as employers can optimise manpower and resources deployment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having employees work from home also help companies reduce fixed costs, such as office rental and workstation set-up costs and staff turnover related costs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As early as 2001, MOM stated that work from home allows workers to better combine their work and personal responsibilities which helps to reduce absenteeism and attrition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Businesses that allow their employees to work from home do grow stronger.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us help our businesses recover from this COVID economy in a way that emphasises efficiency and reduce costs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And through the Productivity Solutions Grant, the Government is also helping to make a work from home policy possible for businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The fourth and final reason for legislating the right to work from home is that it will be good for our economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I cited research showing that a work from home policy reduces employee attrition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What I have not mentioned is that so often, this attrition employees are women.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When you add up the effects on the national level, we see shocking trends.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us talk about female labour force participation rate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is often said that Singapore's only natural resource is our people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Yet, we are not even employing half of our people, our women efficiently.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why is our female labour force participation rate so low?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: According to the McKinsey Global Institute, the culprit is care-giving and childcare responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We need every dollar of that and we need to close that gap.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The solution is to empower our mothers to work from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Teresa, a working mother wrote to me, saying that working from home has meant that she did not have to worry about childcare arrangements and could pick up her children from childcare, bring them to appointments and take care of them when they did not have school.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The right to work from home will provide parents like Teresa and many other employees with legal grounds to request to work from home when they need to without being penalised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will enable those who have been discouraged and forced out of the workforce to rejoin their fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In these hard times, Singapore's economy needs every leg up we can get.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The right to work from home will help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM has previously stated that this legislation can have unintended consequences for the very group it is meant to benefit and protect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, it may discourage employers from hiring groups seen as likely to take up the benefits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is extremely unlikely that getting to work from home hurt someone's career.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, the study found that work from home has been shown to reduce women's likelihood of working part-time after childbirth, reduces the motherhood penalty and potentially increase wage premium for women, especially in the longer run.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, the evidence suggests that legislating the right to work from home would help, not hinder women from succeeding at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Employers can reject the request with specific business-related reasons and employees who want to choose to work from the office can still feel free to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I believe this is a good middle ground win-win proposal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For years, we told everyone that work from home helps with work-life balance, reduces employees absenteeism, leads to higher productivity, saves costs of office space and attracts and retains value employees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It even helped save lives during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All I am asking is that we now make this law permanent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is for those are not married as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At some point in our lives, we will have to care for someone else – be it children parents, grandparents, spouses, partners, friends and other loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We will all need to be care-givers some day and we should have the flexibility to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Working from home also helps with work-life balance and our well-being so it is also about caring for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us emerge stronger, as I have said many times in this House, spend time with those you love.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One of these days, you will either say "I wish I had" or "I'm glad I did".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us give our people a better chance of saying "I'm glad I did".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Various Labour Members of Parliament – from former Secretary-General Lim Swee Say to former Parliamentary colleague Mr Zainal Sapari – have in their Parliamentary speeches over the many years also push for a faster and wider implementation of the PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Hence, NTUC welcomes the announcement to form a Tripartite Workgroup for Low-wage Workers to take concrete actions on this very important agenda.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Uplifting lower income Singaporeans have been a core mission of the PAP Government right from the outset.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The PAP was born from the unions in the 1950s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Taking care of our workers has been a critical part of our DNA as a party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have achieved what few have done over the last six decades, but the task is never finished.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is something that we must and will keep working on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Under the PAP Government and with the support from the Labour Movement, the lives of millions of Singaporeans have been greatly improved: more than 90% of Singaporeans own their homes; our children get much better education; we invested in upgrading skills of our people so that they can stay employed and improve in their careers even as our economy transforms through the decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have made significant progress in the past 10 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This was a big lift and faster than for those higher up on the wage ladder.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It has also helped moderate income inequality in Singapore which is now at its narrowest in almost 20 years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: All these did not happen just by itself.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It was brought about by sound economic policies, and the tripartite partners working actively to intervene to support workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We implemented the “Triple Uplift” formula comprising the PWM, Workfare Income Supplement or WIS, and the National Wage Council or NWC recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Their wages have increased by 30% in real terms in recent years without the loss of jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The PWM also enables them to climb the skills-ladder, improving their future employability and their wage progression at the same time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This has been a significant achievement because the workers in these sectors tend to be older or with limited education and, therefore, are at a higher risk of this employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It required very involved negotiations and firms, companies have to undertake changes of many of their practices to do so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It acts like a form of negative income tax.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Government tops up the income of our workers earning less than $2,300 per month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There are many other efforts, all part of the on-going task of uplifting our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Skills upgrading and job placement efforts by the NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute or e2i, working with Government agencies help many workers access better jobs, better pay and better job prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Bus drivers’ salaries jumped by more than 20% since 2015 with the new bus financing framework supported by the labour movement and National Transport Workers’ Union or NTWU.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In the last five years or so, we have pushed hard on our ITM efforts as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This brought together tripartite partners integrating skills upgrading together with business transformation, productivity enhancement and innovation to catalyse change as a whole of eco-system to also create better jobs and better job prospects for our workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Raising the income of our less skilled and low-wage workers is, therefore, a holistic and a continuous effort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Through Workfare, the PWM and our efforts involving various stakeholders to boost skills and productivity in every sector, we are demonstrating exactly what Mdm Halimah spoke about in social solidarity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Our low-wage workers get an uplift in incomes through Workfare, supported by our taxes through the PWM and by productivity improvements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The upshot is that we can achieve higher incomes for low-wage workers without putting their employment at risk and minimising cost increases for our consumers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I should point out also that the PWM in the existing sectors have also helped lift wages in the other non-PWM sectors as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If we look at the occupations that are traditionally deemed as comprising workers with lower income – clerical support, service staff, tradesmen, operators, cleaners, labourers – there are, perhaps, about slightly over 850,000 workers doing these jobs in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The vast majority of them actually earn above $1,300 a month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: According to MOM, the residual number of low-wage workers who earn below $1,300 is about 100,000 workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: About a quarter of them actually are self-employed so they would not have benefited from any minimum wage, to begin with.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Of these, only about 32,000 are full-time employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, what the Workers' Party wants to achieve with the proposed minimum wage of $1,300 a month, we have already achieved through PWM and many other policy measures, such as Workfare Income Supplement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With this latest tripartite move, we will further reduce this number.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We have, in fact, actually made tremendous strides over the decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But as I said, it is still unfinished business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: As I have just highlighted, this is a very small number of 32,000 to over 50,000-over, about 1.7% of our local workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In fact, the first rung of the wage ladder in the PWM is a form of sectoral minimum wage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Senior Minister Tharman has also called the PWM a “Minimum Wage Plus” – Minimum Wage plus a ladder for wage increase through upskilling.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, the idea of having some form of a minimum wage is not new and we share the same objective to uplift the incomes of low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Where we differ though is the approach to getting there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: All programmes and policies have pros and cons and so too a single blanket minimum wage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Its appeal is that it is seemingly a quick way to raise the wages of workers who have to benefit from PWM – and maybe many other initiatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But there are actually risks to jumping onto this single blanket minimum wage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: First, there is the question of its effectiveness in helping our lowest skilled and most vulnerable workers and not inadvertently putting them at a disadvantage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: It is difficult to find the right a single minimum wage for all sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If it is not set too low, then the benefit to workers in many sectors will be limited and defeats the purpose of having a minimum wage in the first place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But if the Minimum Wage is set too high, then businesses especially the SMEs, cannot afford to pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: They will have to pass the costs on to consumers if they are able to or cut back on employment of workers of lower educational standards or skills, or, in the worse case scenario, go out of business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In an ideal world, of course, a high Minimum Wage will force industries to invest more in technology, invest in items that can raise the productivity and favour the most efficient firms without lowering overall employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But in practice there will be winners and losers and it is our SMEs who are the most vulnerable and our most vulnerable workers will also be at risk of losing out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But in practice it is difficult to arbitrarily prescribe a single higher salary for all sectors and all industries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: There must be a basis for setting the Minimum Wage that reflects the realities of each sector, including the profile of the low-wage worker sin that that particular sector so that it is sustainable, it benefits them and it avoids any unintended costs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Veteran union leaders with long experience on the ground understand the importance of working this out and arriving at the tripartite consensus, so that “low wage” does not inadvertently become “no wage”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If I may share what my good brother in the unions, Brother Toh Hock Poh, will always say when it comes to complex issues, "Ah nay kan duah, wa nang za teo zoh liow, ko tan li la kong" in Hokkien.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Today, let us say we can all agree to $1,300 Minimum Wage proposed by the Workers' Party, a “moral imperative” as Mr Singh puts it in his recent Facebook post.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: How will this number change from this year to the next and on what basis?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In a political contest, a political party will surely come along and say, "Well, $1,500 will reflect higher 'moral imperatives'".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Yet another will come along and say, "$1,300 is good; $1,500 is better, but $1,700 must surely be more 'divine' moral imperatives".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: When this process, this political auction gathers momentum and becomes detached from market realities, the Minimum Wage escalates beyond what employers are able to pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And the jobs of our more vulnerable sisters and brothers in these sectors will be threatened with the risk of unemployment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, I am not so much concerned by what Mr Singh and the Workers' Party is proposing for now, but what it portends for the future – the possibility of a political auction that will price out our lower skilled workers, our brothers and sisters, and disadvantage our smaller enterprises, our SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We are seeing this kind of political processes, this political auction, happening in other countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: At NTUC, we believe the PWM is one way of doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Under PWM, we can engage the different stakeholders of each industry, work out how to address their concerns and challenges, and arrive at a consensus with a basis that they can all actively support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With this sectoral tripartite consensus building approach, it is much less likely for a political auction to happen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We can and should do more to help the lowest paid in our society but we must go about doing it in a way that ensures the upside while minimising the downsides.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The cure surely should not be worse than the problem it tries to solve.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: A third complication, and this is a major one, is the question of migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In most developed countries, the legal Minimum Wage applies to all workers including migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: If the Minimum Wage is driven simply by a "moral imperative", then the natural question to ask is whether it should include non-Singaporeans such as migrant workers, including our foreign domestic workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I do see an online petition going on now in the honour of Mr Singh's name, with all the text he put into his Facebook on the page calling for people to petition to support Minimum Wage for foreign domestic workers as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: So, perhaps, Mr Singh should also take this chance to explain to Singaporeans what the position of the Workers' Party is when you advocate for Minimum Wage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Now, if businesses cannot bear the resulting cost, is there also a "moral imperative" to help our SMEs?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This is a particular pertinent consideration at this time, when we are in a deep COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Many companies, especially our SMEs, such as those in the construction sector, are suffering and not quite out of the woods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I do note that in his Facebook post, the very first line and I quote, "A universal Minimum Wage for the Singaporean worker is not just a moral imperative, it is an act of national solidarity, one that is even more relevant in today's economic environment".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: I have been listening to some of the speeches of many of the Workers' Party's Members in the House yesterday and today, and I must thank them for sharing the Government's view on improving career coaching, reforming our education, supporting our workers, helping our SMEs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: And the Member Jamus Lim's earlier speech talked about supporting SMEs, which I am sure will be welcomed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: But if we juxtapose this together with his speech at the last Sitting about raising Minimum Wages, how does it square away?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Are we supporting SMEs or are we adding more oil to the fire, so to speak?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Perhaps it will be better explained in Chinese, we call it 雪上加霜.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: With the companies in a deep economic freeze now or economic recession, is what is being proposed by the Workers' Party – raising wages through a Minimum Wage legislation – going to add more frost to the snow in companies in deep winter right now?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We welcome such ideas as it would enable consumers to choose whether to support progressive-minded firms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: While introducing a PWM Mark is a good first step, voluntary schemes on their own may not be attractive enough for companies to come onboard.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Government must be prepared to use regulatory levers to help incentivise firms to adopt the PWM Mark, such as requiring companies that access Government schemes or bid for Government contracts to come onboard this voluntary Mark.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: That way, we can also raise the awareness of consumers and service buyers to price the contracts fairly, and build trust towards eventual mandatory PWM for other sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The benchmarks would be a good way, a good starting point, a first step towards empowering workers with greater awareness of wages in their own occupations and their sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This can be done through leveraging various sources of data that we currently have, such as the Occupational Wage Survey Data.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: In sectors with a more variegated employment landscape such as Food Services and Retail, sectoral wage benchmarks may help catalyse more companies to embark on uplifting the livelihoods of our lower wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: This, of course, in time to come, can evolve into a PWM.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: The Tripartite Workgroup could also study lower wage occupations that cut across multiple sectors to see how best to help improve their wage prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Some job roles, clerical job roles, for example, do not neatly fall into one particular sector and it is horizontal across many sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Having employers, Government and union at the same table would enable us to have frank and deep discussions on policy innovations to move the way forward.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: We should recognise what the Government and the tripartite partners have achieved in providing a genuine uplift for the workforce, especially our lower wage workers, and be willing to adopt new approaches.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Indeed, the PWM and Workfare Income Supplement have major new approaches in recent years and we, of course, remain open to new ideas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Achieving social equality and enabling lower income families to improve their lives is never a simple task.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: NTUC and the tripartite partners will focus on this real hard work of uplifting wages of low-wage workers and seek public support for our workers, while hoping to avoid all the possible downsides.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
