text: I was not intending to speak in this debate but in view of the questions that he has put to me arising from a Facebook post, which was a response to another Facebook post or two Facebook posts by the Minister for Manpower and the NTUC Secretary-General, I will put the position out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because when we campaigned in the last election, a Minimum Wage was one of the central pillars of our ambit of the proposals that we had put to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is not a number that has come out of the sky.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Senior Minister of State has been helpful in providing some data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe a newspaper article, just a few days ago, from a former parliamentarian, someone who I think many of us parliamentarians enjoyed listening to, the economist Walter Theseira, asked some important questions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He asked what are the sectors where Singaporeans are earning less than $1,300?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And my question quite simply is, do we need to wait so long to cover these Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can we not consider how we can cover them immediately because it is not a small number.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If you think of 60,000 rental units available from HDB and you compare that with this number, it is significant – it is quite a lot of Singaporeans who need some help.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, my Facebook posts really was not to diss or dismiss the PWM.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was to nudge the Government, to tell the Government, "Hey, wait a minute.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can we move faster on people who are really, really at one end of the spectrum?" So, I think the Senior Minister of State understands that context, so that is not so much the issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, that was the first question, whether we can reach out more quickly to these individuals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And I do not believe SMEs would be significantly impacted, with all respect to SMEs, employers and businesses who have also made their views known also in the mainstream media over the last one, one and a half months, perhaps.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This number of Singaporeans, we can look after them, we can take care of them, and we can do it quite fast.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If there is anybody who can do it for the people who I know as my friends in NTUC, I am pretty sure they are going to work hard with the Government to make that happen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I hope the Government takes them up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second point is about politicisation, which was what the Minister feared.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Are we going to get into an auction when one party says $1,300 and another one says $1,500?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is where we probably have to defer to the experts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The National Wages Council is potentially one forum.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there are also some useful statistics we can use, like the average household expenditure on basic necessities; how much really does it cost for the Singaporean family who is at that end of the spectrum.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And the Minimum Wage or the floor can be set at a number which is realistic and correspondent to that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Actually, the bigger concern I have with the PWM and some of the sectors that the Senior Minister of State has been referring to, is potential profiteering on the back of raising wages for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My question to the Senior Minister of State is what mechanisms are available in NTUC, with MOM, to ensure that companies do not do that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Now, I say this because earlier this week, I just sat in our usual weekly Town Council meeting and I am aware that certain lift maintenance contracts are coming up for renewal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have some numbers from the lift companies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Another lift company, 5%, 10%, 5%, 10%, something of that nature, over a few years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, because we have different contractors, they have different proposals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Now, if all this increase is going to the Singaporean worker, then I am prepared to take on that burden to persuade our Town Council residents that we need to raise S&CC.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am prepared to take it on because Singaporeans are going to benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But my question is, is that a realistic hike in costs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like the Senior Minister of State to share how can we be sure that as the PWM moves forward and particularly for raising of salaries, those costs will go to our workers and will not be translated into profits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I think the Senior Minister of State had a question on the ambit of our Minimum Wage proposal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It does not include foreign manpower at this point because there are other regulatory levers, especially for foreign workers – quotas, levies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I know they serve specific purposes, but I think you will have to implement this and see how best to work the overall manpower situation that SMEs demand and what the economy demands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the important number, it was, I think Senior Minister of State said 1.7% of the population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am sure Senior Minister of State agrees with me that –

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am sure Senior Minister of State agrees with me that we can do and we can move quite fast for this people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I will be prepared to work with Senior Minister of State to ensure that we can actually reach out to these Singaporeans as quickly as the Government can.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because, I do not think it is acceptable that any one, any Singaporean is earning below this number.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And if we can do something about it in double quick time, let us do it.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I must say it is quite easy to propose a Minimum Wage and then when we ask questions about what it is based on and how they will implement it – does it include foreign workers and all – they say, "Government go sort it out".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think if as Brother Hock Poh said, "If it is so easy to do, we would have done it with any long ago".

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Proposing it for panel of experts to do, do research and studies, that could be one way, but that is actually also what the tripartite partners do.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: We look at data, but we incorporate the consensus of all the stakeholders including businesses so that they also must be prepared to price this into their business cost and have a way to also socialise it to the consumers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Indeed, as the hon Member said, when there is a wage ladder that goes up or any cost increase for Minimum Wage, this cost will have to be passed to the consumers at some point.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, there has to be a cost implication in the cost impact.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: That is why I asked the question about proposing a blanket single Minimum Wage across all sectors, which has to necessarily cover all workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because in many developed countries, the concept of a Minimum Wage, as it is applied, includes migrant workers as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, I think we have to be careful about what we are saying here, because to buck the norm, to be different, there must be a real strong justification.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But it also includes people who are technically "employed" but they could be employed in jobs like hawker assistant, helping a family member.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: They are drawing a salary, but they are happy to be just getting $700 a month helping the father or the mother or something like that, manning a store, for example.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: How do you legislate a Minimum Wage to say that the father who runs the store, employing the son as as a worker, as an employee, has to add a cost on and mandate it?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Those are the challenges when you go down to the bottom.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If I may use Brother Hock Poh's words again, he said "Wo jiak yam bi li jiak bee zuay" or I eat more salt than you eat more rice; "Tak chek jin ho", but "ai zor jin gan kor" or easier said than done.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, his point is this, reams and reams of data and research is good.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: But in practice, is always harder to do, because there are practical considerations, there are pushbacks.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that is why a negotiator approach with stakeholders is the most important.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: In the area of working with our stakeholders, I believe that that is why when we work on the negotiated outcome, there is always that balance that can be struck.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And I think collectively we ought to socialise Singaporean consumers to the need to up the wages of those at the lower end and demonstrate social solidarity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I would just take the opportunity to just clarify a few points and perhaps obtain some clarifications as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One of them is that Senior Minister of State mentioned a few times that a lot of these affect real lives and I have no doubt that they affect real lives because that is precisely what we are fighting for.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But, with all due respect, as much as it will be lovely to always rely on folksy wisdom and beliefs by labour union leaders, at the same time, it is important to realise that when when we talk about studies that show that the Minimum Wage does not lead to any appreciable increase in unemployment, this is based on careful consideration and not just beliefs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is worth reminding ourselves that there was a time in the 16th century, when people believed that the sun revolved around the Earth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But that belief is not in fact the same as evidence and all evidence from countries all over the world demonstrate that a Minimum Wage has minimal impact on unemployment as long as it is not set too high.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But why we believe as well that it is important to be open to other possibilities is because we, likewise, do not want this number to be politicised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There are lots of numbers that can be politicised, the interest rate can be politicised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We ensure that the central banks do not politicise the interest rate by making sure that they have independence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I will just close by pointing out one thing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is that I do not believe in schadenfreude.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We have been throwing out Chinese idioms so I will define that 幸灾乐祸.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I do not think that supporting SMEs, as I said in my speech just now, is exclusive from supporting a Minimum Wage, which I mentioned in my maiden speech.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In fact, I would just remind everyone that Henry Ford who invented the automobile understood this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: He said he has to pay his workers enough so that they can buy his cars.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, with the skills increase, the person would then be justified for wage increase, based on the larger job scope or a more productive outcome in the work delivered.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I am more referring to a case where like the Labour Annual this year in May, talked about extending the PWM to the lift and escalator sector and I believe there is one more sector, I am not sure whether it was waste management, but one of them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Apart from that, if there is a reason for a vendor to assert that actually the cost is being overstated here and PWM is being used as an excuse to increase costs, what recourse would the Government consider?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Will there be a committee that we can potentially go to to address some of these matters?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Otherwise, there has to be somebody who is prepared to price his service or his product competitively and reasonably.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Just some points of clarification to the Senior Minister of State, Dr Koh Poh Koon, who gave a spirited defence of the PWM model.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We have said that we do not think that PWM and Minimum Wage are mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My first question is really how long does the Senior Minister of State envisage the rolling out of the PWM to all the vulnerable workers who are now earning very low incomes; how long would that take?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The number could be 100,000 or 36,000 depending on the definition used, but how long we are going to take to address the needs of that group?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why does Minimum Wage inevitably become politicised but the PWM model does not also become a political football and become politicised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Third point of clarification is really on how the Minimum Wage may hurt our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, how does such a small number actually effect a very substantial hurt or a disadvantage to SMEs if the number is basically small?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In making this point, I would note that some discussions publicly that have happened about Minimum Wage within the business community, that have been reported in The Business Times and so on, have shown that many business owners are in fact open to a Minimum Wage if it is not set too high because they also want to pay their employees with dignity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The last point is really on the Senior Minister of State who talked about the contrast between Minimum Wage and Progressive Wage Model that with the Progressive Wage Model, you are less likely to lose jobs because that is a negotiated outcome with employers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But would the Senior Minister of State accept that you can have a process to set a Minimum Wage nationally, with reference to research and facts that involves consultation with employers before that Minimum Wage is set, so you do not surrender that advantage as well.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think in my speech, I did explain that different sectors have different eco-systems, different kind of skills requirement and therefore different starting pay even for certain lower job roles.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: And therefore, if at a national level, it is very hard to decide on one number that everyone can agree to as their starting pay.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: How would that process be to make sure tat there is convergence on one single number – to have the lowest end of a cleaner and a lowest end of a clerical staff – all having the same minimum wage that is acceptable across different industry sectors?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, that is a practical challenge that cannot be overcome so easily with a single Minimum Wage.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Bear in mind that this segment of workers, some of them could have disabilities that may not be able to embark on the kind of jobs without Government support to begin with.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, by giving some of these Workfare supplements, we actually top up the kind of wages because otherwise, an employer may not be prepared to employ someone with a certain disability that may not be able to fulfil the full function of the job scope.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: This is where you will end up leading to dis-employment for a particular segment of vulnerable workers.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: So, it cannot be a one-size-fits-all because there are different segments of people, different industry demands.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: I think the process will be something that we want to do now, talk about it, discuss it, work out some schematics.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Obviously, we have to look at the economic situation as well because this will be probably the wrong time to push for increased wage costs onto our SMEs who are already suffering.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Why would the PWM structure be less likely to be politicised?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: It is not decided politically by one party.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The employers naturally will push back as well if what we are proposing for the sector is not sustainable to them, business-wise.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: If what is being pushed from just a political base would put them out of business and make them non-competitive, there will be a natural push back.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Otherwise, if it is just a single number that is decided based on politics, I think this is where the danger of the slippery slope occurs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: One on the issue of heterogeneity, needing each sector to have their own specific Minimum Wage.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I would actually put it across even more simply.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The other point is I think it is actually a bit disconcerting to bring in special cases like disability and the individual that happens to work part-time for his father, or even to talk about earning more than one $1,300 if someone works overtime, because honestly these are, if I may use the term, straw man.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We are not comparing these particular special cases.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: We are talking about individuals without disability that happen to be working just regular full-time work week and are nevertheless struggling to make ends meet.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I also do not feel that we should let them, in as rich a society as we are, flounder on their own.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If not, it may actually lead to no wage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, could I seek clarifications from the Workers’ Party on whether they actually recognise the downside risks of low wage becoming no wage, especially when technology automation is increasingly being adopted?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not believe any of us made that specific remark.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I would like to ask the Member in return: is he agreeable to pay the 100,000 workers, specifically narrowed down now to 32,000 workers, $1,300 as a business employer?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: I think as a business owner, the responsibility is not to a specific sector of employees but to the entire company.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: Sustaining a business means providing jobs for the whole company.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, a business owner needs to look at sustainability, and it is the responsibility of a business owner to look at productivity increase because that is what makes businesses profitable, viable and then scalable to be able to provide more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, an arbitrary Minimum Wage may actually be more negative for a business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: We need to look at it as a holistic approach, helping businesses upskill their employees, helping businesses to grow their business.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: So, as the businesses grow, we can provide more to our workers and we can actually hire more workers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui
text: I think that is what businesses are looking towards in terms of good effective policy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Actually, to be honest, that is a really big debate going on and I think to avoid just discussing this purely on theoretical or rhetorical menace, I would like to ask both sides of the House, including the Senior Minister of State, from the position of someone who is also declaring my interest as strategic advisor to Daughters of Tomorrow where we work actively with employers and businesses to advocate directly to them for what we call livable wages for the employees.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Is there anything that Senior Minister of State Koh might want to share that Members of Parliament, backbenchers, or even community groups can do to help the Government in this effort to encourage more employers in different sectors to think about different ways and using different angles to encourage them to pay the employees more, and in return reap the benefits of a workforce that has higher morale and give higher loyalty to the companies and businesses.

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: The first thing he is asked is: do you have the skills that I need to do the job, and for the skills that you have, what am I prepared to pay you?

speaker: Dr Koh Poh Koon
text: Because the employer will then feel that these jobs that he can do with these skills are justifiable for the wage and costs that I am going to bear for which I can actually be competitive as a business and recover it through my my business.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting for a minimum of 20 minutes.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Because it is not progressive, so it is a maximum of 20 minutes as well.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will take the Chair at 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.08 pm until 4.30 pm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Many Members have spoken on the challenges and concerns of our workers across all segments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our infection rates have gone down and we have been able to proceed with the slow and steady re-opening of our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Yet, it would be a mistake to think that we are going back to pre-COVID-19 norms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As other speakers in this House have observed, it is unlikely that things will be the same again.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Many industries will take time to recover and, when they do, they will look quite different from what it is now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The way we work has already changed and will continue to change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For instance, companies and workers alike have had to adapt to telecommuting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: On the contrary, the pandemic has spurred the pace of digitalisation, upskilling and improving the resilience of our workforce and supply chains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Government has put in place substantial effort and resources to help our businesses and workers deal with the impact of the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Right now, our focus must be to help our businesses and our workers to emerge stronger from this crisis and to seize new opportunities ahead.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We should work on the basis that short-term relief measures will continually and eventually taper off.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is why economic agencies under MTI as well as agencies that lead the ITM sectors, such as MAS and IMDA, are intensifying efforts on job creation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: MOM and WSG will work with these agencies to support employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Well before the JSS phases out, we have introduced the Jobs Growth Incentive or JGI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The JGI will provide salary support for businesses which bring forward their hiring plans and hire more locals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package is our key push to help our workers to enter new jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Where this is not yet possible, we are helping jobseekers to acquire the skills that will put them in a stronger position when the economy begins to recover.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It pools together jobs and training opportunities for Singaporeans across the public and private sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Under this Package, we have curated 117,500 jobs as at end-August, including jobs, company-hosted traineeships, attachments and training opportunities and training places.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: With the exception of SGUnited Traineeships which are designed for fresh and recent graduates, these opportunities are all open to mid-career individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: More than 33,000 jobseekers have been placed into SGUnited Jobs and Skills opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about how the Government determines the number of job opportunities available under the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package and the job roles created by the top hiring sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have been putting out the total number of committed opportunities available under the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package in our weekly Job Situation Report.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The number of committed opportunities is based on approved places under the various SGUnited Jobs and Skills programmes, such as, one, career conversion programmes, traineeships, company attachments and training courses; two, public sector and other Government-funded jobs; and three, private sector jobs that are advertised on the national MyCareersFuture.sg jobs portal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Not surprisingly, the key contributors are growth sectors, such as information and communications, healthcare, professional services, finance and insurance and manufacturing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Examples of jobs in the top five sectors include: software, web and multimedia developers, nursing professionals, management and business consultants, financial analysts and engineering professionals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But I should also point out that even in sectors badly-hit by COVID-19, there is hiring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In tourism and retail, for example, business models are changing fast.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Employers see a need to reskill existing staff as well as to bring in fresh talent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is, therefore, important not to write them off.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: To help our local jobseekers access and get more information on the available jobs and skills opportunities, Workforce Singapore (WSG) has organised various career workshops, seminars and walk-in interviews, reaching about 38,800 individuals between July and September 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have also brought career matching services closer to the heartlands.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, we have launched the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Centres in phases since early July and, by end-August, one had been set up across all 24 HDB towns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Although all satellite career centres were only in operation from end-August, Career Ambassadors have advised around 4,200 jobseekers by now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We are heartened to hear Mr Liang Eng Hwa sharing that his constituents have found this to be helpful and that many were able to secure jobs after going to these centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: That being said, when so many businesses are restructuring, mismatches in jobs and skills must be expected.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We recognise the tremendous adjustments needed by both jobseekers and employers to give each other a chance even if they do not look like perfect fits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Many jobseekers have shown such courage and resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For jobseekers who are prepared to take the leap to change vocation or join a new sector, our career conversion programmes and company-hosted traineeships and attachments can help to make this switch easier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: At the same time, we are also seeing businesses changing their mindsets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Instead of looking only for jobseekers who already have the experience and skills, businesses often find that when they widen their search, they find good candidates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Government has been working closely with such forward-thinking companies in the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And in doing so, these companies have created new opportunities for Singaporeans while placing themselves in a good position for economic recovery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng has highlighted that mature workers aged 40 and above are likely to face greater difficulties in making a career switch.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Moreover, under the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package introduced in the Unity Budget earlier this year, we have ramped up our career conversion programmes to more than 14,000 places this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This year alone, our career conversion programmes have helped 6,100 mid-career jobseekers to acquire new skills and switch into new occupations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These include close to 100 Professional Conversion Programmes or PCPs, covering across 30 sectors, and specialised career conversion programmes under the Tech Skills Accelerator or TeSA for the ICT sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For mid-career jobseekers who may not be able to secure a job straightaway, the SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme provides attachment opportunities hosted by companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These opportunities provide jobseekers with valuable industry-relevant experience and help them to build up their skillsets and networks, while receiving an allowance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Government will co-fund 80% of the training allowances for trainees under these programmes, while the organisations fund the remaining 20%.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The public sector has also introduced a Work and Skills Immersion Programme in capability areas, such as ICT, food science and technology, social services and healthcare sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Open to fresh graduates and mid-career switchers, successful applicants are employed full-time, typically on a two-year basis, and will receive structured on-the-job training, preparing them to take up roles in the economy once we recover.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Miss Cheryl Chan has also pointed out that our upskilling and reskilling strategies need to take into account certain vulnerable groups, such as special needs individuals, and we agree fully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Open Door Programme helps PwDs enter suitable jobs and integrate them into the workplace by providing support for job placement, training and cost of job redesign.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Open Door Programme training grant was recently enhanced in July, with more course fee subsidies of up to 95% and training allowance of $6/hr, as well as a new training commitment award of $100 per completed eligible training course.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The training courses are curated to ensure that they equip our PwDs with industry-relevant skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This includes courses in software and technical design skills, and courses that help PwDs work in emerging sectors like logistics, or in new jobs that may involve automation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: There are also customised Train and Place Programmes for specialised jobs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And looking ahead, SG Enable is also working to expand courses in sectors with long-term growth opportunities, such as healthcare, education, banking and finance and computing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: On our foreign Work Pass policies, there was already an intense debate last month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, I will just summarise some of the points that were brought up by Members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Government will continue to make adjustments to calibrate the flow, keeping in mind Mr Liang Eng Hwa's reminder not to over rely on foreign manpower.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: To that end, we update our foreign worker policies on a regular basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We will also cut S Pass quotas for the construction, process and marine shipyard sectors from 20% to 15% from 2021 to 2023.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: At the Employment Pass or EP level, MOM has also tightened the framework recently.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is why we raised the salary hurdle – to nudge employers towards better quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And this also means that applicants who do not meet the higher hurdles must come under the S Pass framework, where there are quota controls.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have extended the job advertising duration from 14 to 28 days.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: When assessing EP and S Pass applications, we will place additional emphasis on efforts made by employers to build up and retain a strong Singaporean Core.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We will also be engaging an expanded group of employers to review their hiring practices, including firms whose Singaporean Core has been weakening, or whose EP and S Pass workforce are also overly concentrated from a single foreign nationality source.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Members such as NTUC Deputy Secretary-General Koh Poh Koon earlier have spoken passionately on supporting our lower wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We all share the same aspirations in this House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As various Members have also spoken earlier in clarification of Dr Koh's speech, we do not want any Singaporean to be left behind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We want to uplift and care for our fellow workers as best as we can.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This Government and our tripartite partners stand in solidarity with our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We are progressively narrowing the gap between the incomes of our low-wage workers, and those in the middle.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As for the overall workforce – that means those with PWM and those without PWM collectively – real incomes of our full-time employed resident workers at the 20th percentile have also increased cumulatively more than the median.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: There has certainly been progress, if you look at our measures and how the whole eco-system works.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But more importantly, we have done so, while keeping unemployment low for years, up till COVID-19 broke out early this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The risk of disemployment is a key factor that the Government is very sensitive to.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: With regard to literature, the fact is that the jury is still out there.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Economists have not conclusively found that Minimum Wage will not create disemployment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In fact, I am told it is a very hotly contested area and economists continue to debate this issue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Recent studies have found that the range of estimates for the disemployment effect of Minimum Wage is wide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Moreover, studies have shown that the disemployment effects could be stronger for certain groups of workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For example, Harasztosi and Lindner found that the disemployment effects due to increases in Minimum Wage in Hungary were considerably larger in the tradeable and exporting sectors than in the non-tradeable or service sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Others, such as economists Meer and West have shown in their research in the United States that Minimum Wage may not cause immediately disemployment effects, but still impact job growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Some studies, when you look at it, they relate to disemployment from the averages perspective.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But I think it is also important when you look at some of this evidence, the preponderance of evidence show that low-skilled workers are actually most at risk when you talk about job loss.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, we need to deal with the specifics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Look at the natures of our profile of low-wage workers in Singapore and the nature of how this would affect them in specifics.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We are not ideologically against Minimum Wage, PWM or what have you, but I think what we want is the best from each of these systems that will benefit Singapore, benefit our low-wage workers; but at the same time, we avoid the downsides and the trade-offs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is very important for us and that is why we take a very serious view on disemployment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I think it is important that we support them beyond just the wages, and we also have Special Employment Credit to offset their wages and improve their employability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Silver Support is also provided to support retirement adequacy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, on top of the wages that they get, Government supports them with a slew of measures to uplift their income to support their homes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is also important to inculcate care and respect for our low-wage workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: With Workcare, we will improve low-wage workers' working environments in appreciation for their work, such as through the provision of proper rest areas for outsourced workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I think the question would be this – can we be a nation with a strong social compact but without Minimum Wage?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: When we think of countries with high standards of living, strong social policies, and with good and advanced economies like us, we often think of Scandinavian countries like Norway, Denmark and Sweden.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Like Singapore, these countries do not have a single Minimum Wage, and yet they still have vibrant, cohesive societies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In place of a single Minimum Wage, these countries have robust dialogues between stakeholders, resulting in collective agreements on wages at the sectoral level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is akin to our sectoral tripartite approach in our existing PWMs and future tripartite efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Tripartite Workgroup for our low-wage workers, will be studying this important issue with an open mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: They will work to refresh the consensus on what works best for our low-wage workers, and to ensure that more of our low-wage workers can benefit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Dennis Tan have asked about the criteria for SIRS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is a significant expansion of an already sizeable programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have already been exercising flexibility in the qualifying criteria to support more self-employed persons, or SEPs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And for the remaining one third, applicants may have been earning much higher incomes, they could have resided in higher value properties, or own two or more properties with their spouses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As SIRS was intended to support SEPs, employees who lost their jobs or experienced income loss were redirected to the COVID-19 Support Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Where there were other areas of need, we have referred unsuccessful applicants to the appropriate agencies for follow-up assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: On the suggestion by Mr Saktiandi Supaat to allow citizens in need to tap on their CPF balances early, as announced by Deputy Prime Minister Heng in August, the Government is studying appropriate ways to provide support to working Singaporeans, including SEPs, in the event of prolonged loss of income, beyond existing schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We take these ideas seriously and will study them closely; rest assured.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: MOM will continue to make every effort to ensure that Singapore and Singaporeans are not just able to tide over the immediate challenge ahead of us, but also are set in good stead for the future beyond that.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe we have seen our Government do this in the past six or seven months with five Budgets that have been rolled out to deal with the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on Singaporeans and Singaporean businesses.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Government has done a good job, so far, with regard to immediate crisis management and to meet immediate needs, of our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The fact remains that there are, to paraphrase Deputy Prime Minister Heng, "profound uncertainties ahead".

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I am heartened that the key phrase in the Statement is the strategy to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In other words, now that we are out of that immediate danger, what can we do to navigate the river to be mindful of the currents to ensure that our boat sails in that right direction; being mindful, of course, of all the crocodiles that are around us.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I would to like to see how opportunities could be explored during this period in the Sports & Fitness and Arts & Cultural industries to make them a more essential part of our community and society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: COVID-19 has indeed had a significant dampener on sports.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: You need to have spectators to have meaningful sporting activities, and just even play together, you need to have people come together, and understandably so we could not do that in the first few months of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to focus now on opportunities for those in the arts and culture industries.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: No doubt, many of the practitioners, professionals and organisations could rely on some of the schemes such as JSS & SIRS for support as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, MCCY and MOE could leverage on the performing expertise of our arts professionals to engage and employ them even as auxiliary educators of sorts for them to come into the schools and bring real-life artistic experience to our students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Using our arts performance like this would, I believe, be a win-win situation because it will allow our arts performers an alternate revenue stream, something else they can do besides their actual performing and it also allow our students to be exposed to and be taught by and be nurtured by as it were, actual, professional arts practitioners coming from the arts industry.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that some schools do engage professionals now on an independent ad hoc basis, but what I proposing is, perhaps, having a dedicated core of arts and culture professionals who are actually considered auxiliary MOE educators and having these educators being deployed in a structured formal manner to every MOE school in the country, and through this way we also educate and bring our young people or young adults into the world of arts and culture through forms such dance, music, singing and so on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe it was Cultural Medallion recipient Jeremy Monteiro, himself is a world renowned pianist who said, and i quote, “It would be a waste if local musicians, who have years of experience in the industry, but no formal education, are not allowed to formally teach part-time or full time too.” The same, perhaps, could be said of theatre practitioners or dancers as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If our concern is that such professionals might not have sufficient teacher training, then I strongly recommend that MCCY, perhaps, work with MOE to see how these professionals could undergo basic teacher training certification in the fundamentals of education, for example, how to impart education, how to work with curriculum and so on while concurrently actually bringing their art and their craft, in working with the students.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that incorporating more of the arts and culture into our school’s curriculum and involving more of our arts professionals in the delivery of this curriculum is a huge step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I end my speech in support of the Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I think it is important to be clear what the literature says and I wonder if he could clarify.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: He did cite single studies which show that the Minimum Wage, perhaps, may generate occasional instances where unemployment levels may go up but we should be clear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is always easy to cite individual studies and that is why in academia we do not rely purely on a single study to support our case.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Rather we do something called meta analyses so these aggregate and evaluate the totality of the results.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If you look at the totality of the results, I think it is fairly clear that – and I am happy to cite a specific study.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, for the case of the UK you can look at the study by Dube in 2019; for the case of the US, you can look at, in addition to the famous Card and Krueger study in 1995, more recent evidence as well, for Brookman in 2010 for international evidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The point is, look, I am not trying to make this a battle of studies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But I think we need to come to some kind of agreement that we do not make proposals about the Minimum Wage on the basis of a single study that favours the outcome that we have approached the issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: This would fall far below the minimum wage of every, almost every other developed country and all these studies have been based on Minimum wages that are much higher than the number that we are proposing here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I think it is important to keep that in mind.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: First, I thank the Member Jamus Lim for his, I suppose, clarification.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: The point I made earlier was that this is not about studies and not about particular studies actually.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Or actually, we did have Minimum Wage through our PWM or Minimum Wage Plus to some extent.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, conceptually, ideologically, we have clearly said that we are not against one idea or the other.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We can throw studies at each other and, like I said, it is hotly contested, even among academia.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: What is important is this: that we want to reap the maximum benefits of what these studies have shown and how others have applied it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I have also shared others, like in Norway, Sweden, Denmark, have also shown strong, social solidarity without implementation of a single Minimum Wage, using the same approach that we have had – using sectoral consensus to make sure that we have uplifted our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Studies aside, \what we have to look at is our local context.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, I have shown that at the 10th percentile, as I said in my speech earlier, we have seen wage growth.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I do have to also reiterate the fact once again because the Workers' Party tends to forget this in its deliberations always that our system works in tandem as a holistic system, it is a whole system.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is not just PWM but Workfare that we use to top up.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think many of your residents too would have enjoyed Silver Support in their old age.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: This is exactly the profile that needs the most help and we top up the income so that they are not left behind.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: And that is why I think it is important that beyond putting studies, showing analyses, meta analyses and what have you, but really getting down on the ground, working in consensus meet the employers too and making sure that the downsides are managed and do not impact our lowest skilled workers who are likely at risk when it comes to job loss.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, the risk of disemployment is something that we are very sensitive to and that is why we have the Tripartite Workgroup on the Low-wage Workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We need to study this quite carefully as we chart the path ahead.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it is not just something simple, you could do it within a short span of time without understanding the impacts, the consequences for our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, it is not about academic and studies but, really, lives of Singaporeans and how we want to uplift our low-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, if you have a fresh perspective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yes, thank you and I will just note them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I am really happy that Senior Minister of State Zaqy has raised the example of Scandinavia because, in fact, it is true that Scandinavia does not have a Minimum Wage but that is in part because they also have unionisation rates in the order of 70% to 80%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, there is a very strong collective bargaining representation there.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: In fact, part of the reason why they do not want the Minimum Wage is because they do not want to get into a situation where a Minimum Wage might push wages down below a certain mark which, as I explained, is not in fact the lived reality of our low-income workers who are struggling with some of the lowest wage rates, even with the $1,300 that we proposed as a Minimum Wage among developed countries.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, let me put it to the Member again that, yes, we do have a similar system, the tripartite negotiation but we are a much smaller country and you cannot say that our wages do not increase.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: It is one thing to say that the system has not worked.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: On the other hand, I put forth the numbers to show that the system has.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, if you tell me that the low-wage workers have stagnated in the last 10 years, I say the numbers show otherwise.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: I think it is not just about academia or theory out here.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: We have worked the system, we have worked and the unions have worked the ground too, employers have been working with us and our system works too.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: So, we all have our uniqueness but the issue here is: is our system working?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Have the wages of our lowest 10%, for example, if I take it to that level, has it gone up?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I want to pose four questions to the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We do not have time to pose four questions, I have said that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Do you not think this is a very bold idea or that —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, we have been discussing this for the past, quite a long bit of time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We can always put in new measures to support the implementation of a new Minimum Wage or living wage.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because in terms of the level of competitiveness, the level of Minimum Wage or living wage that we are proposing is actually very low level.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, it would not affect the overall wage level immediately.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Every part of Singapore, coming together, for a beautiful, tightly knitted, cohesive fabric.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These diverse strands of our social fabric include our arts, culture and sports sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Darryl David has spoken passionately about these three sectors and I will address his queries.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These sectors make the Singapore tapestry even more beautiful, vibrant, and meaningful.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These strands coe together, to represent the heart of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In recent times, like the many threads which make up the fabric of our society, these strands have come under strain.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has fundamentally affected the way in which we interact and socialise with one another and has threatened to unravel some of these threads.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we know that even as we battle the pandemic, it is critical for us to ensure that each of these threads – our arts, culture and sports sectors – remain vibrant, cohesive and remain very much a part of the Singapore Tapestry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We must continue to sustain and develop them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And they, in turn, must continue to be an avenue through which Singaporeans fulfil their aspirations, dreams and desires.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These threads must also continue to connect Singaporeans from all walks of life and be able to inspire and imbue a sense of pride in being Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our sportsmen and sportswomen, past and present, have been a source of inspiration to many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We share the joys of their success and we feel the pain of their defeat.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The events and programmes of our arts community reach ever wider and growing audiences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They also teach and they inspire us in a way which almost nothing else can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of this is possible because we have, over time, nurtured the best talents, helped them along in their journey, developed them, given them a boost in their chosen craft, built a platform from which they can showcase their talents.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we owe a lot also to our community of trainers, coaches, instructors and freelancers, all of whom contribute richly to this landscape.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As Mr Darryl David says, we must do what we can to rally behind them during this difficult time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whilst some sectors have seen a measure of recovery, the past few months have really not been easy for those in the arts, culture and sports sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Fundamentally, these sectors thrive on large group gatherings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Theatre, performances and competitive sport – they all play to an audience.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These measures are necessary but we must not forget that they have severely impacted the viability of businesses and the livelihoods, particularly of freelancers in these sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the almost three months that I have been at MCCY, I have met a broad range of people across the various sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have met with many leaders of our National Sports Associations, talked to athletes, coaches and freelance instructors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have also heard from artists, musicians and arts educators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many have been so very generous in sharing their views and vision with me, giving me a good grasp of the industry and good ideas for the longer term development of these sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But they also spoke candidly about their here and now, their immediate challenges, and I think all of us in this House understand those difficulties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over the past few months, MCCY has rolled out dedicated support measures for our sectors to supplement the assistance they already receive from the broad-based Government measures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We understand what many are going through and we know that we must, where we can, help them further.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also supported practitioners to hone their digital skills and expertise in areas, such as business literacy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And many of them, in turn, support the industry as a whole.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, the Jazz Association of Singapore – Mr Jeremy Monteiro is their Music Director, someone that Mr David mentioned earlier – they were one of the first recipients of the Digital Presentation Grant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They went online overnight and launched multiple digital programmes, including JASS@Home, a digital concert in celebration of UNESCO's International Jazz Day 2020.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I attended many of their presentations – high quality, innovative, entertaining but I think, most of all, comforting, to the many Singaporeans and, especially, in these times.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On top of that, in the true spirit of giving back, JASS has also started their own Crisis Fund to assist local jazz musicians affected by the crisis with short-term financial aid.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, JASS receives a grant from the Government but they also pay it forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Bhaskar's Arts Academy was also awarded the DPG for DashaTanMatra (10 Subtle Elements), a series of 10 mini digital presentations of new dance, music works, webinars on Bharatanatyam, and re-adaptation of past repertoires.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to support the industry as they seek to go digital.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another practitioner I met recently was Ms Emmeline Yong.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She was an investment banker in New York.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She gave it all up, returned to Singapore to pursue her passion in visual arts and she set up Objectifs in 2003.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Objectifs is an example of an arts organisation that MCCY is committed to supporting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has a strong sense of mission to nurture and also provide a platform for other practitioners and freelancers to hone, practise and exhibit their craft.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: With the support of the ACRP, Objectifs put up free photography and videography courses for arts practitioners and other freelancers to help them create strong social media content to outreach, a campaign to pitch their offerings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To better support freelancers or smaller set-ups, the Arts Resource Hub (ARH), set up under the National Arts Council (NAC), provides targeted support for all of them, including co-working spaces, talks, clinics on financial planning, probono legal support, digital tools and copyright – a broad spectrum of what is needed, giving them a platform and tools for these artists to pursue their craft and also build on their dream, much like what JASS and Objectifs have done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the immediate short-term, the ARH has also provided freelancers with aggregated information and assistance to help them tap on the broader Government programmes like the Self-Employed Persons Income Relief Scheme (SIRS), COVID-19 Support Grant and the SEP Training Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, MCCY has also worked with people within the community spaces to develop platforms to bring digital experiences and also blended programmes, which are often hybrid in nature, to blend or both in-person and virtual and finding platforms to bring more of these to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, #SGCultureAnywhere by NAC is an integrated campaign that profiles the best of Singapore arts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our cultural institutions and major arts companies have also made their content available on new digital platforms, such as SISTIC Live.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those of you who have not gone on SISTIC Live, I encourage you to give it a try.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In sports, we developed ActiveSG Circle as a virtual sports centre to encourage and inspire Singaporeans to get active, as well as to provide a marketplace for sports and fitness instructors and their potential students and trainees to get in touch with each other.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through the Circle, she has discovered new ways to reach out to both existing and also to new students, with reasonable fees, to make these classes and these interactive sessions a lot more accessible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SportSG has also introduced Blended, an initiative to encourage sport event companies and organisers to transition to events that blend virtual and physical participation which Singaporeans can look forward to more of in the coming months.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This format will certainly be with us for some time and we will continue to study how we can support them better so that instructors, coaches and other freelancers alike can continue to reach out to an audience and, as far as possible, even in these times, to continue with as much as they would have done in normal circumstances as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: MCCY will provide immediate assistance to critical segments with special talents.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We know that if we lose these talents, inadvertently or otherwise, in this pandemic, it could take years to recover.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It would set us back in our efforts to promote arts, culture and sports in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for the arts and culture sector, we will be providing an Operating Grant under the ACRP to support arts and culture organisations and also those in closely-related sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They hold key talent capabilities in our eco-system and we must not lose them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We hope organisations that receive this grant will provide work opportunities for the many employees in this sector, including the freelancers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Added to the earlier announced $25 million package, this makes for a total of $50 million available to the sports sector.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is made up of a diverse range of different institutions, from the National Sport Associations (NSAs), to the private academies and clubs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are private leagues that run the sports facility as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, of course, the whole mass of coaches and freelance instructors, they all make up a very rich and vibrant sports eco-system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They all play an important role in our collective efforts to build a strong pipeline of athletes to mould and shape them and to support them on their quest for competitive success on both the domestic and international front.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many private academies and clubs, in particular, complement the efforts of our NSAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They enrich training and talent development, and they also offer a range of different competition opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Take the Aquatic Performance Swim Club or APSC, or the APS Swim School, for example.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a private swimming academy which has, over the years, contributed significantly to the identification and talent of Singaporean swimmers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Since 1996, the APSC has channeled swimming talents spotted from the APS Swim School into specialised competitive swimming training, diving and also synchronised swimming.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have also provided competition opportunities across a range of different levels and through its many myriad of events.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We understand the impact that COVID-19 has had on these private academies, such as APS and others, the leagues and facility operators and we understand the challenges they go through.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many of them need some measure of support, if nothing else, to tide over the period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Recently, the Cage and other such similar sport facility operators also reached out to me to share their concerns.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They spoke about the inevitable loss of revenue because of the safe management measures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And they had difficulties affording rent and continuing to sustain the salaries of their staff.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we can well understand how these restrictions have impacted their ability to operate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SportSG has worked with many such businesses to allow them to resume some programmes and activities safely, coming out of the Circuit Breaker.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I am sure Members in this House will agree that we do not want these operators to be a casualty of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our sporting landscape, with its broad spectrum of different players and options, will be the poorer if that happens.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While the resumption of sports activities since June has alleviated some immediate operational concerns, we recognise that there is still the longer term sustainability and survivability.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I think that is a major area of stress for many of these operators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This grant will also ensure that our critical sports businesses which contribute richly, as I have said, to our athlete pipeline development and training, do not close down due to the pandemic, do not marginalise the programmes that are available for athletes, allowing our athletes to benefit from the best training programmes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The last few months have shown that going digital is paramount, in fact, completely necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It allows our businesses and freelancers to reach out to existing audiences, to newer and also wider audiences, allowing higher quality content to be developed and also a degree of interactivity, despite the fact that you are communicating across two screens.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We recognise the work that they do and we have extended this programme to them, aiming to support 100 projects, which will, in turn, see the participation of about 450,000 Singaporeans in sports programmes over the next six months.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will also set aside an additional $4 million for sports businesses and freelancers to enhance the quality of their own digital productions to become even more interactive and more engaging and attract a greater following on their platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, we will work with MOE and other partners to ensure that our students continue to have access to high quality arts experiences as part of their holistic education.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The intent, Sir, is to continue to nurture and develop an appreciation, and hopefully, eventually ignite a passion for the arts in our young.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The young will make up our audiences, our supporters and our patrons, and of course, the practitioners, in years to come.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have noted Mr Darryl David’s suggestion to engage our arts practitioners as auxiliary educators in schools.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, to ensure that students can benefit from the knowledge and experience of our arts practitioners, which I agree with Mr David it is a critical resource, NAC has worked with NIE International since 2012 to develop a course on the Essentials of Teaching and Learning for arts practitioners, precisely to become arts educators.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: NAC has also worked with other partners such as the Social Service Institute and SEED Institute to develop relevant pedagogical skills to complement what they are already do and are able to practice so that they can then seamlessly work with children with special needs and pre-schoolers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One needs to merge or blend what you have in your own experience as an arts practitioner with the relevant pedagogical skills so that pre-schoolers and those with special needs can also benefit from such education.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: NAC is working with arts educators to convert their student-facing programmes, such as the NAC Arts Education Programme, into digital or blended forms in the same way as we do for so many other programmes so that they become more accessible and we can reach a wider audience.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: NAC has also paired up with NIE to develop an e-learning primer and an e-pedagogy course for the arts, which will be launched in December 2020 and made available to arts educators at no cost.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Today, I am sure Mr David knows, museum-based learning forms a key component of the Primary Arts syllabus, with a recommended learning journey for Primary 4 students to the National Gallery in Singapore or to the Singapore Art Museum.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On top of that, all Primary 6 and Secondary 2 cohorts will also visit the Asian Civilisations Museum and the National Museum of Singapore respectively, to enhance their learning and also to complement what they are taught in school, out of the classroom, as far as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is a certain messiness in the way in which the sports and arts practitioners are organised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is not only inevitable, but perhaps also useful to keep the sector fresh, and maintain some of that carefree entrepreneurial spirit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Hence, MCCY and our agencies have taken a light touch towards freelancers in the past, recognising the value of spontaneity and flexibility in their work – one day you can work on your own, another day you can come together and collaborate with another institution, but there is that spontaneous freedom.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But COVID-19 has thrown into sharp focus the importance of having some dedicated organised framework to look after these freelancers to support their efforts, to help them apply for and get into the programmes that the Government has put up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We, my colleagues and Minister of State Low Yen Ling in particular, have reached out to many freelancers, and we will continue to do so – to help them to level up and to allow them to bring in more diversity to their craft.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The sport freelancers I have met have also expressed their desire to do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To encourage more to sign up for this programme to raise their coaching expertise so that once we are back – closer to what was normal before – these coaches will become more relevant and have more skillsets to impart to their trainees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Likewise, for arts freelancers, MCCY and NAC, through the ARH, will work with them to step up on efforts to help them tap on available resources, to support them, identify and facilitate also work opportunities, skills upgrading, and also help them leverage on digital technology.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It might not always be as easy for freelancers to be doing this on their own.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We recognise that and we have a team set up to look into their needs, and to see how best to organise this, to organise the efforts to pair them up with available programmes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We encourage our freelance artists in the community to contact the ARH directly should they need assistance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are facing both short- and longer term challenges.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
