text: The Government is committed to helping as many as possible in the sector to pull through, to remain viable, and to continue to play a rich part in the Singapore Tapestry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the immediate short term, the financial measures that I have outlined briefly will help.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we know that the most sustainable way to help our sectors is to allow for the activities to resume not only at scale, but also safely.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are as eager as our artists, and our athletes, and the wider community for this to happen, and we have been working towards this goal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Recently, my colleagues and I attended several live performance pilots, including those by the Singapore Dance Theatre, Bhaskar’s Arts Academy, Singapore Symphony Orchestra, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are reviewing now how we can fully resume and scale up live performances for the sector, with the appropriate measures to always prioritise the safety of our audiences, the performers and the crew.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the coming days, we hope also to progressively reintroduce programmes at museums in a safe manner as more social activities resume.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singaporeans can also look forward to the return of the Singapore Premier League this Saturday, after a hiatus of more than six months.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The teams have resumed training, initially in small groups of five, subsequently full-squad training.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I met a few of them when I visited the Lion City Sailors Football Club at Bishan stadium a few weeks ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I could see that they were all keenly motivated by the desire to get back onto the field and to compete.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are also working with health authorities to pilot the resumption of spectator sports and mass participation sport events in the near future.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, we will have to find new modalities for mass participation events to avoid large concentrations of people at one place and also to consider the use of blended models in some of these events.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One such example of a blended event pilots is the “Run as One” event, where small groups of runners were given time slots to compete across a fixed route over the course of two weeks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, you are given the best example of own-time-own target – go at your own time but complete the distance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nowadays everyone has a fitness tracker, and you can track your time and the distance covered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These examples give us some options in how we will introduce or reintroduce mass participation events.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These pilots also allow us to test and refine the sports formats, with the goal of making them as safe as possible and also to try to maximise the amount of interactivity and fun that participants and spectators want to enjoy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, we have been working closely with religious organisations to resume more activities safely.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My colleagues and I have visited many such religious organisations, or the ROs, over the last couple months.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is encouraging to see they have adapted so very quickly, put safety as the primary consideration, and have been committed to working closely with the Government, placing the well-being of their devotees first.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We continue to be in constant dialogue with our religious leaders.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Much as these will help many tide over this period, we also know that it will take more than just financial assistance to sustain and to develop these sectors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: People must be able to see and also appreciate, the intrinsic value that arts, culture, and sports can bring to our community.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It allows us to rally behind our athletes, our Team, our sporting heroes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It builds and it shapes Singapore, and the kind of Singapore we want to live in, in a way which nothing else can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Singaporeans have turned to the arts, culture and sports to find respite, inspiration, and even to uplift spirits over the last few months in these times.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I urge all of us to support them as much as we can.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Whether it is for the established artists, or the nascent sporting talent, they all thrive on having an audience.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will perform even more gracefully – I am sure, compete more vigorously when they are cheered on by an appreciative audience.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I hope we can also be receptive to the new ways of consuming the arts, culture and sports.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some of the programmes, like Bandon that I mentioned earlier, please get onto them, please experience them for yourselves.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Support them as they bring better content, programmes and events to you.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To our practitioners in all these sectors, I encourage you to stay determined, continue to hone your craft, build your skills, train, compete, perform.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Each of you will continue to be a vital part of the Singapore Tapestry, bringing together rich patterns and colours drawn from each of your diverse contributions and special talents, and your own achievements in arts, culture and music, and sports.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All of these threads make for a more vibrant, exciting and cohesive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Be assured that we value the work that you do, and the Government will support you.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: But as with all things, I think we need to begin with a goal in mind.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan
text: We have given a lot of tribute to how the Arts and the Sports make up the Tapestry of Singapore, provide social cohesiveness, but I would like to encourage and seek the Minister's clarification on whether there is any thinking right now, or there will be any thinking in the near future, about planning for the Singaporean arts scene to become internationally successful and viable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It had given us a lot of food for thought and really, we took on board the points as we looked at what else we could do, how else you could support the immediate short term of the freelancers, the coaches and the performers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But more importantly, I am very cognisant of the points she makes about the longer term vision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is precisely because we have to have the ability to have the longer term to be able to prepare our artists today and to protect them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The culture Academy is really a set up to look at the short-term needs, the industry and also to chart the longer term goals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In fact, just this morning I had a meeting with many of our Arts Institution heads.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We had an interesting dialogue and the same question has come up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And if Ms Tan is looking for recognition, just look at the exhibition today at the National Museum, started on the 8 October 2020, the Venice Biennale exhibition, Music For Everyone, and you will see that actually that exhibition has been on the world stage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Events like that in the past, as well as events in the future, will continue to nurture to grow and will give each of these artists as best a pipeline as possible, as best a development pathway as possible for them to shine on the world stage because ultimately that is what we want.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, to offer some perspective on the truly extraordinary measures that the Government has taken in its Budgets to deal with this crisis, such that we are even in a position today to debate about the way ahead.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Second, to highlight the struggles that Singaporeans continue to face in the immediate term and what more we can do to support Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And third, to look ahead and seek clarifications on the Government's strategy to invest in our long-term capabilities and priorities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, on what has been truly extraordinary in the Government's four Budgets this year and the latest set of support measures.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: More than $4 billion, directly into the hands of households, to boost the Government's support for households in these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Six billion dollars that it is setting aside, amidst a crisis, for future GST Voucher payouts, because the Government knows that the GST Voucher scheme is a permanent commitment.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, I completely disagree with the hon Member Mr Leong Mun Wai, who suggested yesterday that, because the Government is putting $6 billion into the GST Voucher fund, he has raised apprehension about an impending GST hike and in fact, the $6 billion should be spent elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: More than $10 billion in total that the Government has set aside again during the crisis for our strategic, long-term needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: More than $10 billion that the Government has remained committed to, despite all the fiscal exigencies of the crisis.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I thought these bear mentioning, because it is so easy to underestimate the scale of the Government's response to the crisis, so easy to overlook the Government's fundamental commitment to think long-term and so easy to take for granted the resources that we now have to sustain our response to the crisis while building a better future together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I hope that by highlighting these, we would have a better sense of perspective as we debate the Government's strategy to emerge stronger from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The COVID-19 Support Grant aims to help Singaporeans cushion the impact of the pandemic on their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is meant to work alongside ComCare assistance, which remains available, and indeed has been enhanced for the lowest income households in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, ComCare is designed for one particular segment.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One of the criteria for the COVID-19 Support Grant is income loss of at least 30% for three months.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One resident in particular lost 30% income for two of three months and 29% in the remaining month.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: He did not get the grant, despite my appeal for him.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I was told there were no extenuating circumstances in his household to justify an exception, as his other family members are working and so the gross household income should continue to be sufficient for their needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And while the responsible policymaker would make sure that the next $1 in income support is given to the household that needs it the most, I urge that we also consider what the next 1% point drop in income would mean for a household in the middle income segment.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The median income in Singapore is about $4,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Take a 25% drop, that represents $1,000 less each month.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A resident in this situation would not qualify for the COVID-19 Support Grant at all.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And we can point to the $3,000 that the resident still draws each month and say this is sufficient.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I urge that we consider from the resident's perspective, his or her lived reality, his or her expectations, burdens and commitments, and what that $1,000 loss might feel for him or her.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I therefore suggest that we pro-rate the COVID-19 Support Grant, based on the extent of income loss up to 30% and avoid the all or none cliff effect of the current criterion.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In making this suggestion, I am well aware that wherever we draw the line in a policy, there will always be those on one side of the line who feel like they have missed out.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And yet, in many of our policies, we have drawn not one, but multiple lines, such that it is a gradient rather than a cliff.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is the case with housing grants and this is the case with healthcare subsidies in the Pioneer and Merdeka Generation Packages and CHAS.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Pro-rating the COVID-19 Support Grant would provide calibrated relief for more middle income households and better cushion the lingering economic pains of the pandemic for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: More importantly, if we cut through the statistics and think about the thousands of Singaporean jobseekers as individuals, with lives to build and families to feed, grappling with the uncertainties of a search that has been going on for months, trying to stay strong amidst the deflating radio silence after that application that was sent out weeks ago, or after that interview last week that seemed to have gone went quite well – then it becomes abundantly clear to us that we not only need to walk alongside each Singaporean each step of the way, but also deliver outcomes for these jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, I urge the Government to double down on job matching and get many more openings filled much more quickly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One of my residents was holding a full-time job.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: She successfully applied for another role, in a different sector and was told that her first day will be in April.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, she resigned and started serving her notice period.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Then, the global economy worsened, the department she was slated to join got shut down and the offer that she had accepted got withdrawn.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: She ended up with nothing – she could not go back to the company she had resigned from and there was no other opening in the company she was slated to join.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: She has sent out more than 80 applications.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In her words, "anything to get me started, I applied." And in her words, from "using various platforms, cold-emailing, career fairs, I have tried them all." She is 25 years old.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Another resident of mine was manufacturing vaccines with a major pharmaceutical company here, but was let go after her contract expired.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Her applications for similar positions had been without success, despite relevant experience.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In her words, "it doesn’t make sense." She had also applied for other positions in MedTech and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: She tells me she simply hopes to support her ageing parents, who probably cannot for work much longer.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: She says her "mind is dropping to almost negative now".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: She asks me to put myself in her, quote, "dusty shoes".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Then there is this other resident, 44 years old, holds a Master's in Chemical Engineering, retrenched three months go – still searching and still interviewing.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Yet another resident, this one, in his 50s, with more than 25 years of managerial experience.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In his words, "when recruiters see my age, they just pass me over." He told me he does not mind at all a lower pay or position and he told me he wished his career coach would have more time for him, because in his view, time is of the essence in certain openings.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There is the resident who was an air stewardess and is now signing up for a training course with monthly allowance under the SGUnited Skills Programme to become a healthcare assistant.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And there is this resident, who switched from being a bar executive in one of the top bars in Singapore, to being a lift technician with one of the top OEMs in Singapore in the market.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I told him I hope he would consider joining our Town Councils some day.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We have to match these jobseekers with available opportunities much more quickly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And we need to do this because we must maintain hope amongst our people and maintain hope in our society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Anecdotally, a big part of the challenge in job matching has been about expectations, concerns and mindsets, on the part of both jobseekers and employers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, we need an intensive relationship-management approach, focus on building the relationship with each employer and jobseeker, really understand and work the accounts, broker a match with persistence and finesse, and ultimately, convert and secure a placement.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think we are know where we want to go.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We are aligned in terms of our objectives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I am asking that we resource much more decisively because we need the outcomes for Singaporeans a lot more quickly.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, I would like to look ahead and seek clarifications on the Government's strategy to invest in our long-term capabilities and priorities.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Deputy Prime Minister and the Finance Minister has said that the latest set of support measures would not draw further on past reserves but be funded by the reallocation of reduced spending, as well as deferred development expenditure.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This includes more than $3.5 billion for transport infrastructure, more than $0.5 billion for healthcare infrastructure, more than $0.5 billion for waterworks and land preparation for the AgroTech zone at Neo Tiew and more than $150 million for MCCY.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Given the Government's weak revenue outlook for the next few years, I share hon Member Mr Liang Eng Hwa's concerns about how we might be able to fund these deferred projects in future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I appreciate the Government's commitment to minimise its draw on past reserves, but I wonder if current revenues originally budgeted for strategic development should be set aside in a fund for deferred spending while additional, exceptional COVID support measures continue to be funded exceptionally with a further but prudent draw on past reserves, instead of reallocation of deferred development spending.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These investments concern our long-term connectivity with the world and within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They concern our healthcare capacity, and our capacity to stay healthy through community sports.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, we would have very hard and very important choices to make.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   	To combat COVID-19, the Government has announced four Budgets decisively and introduced additional assistance measures in August.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Government has allocated tens of billions of dollars to tackle the immediate challenges.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The scale and decisiveness of these efforts are evident to all.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the economic impact of the pandemic on Singaporeans will not abate soon.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I urge the Government to continue to address the immediate needs and concerns of Singaporeans while looking into the future planning and implementing the Emerging Stronger strategy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I would also like to urge the Government to put in more resources to improve the success rate of the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Programme to give more hope to the many workers who are still looking for jobs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In English): Sir, in conclusion, I ask that the Government provide more calibrated support for the broad middle, more effective job matching for workers across all age groups and age groups, and more clarity on our long-term investment strategy in key capabilities that will shape our survival and success.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I am confident that we will remain a hopeful and united people, determined to build a better future for ourselves and future generations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to offer a comparative perspective as to how we fare in relation to Asian countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With your leave, Sir, may I be allowed to use the LED screen to flash the slide?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We see here, Sir, that Singapore is first among 12 Asian countries, in terms of the fiscal commitment to the COVID-19 fight.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This compares to Japan, which is second, and comparatively, it comes in at 15.9%; South Korea comes in at 14.4%, and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, from this perspective, Sir, we can see we compare relatively well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Sometimes, we have to spend more; sometimes, we have to spend less.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And the Budget itself is replete with some examples of this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Just a few hours ago, the hon Minister Ms Indranee Rajah, gave an example of how sometimes we need to spend less when she announced the Baby Support Grant scheme.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She took pains to explain that the grant is aimed at couples who were put off by the COVID-19 pandemic and to encourage them to start and raise families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She also explained that for lower income families, there are already a number of grants and programmes to help them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, from that perspective, it may not make sense to extend the grant and spend more money.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On the other hand, there are programmes where we have to spend more to spend well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Well, we have the COVID-19 Support Grant which was extended by the hon Deputy Prime Minister Mr Heng Swee Keat.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The extension now would cover Singaporeans who suffer a fall in income or lost their jobs after December 2020.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is welcome relief for the affected families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He also extended the Workfare special payment to Singaporeans who did not receive Workfare last year, but did so this year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And, in this way, many low-income families, mind you, the WIS is triggered in relation to low-income workers earning $2,300 per month or less, so more low-income families would benefit from this extension.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I think although we spend more, we spend it well to help these families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In my speech, I would like to concentrate on three budgetary measures for individuals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: First, the Special Financial Relief Programme (SFRP) (Unsecured).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Under the SFRP (Unsecured), the savings for an individual can be significant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The average card interest on outstanding sums attracts 26% per annum.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Converted loans under SFRP (Unsecured) are imposed 8% per annum over a five-year tenure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, Singaporeans facing debt pressure are well advised to consider the SFRP (Unsecured) during this extended period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In my respectful view, the take up rate is low and can be improved.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I think the pool of Singaporeans who are heavily in debt is bigger.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I say this because in 2017, MAS introduced measures to tighten unsecured credit limits to those heavily in debt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In that announcement, MAS stated that there were an estimated 60,000 borrowers in this pool or 4% of total unsecured credit users.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I would assume that this pool should have grown during this crisis with the declining economy, falling income and loss of jobs affecting some families.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But if I am right, I would suggest more proactivity on the part of the Association of Banks in Singapore or ABS and the Credit Counselling Singapore to publicise this programme more so that they can reach out to individuals bogged down by this debt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It can also be made compulsory for financial institutions to consider inviting the debtors to SFRP (Unsecured) before considering legal action as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Before leaving this topic, it would be remiss of me if I did not commend the Financial Institutions & ABS for coming together with MAS and the Govt to implement SFRP (Unsecured) to help Singaporeans facing debt pressures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Financial Institutions could have just insisted on the strict terms of their contract; they would not be wrong but they did not.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is a great example of SGUnited and how banks are helping Singaporeans facing the debt pressure as a result of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Next, I suggest a re-look at the funding model for skills upgrading for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Skills upgrading for Singaporeans is an important pillar in our Roadmap for the Future as outlined by the hon Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng said "We will…need extensive upskilling and continual reskilling of our workforce, to equip our workers to continue to get good jobs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We want to do so for every worker at every age."  On the point about "doing so for every worker at every age", I wish to share an e-mail that I received from Mr John Tan, my resident.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He is married with one bubbly son who is two years old.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He applied for a three full-day Certified Associate in Project Management (CAPM) course.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He pointed out that for Singaporeans aged 21 and above, they get 40% subsidy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The original course fee was $1,016.50, with GST, so he had to pay $641.50, with GST.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I do appreciate why we need to incentivise our older worker to upskill by providing them with a higher subsidy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Given the current challenging environment, there is an opportunity to up the tempo for upskilling and re-training even amongst our younger Singaporeans, so that they get into better-paying jobs with better prospects.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I therefore suggest that we use a tiered approach that incentivises Singaporeans to re-skill as they get older instead of backloading the extra subsidies only when they reach 40.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In this way, we will be able to nurture a reskilling attitude in all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon on Deputy Prime Minister said "In the design of our support schemes, we have been deliberate in channelling additional support to vulnerable groups, to help them access opportunities and stay in good jobs".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In that speech, she made a point that how we treat persons with disabilities is shaped by the attitude of society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I fully agree with her and I would say that a similar point can be made in relation to ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In my speech in February 2020 on occasion of the Unity Budget, I applauded the introduction of Enabling Employment Credit or EEC to incentivise employers to employ and retain persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I also said that a similar credit scheme should be provided to incentivise employers to employ ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I shared the story of Mr R, an ex-offender who was earning a depressed wage on account of his background.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I continue to meet several residents who are ex-offenders who find it difficult to get jobs or are being underpaid during this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Minister for Home Affairs shared useful statistics on the plight of ex-offenders just yesterday pursuant to my Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He informed that the economic downturn brought about by COVID-19 has made the job market more challenging for ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Yellow Ribbon Singapore has stepped up its efforts to help these offenders and I must pay tribute to Yellow Ribbon Singapore and its partners for their stupendous work in getting work for ex-offenders so that they can complete their rehabilitation and reintegration into society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This year to date, I do not have a percentage but 1,534 ex-offenders have been employed, thanks to Yellow Ribbon Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These figures are lower-bound estimates as they do not include self-employed persons, such as delivery riders or private hire car drivers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: A lot of hard work has been put into this, so as to achieve these figures, but I think we can do much more.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Even though we assume that we have another 20% in self-employed jobs, I would suggest that our Government and whole of society can do much more to bring down the roughly 30% unemployment amongst our ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Deputy Prime Minister's objective outlined in his Ministerial Statement about channelling additional support to vulnerable groups.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It will be a good signal by our society to ex-offenders that we remain invested in their rehabilitation and reintegration even in these challenging times.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I seek the hon Deputy Prime Minister's views on this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The suggestions I have made are intended to ensure that Singaporeans who join our workforce continually upgrade themselves to grab the opportunities our future brings and to strengthen the inclusivity element of our Government’s strategy to emerge stronger from the COVID-19 pandemic as outlined by Deputy Prime Minister Heng in his Statement.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In response, I have some clarifications and recommendations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We are all aware just how COVID-19 has severely disrupted businesses and livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Air travel has ceased, borders are closed and our daily average of about 100,000 Malaysian workers commuting from Johor is significantly lower.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many local factories are extremely short-handed and facing harsh challenges.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some of these factories are located within the Woodlands Industrial Area, which happens to be in the division I look after.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My volunteers and I tried to assist by attempting to match some of the residents who were seeking jobs, especially within 2 km of their homes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We always knew that there is a stark mismatch between the jobs and the expectations of jobseekers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, this pandemic has forced us all to rethink and recalibrate our approach to address the mismatch between the employers and the job seekers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Since the middle of this year, I have been actively planning and organising both online job webinars and physical job fairs with support from NTUC e2i for our Sembawang residents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We partnered several MNCs and home-grown companies in the electronics and manufacturing industries to be part of these job fairs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some of the jobs available involve operation of complex machines that are far more automated compared to the older labour-intensive assembly lines.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singaporeans are not enthusiastic about the opportunities to work in these manufacturing companies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: After speaking to the hiring teams, I had a better understanding.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To be able to apply for some of these jobs, you need a NITEC certification or even a diploma for more technical job roles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If you have a driving licence, you could also make more than $2,000 per month.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is obvious that many job seekers will shun job opportunities in the manufacturing industry because the entry pay is simply a non-starter.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There is a concern that should the borders remain closed, many of these factories will be unable to fulfil their orders, this is especially so for high growth industries like semi-conductor manufacturing.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The labour shortage situation will inevitably threaten the future of these companies and also affect Singapore’s economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is the biggest contributor to our economy.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Over the weekend, two pieces of good news were announced.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: First, MNCs are staying firm on their growth plans in Singapore despite the COVID-19 pandemic and they include companies in the semiconductor sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Second, a new task force will be formed to study how to raise the wages of low-income workers and to push for productivity growth.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Now, due to the crisis situation, we do not have the foreign workers to help our factories.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, should these companies have to wait for circumstances to improve and while waiting, hope not to have a painful death or should they take this opportunity to rebuild our Singapore Core?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to address the criteria for job offers, instill better working conditions, implement job redesign and relook at how workers are remunerated.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Another question is: how can Progressive Wage Model be applied directly to these manufacturing companies in order to assist them, to be able to attract local workers instead of always having to rely on daily cross-border commuting foreign workers?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Instead of providing a COVID-19 Support Grant of $800 for three months to Singaporeans and PRs who are still searching for jobs, this $800 could become a contribution of $400 per month for six months as a top-up to the current pay of $1,400.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: A manufacturing industry worker could easily get $1,800 per month instead of remaining jobless.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As Singaporeans, they will still qualify for Workfare Improvement Supplement while the manufacturing companies could attempt to address the short-term labour shortage by hiring available Singaporeans and PRs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Similar to the manufacturing industry, you hear the same problems with the nursing homes and community hospitals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Currently, 60% of the community healthcare sector staff are foreigners and 40% are locals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With rapid ageing in Singapore, the demand for healthcare assistants will only increase, and if it continues this way, the supply will be very limited.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I met several housewives who have prior care-giving experience and are keen to join the healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, the entry salary of $1,400 to $1,600 per month is a key deterrent because the net take-home income after deducting their CPF, meals and travel expenses will only be a few hundred dollars.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I am certain that if the monthly salary is around $2,000, they will be more likely to consider such job offers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Workers must feel appreciated and taken care of.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Only then will they give their best to be positive and productive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The pandemic has led to permanent changes across industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even as COVID-19 continues to rage on in many parts of the world with new waves of infection, Singapore is, indeed, in an enviable position to shifting focus to recovery and growth and seizing opportunities in a new world order.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Much has been done to cushion the impact of COVID-19 on workers and businesses and it is now time to press the reset button and focus our efforts on building new capabilities for the post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The impact of the COVID-19 pandemic is expected to be protracted, so it is prudent that we adopt a financially sustainable approach as we settle in for the long haul.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To this end, we must ensure that the COVID-19 response measures are targeted, prudent and implemented cost-effectively.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must also critically review and prioritise future expenditures, in line with tighter fiscal space.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must ensure that the choices we make are prioritised to deliver the best outcomes for our people and businesses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With sharp deterioration in growth outlooks expected of all major economies, Singapore’s revenue outlook will remain uncertain and challenging for several years to come.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I guess we were all worried when the Deputy Prime Minister spoke about the need for higher taxes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Given the gloomy economic environment, residents are understandably concerned about the impending GST hike.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Travel disruptions will surely impact GST collections from foreigners and tourists.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The exponential growth of e-commerce may yield substantial GST contributions if the tax regime is enhanced.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We may not be able to avoid raising taxes to fund our rising expenses, but we must continue to find ways to keep taxes and transfers progressive and fair.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have spoken about wealth tax in my earlier speeches.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: COVID-19 has accelerated structural shifts and we must redouble our efforts to equip our people with the necessary skills to thrive in a post-COVID-19 world.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Singapore has the foresight to launch SkillsFuture more than five years ago.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The movement was driven by the imperative to have Singaporeans develop new capabilities for the future and embrace a culture of lifelong learning in order to ride the waves of change brought upon by rapid technological disruptions and economic restructuring.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This imperative is now more urgent than ever.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst the SkillsFuture movement has galvanised much awareness on the need for lifelong learning and led to greater participation in training programmes, Sir, it is less clear how SkillsFuture training is linked to the attainment of distinct quantifiable skills, career advancement and wage growth.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I often hear the frustrations of residents, particularly those who have been retrenched, that their efforts to attend training courses are not matched by recognition accorded by prospective employers and made very little difference in their job search efforts.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many employers, especially the SMEs, are at a loss as to how they may identify the right training programmes best suited for their employees to support the restructuring of their business.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With growing acceptance of remote working, businesses are widening their talent search for skillsets and deep knowledge beyond Singapore’s shores, under the Work From Anywhere in the world policy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is, therefore, of paramount importance that we support our adult workforce with an education regime capable of equipping them with skills and capabilities that match the labour needs demanded by employers and industry robustly.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Starting from a position of strength, SkillsFuture 2.0 must evolve to foster stronger linkages between training programmes, skills acquisition and improved career prospects.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: To achieve this, I call for a Government-led effort to introduce a new category of training programme, maybe called Industry Skills Training (IST) Scheme.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A key feature of this IST Scheme is the requirement to address labour force demands, with the strong involvement of prospective employers and industry group in training design and delivery, in collaboration with the training providers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Swiss and Swedish Vocational Training Systems are useful references in designing the IST Scheme.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Governance framework of IST programmes must facilitate clear identification of training needs and accountability of training effectiveness and quantifiable outcomes, with the industry and employers both playing pivotal roles.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The programmes should be anchored upon a clearly laid out, systematic skills ladder for the respective sectors organised along ITM clusters and include training for new business models and solutions within that sector.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Skills certification should be portable and should, if it works, right skills are being charted, correlate with pay levels.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: IST programmes should provide a clear training pathway for new entrants to the industry as well as for existing employees.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Where appropriate, credit-bearing structured internships should be an integral part of the training.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Training providers should be incentivised to achieve positive employment outcomes linked to their training and not just focused on the delivery of these programmes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is time we pivot our assistance to support our people rather than simply preserving any and all jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The biggest hurdle for many is the documentary evidence of income reduction, requiring the co-operation of employers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For example, one of my residents told me that her employer threatened to terminate her services altogether, if she reported her pay reduction in order to qualify for CSG.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Less educated senior residents who work in low-wage jobs struggle the most with the application process.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even though residents find comfort in the extension of CSG support till the end of this year, many are unsure about how they may meet the requirement to prove to the authorities that they had made sufficient effort in job search and training in order to qualify for this support.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The scheme should allow room for unique circumstances and empower approving officers to apply good sense and compassion in hardship cases that may not neatly fit the criteria.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We need to provide for families a sustained level of basic daily expenses, medical coverage and retirement adequacy should their livelihoods continue to be disrupted.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We cannot stop at the time that we have indicated if the situation continues.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This may be just the catalyst that reskills, transforms and strengthens Singapore’s greatest resource – our people – and catapults us into the forefront of an international recovery when the tides are with us once more.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members have raised many useful points over more than 12 hours of the debate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, if I take 20% of your time, there would be still be 80% of the points that will not be addressed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But my respective Ministry colleagues will review them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Keeping the pandemic under control remains our top priority.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As I shared last week, we are in a stable position.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have a plan to further re-open our economy safely.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we must stay vigilant, to stay ahead of this virus.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our economy is also showing early signs of recovery.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The International Monetary Fund or IMF's latest projections for global growth in 2020 is -4.4%, a less severe contraction than the June forecast of -5.2%.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But the IMF also warned that recovery is prone to setbacks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Although it seems we have turned the corner, we are not out of the woods.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just last week, the World Health Organization recorded the largest one-day rise in cases, with an increase of more than 338,000 cases globally.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our economic trajectory also hinges on how other countries manage the pandemic and reopen their economies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And even if our GDP growth figures rebound, the jobs situation will remain challenging for some time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is, therefore, critical that we support our workers and businesses through this crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Several Members shared their views on the COVID-19 support measures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the start of the crisis, no one could predict how severe the virus situation would become and how badly our economy would be affected.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: COVID-19 is both a health and economic crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It has caused both a simultaneous supply and demand shock as trade links were disrupted and consumer demand plunged.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In the face of an unprecedented crisis, our priority was to flow support to as many affected people and businesses, and as quickly as possible.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Jobs Support Scheme, or JSS, is one example of this support.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: SMEs, on average, receive more than five times as much JSS support per dollar of revenue compared to the average JSS recipient.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our schemes and programmes have dampened the adverse economic impact of COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They have also kept our unemployment rate in check and reduced long-term scarring on our economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As the COVID-19 situation in Singapore stabilises, the next pressing task is to help our economy recover.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our support must therefore evolve from "resuscitate" to "rejuvenate".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are also pivoting from broad-based relief to more targeted support, to better cater to the needs of our sectors and firms.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, those that will see greater demand in the post-COVID-19 economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I encourage these firms to make full use of the suite of capability development grants to expand and grow.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The JGI will also support them to hire more locals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The second category are firms in sectors that are suffering a temporary drop in demand now but will eventually recover.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will help them recover faster and emerge stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For the tourism sector, the SingapoRediscovers Vouchers will help encourage domestic consumption.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For the aviation sector, the Enhanced Aviation Support Package will help firms retain core capabilities to position for recovery.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I share Mr Sharael Taha's view that being an air hub is strategic to our economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For the arts and sports sectors, Minister Edwin Tong has just shared further details of the Arts and Culture, and Sports Resilience Packages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I hope these will alleviate Mr Darryl David's concerns for the sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: However, there could also be cases where a firm's potential failure due to this crisis would significantly impact Singapore's competitiveness or national security.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In such instances, we cannot preclude the possibility of Government taking some action to ensure these strategic capabilities are preserved.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The exact form of support will depend on the circumstances.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But the bar for any Government action will be high.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government will also exercise prudence and ensure public funds are well used.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The third category are firms where the outlook remains bleak as there are fundamental changes in their operating environments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They will need to reinvent themselves and pivot into new products and sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Minister of State Alvin Tan mentioned yesterday, the Government is finalising a set of measures to support nightlife businesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I agree with Mr Saktiandi Supaat that as firms recover, we need to taper the support carefully to avoid a cliff effect.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In addition to the extensions of financing schemes and payment moratoriums, customised restructuring schemes will also be available for those who need more tailored support.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will continue to monitor the situation and adjust where needed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Taken together, these measures will help our firms recover, in a more targeted and efficient manner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Given the scale of this crisis, we may not be able to save every business and every job, but we will support every worker.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We launched the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package earlier this year to create opportunities in jobs, traineeships and skills training.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are working on the next bound of tripartite efforts to develop more opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan asked if we could accelerate job matching for our displaced workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, we have been working to speed this up through multiple channels.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There is now an SGUnited Jobs and Skills Centre in every HDB town.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have also held multiple career fairs at locations islandwide.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As a result, we have seen a steady increase in placements.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In this period of restructuring and recovery, I urge both employers and jobseekers to keep an open mind and be willing to adapt and adjust.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members have also highlighted concerns over a few groups of workers who are at higher risk of income loss or who face difficulties finding a job during this period.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I agree with Mr Yip Hon Weng that we must intensify our efforts to help our retrenched mid-career workers reskill and find new employment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is why we introduced additional support for them via the SkillsFuture Mid-Career Support Package and the SG United Jobs and Skills package.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I also encourage our mid-career jobseeker to stay resilient and adaptable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As Mr Vikram Nair pointed out, "creative destruction" is inevitable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Changing industry and potentially taking a pay cut for now is certainly painful, but will put you on a better footing in the post-COVID-19 economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, I urge companies to be receptive towards hiring mid-career workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They have much to offer with their wealth of experience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Denise Phua will be pleased to know that this same 50% support is also available to employers who hire persons with disabilities, regardless of age.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I also agree with Mr Murali Pillai's idea to extend the 50% JGI support to ex-offenders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I have asked MOM to take this up.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They will announce more details in due course.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Another group of concern is our self-employed workers, as Mr Dennis Tan and others have highlighted.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This was why we introduced the Self-Employed Person Income Relief Scheme, or SIRS, to provide relief to those with less means and family support.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The three payouts were sized to cover affected self-employed persons till end-December 2020.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government is studying how to continue supporting this group of workers beyond 2020.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But like other support schemes, we will need to taper towards normalcy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will provide an update before the end of the year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Another group we are watching out for is our lower wage workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I agree with Miss Cheryl Chan that we need to extend holistic support to uplift our low wage workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, many of them are in frontline service jobs which have been disproportionately affected by the pandemic and safe management measures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For those who are retrenched, we will support them under the SG United Jobs and Skills initiative.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So far, we have facilitated the placement of 17,000 non-PMET workers into new jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is more than 50% of the 30,000 placements facilitated as at end-August.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As mentioned at my Ministerial Statement last week, we will expand PWM to more sectors over time to benefit our low-wage workers, while making sure that businesses can absorb this change.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I agree with Senior Minister of State, Zaqy Mohammed and NTUC Deputy Secretary-General, Dr Koh Poh Koon for their cogent explanation on the strengths of the Progressive Wage Model.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, we should avoid a blunt approach, especially when we are in the midst of battling this crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Let us focus on supporting our workers and businesses especially SMEs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I commend our tripartite partners for agreeing to form a Tripartite Workgroup on Lower Wage Workers to study how to expand the PWM to more sectors and push for greater productivity growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I fully support this tripartite partnership and look forward to their recommendations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Besides the Progressive Wage Model, we also have the Workfare Income Supplement, or WIS, which Mr Fahmi Aliman mentioned.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This boosts the wages of our workers who earn below $2,300 monthly with an income supplement of up to 30% through cash and CPF payouts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: PWM and WIS must be seen as an integrated package.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: She works as a cleaner and earns $1,500 each month, thanks to the PWM.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On top of that, she receives Workfare payments at $333 per month.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Taken together, she has a monthly income of at least $1,800.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Auntie Geok also benefits from the one-off Workfare Special Payment of $3,000 this year, to help tide through this difficult COVID-19 period.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Besides our at-risk and vulnerable workers, we are aware that COVID-19 has affected the livelihoods of many Singaporeans at large.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For those who faced job or income loss, we provide relief through the COVID-19 Support Grant, or CSG.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have designed our schemes to ensure support is targeted towards those who are most in need.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As with any eligibility criteria, there will be exceptions along the margins.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In summary, let me reassure Members that we remain determined to support our firms and workers through this period.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While we have made a shift to prepare our firms and workers for recovery, we recognise that the COVID-19 situation remains uncertain.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will continue to monitor the situation closely, and provide additional support where necessary.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In my Ministerial Statement last week, I sketched out the broad strokes of our economic strategy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am glad that many Members have contributed many useful ideas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa puts it well. "The crisis has hurt us as a country.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we should also capitalise on this crisis to write another exceptional chapter of the Singapore story." Unlike other countries, Singapore is both a city and a nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Cities are nodes sitting at the cross-roads of many flows – goods, capital, people, and ideas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Nations are communities with a common identity and destiny.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They look out for and care for one another.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore is a global city – open to new and exciting flows.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we are also a nation – we have to make a living for ourselves, stay united and defend our independence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Managing this unique dual identity is critical to our success.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have to stay open to the world while forging our own identity, stay globally connected while remaining independent, and embrace diversity while being socially cohesive.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These seemingly conflicting objectives are not choices, but necessities for us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And they will always define us as a country, and guide how we manage our economy and society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This dual identity has shaped our economic journey.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Since Independence, we have adopted outward oriented policies, embraced free trade and welcome foreign multinationals to base themselves here.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over time, companies like Infineon, Johnson & Johnson, and Rakuten have established regional and global operations in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They bring their know-how and business networks to Singapore, and create a vibrant ecosystem to nurture our local companies and start-ups.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These foreign firms also give our companies opportunities to become part of a global value chain.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, Zumata, a local start-up, was engaged by Sompo, a global Japanese insurance player, to automate the handling of customer queries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Sompo ended up applying their prototype solution not only in its contact centre in Singapore, but also in its Philippines outfit.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Through this process, Zumata was brought into an overseas market as well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is these kinds of synergies – between foreign and local firms, between MNCs and start-ups – that will continue to anchor Singapore as a true Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh had correctly reminded us that such collaborations ensure our survival and prosperity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They bring good jobs to Singapore, and ensure that new businesses continue to seed themselves in our soils.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is why we have always been relentless in encouraging our people and firms to upskill and transform themselves; to ready themselves for such new opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And this is how we make sure jobs and industries are future-proof – exactly what Mr Leon Perera spoke about.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim also spoke about activating a Plan B, to get local firms to transform and go regional.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The fact of the matter is that this economic transformation has been our plan all along.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And in fact all of these years, we have been reinventing our economy over and over again.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Assoc Prof Lim mentioned the Government has spoken about technology, innovation and enterprise since 2016.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Twenty sixteen was also when we started our Industry Transformation Maps, or ITMs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But we have a broad base of companies, numbering several hundred thousand.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Uplifting all of them, along with our workers, is not a straightforward matter.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our agencies like Enterprise Singapore, and in fact, all our economic agencies and our tripartite partners have been working decisively and closely with businesses on their transformation journeys.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It has given us added impetus to help our businesses find new opportunities and take new strides.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And I know businesses are doing what they can.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Business owners I spoke to, tell me about how they are working to transform their operations and upskill their workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will double down on our efforts to support them in this journey.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And this is what the next iteration of the ITMs seek to achieve.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We are consulting widely across industries and firms as we refresh our ITMs – as part of our preparation for ITM 2.0, as Mr Edward Chia mentioned yesterday, and many Members have given helpful suggestions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Chia raised a very good point about how supply chains are being reimagined, and how this is a good opportunity for our firms to further expand themselves into the region.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr Chia's other point on how innovation can be augmented by the "two-fold engine" of technology and design, is also useful.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This will help our firms differentiate themselves in this age of the online marketplace.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Another way firms can differentiate themselves is to offer innovative products and services born out of cross-cluster synergies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Shawn Huang had insightfully observed that we need to recognise and harness adjacencies across industries and across jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, all of these will bring about the potential for systems-level innovation across our economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Teho Ropes & Supplies is a local firm that provides systems solutions to the marine and offshore industries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Through the platform, it was matched with Ent-Vision, a local AI start-up.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ent-Vision tapped on its experience in supply chain and logistic solutions to build a machine-learning system for Teho that automated the labour-intensive customer quotation process.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, Ent-Vision built on this newly gained domain knowledge to develop a new product and segue into the maritime sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Green Economy also presents opportunities for firms to seize early mover advantages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These opportunities range from clean energy solutions and low-carbon technologies, to innovations in the built environment, and the development of green financial tools and markets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We invested R&D in these areas early, as part of our 2020 Research, Innovation and Enterprise plans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The next step, as Miss Cheryl Chan rightly identified, is to equip our people with the know-how.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Work in under way on this very important area.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example we have set up the Energy Efficiency Technology Centre to offer training programmes, on top of existing SkillsFuture courses that will train Singaporeans in sustainability sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The objective of growing our firms is ultimately to create quality, well-paying, and sustainable jobs to benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Foo Mee Har highlighted a pertinent point, that the future of work may be very different post-COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The rise of digitalisation and the gig economy will make the job market more volatile.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Job types and work arrangements will also evolve, as Ms Yeo Wan Ling and Mr Louis Ng had pointed out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, Singapore is facing an ageing population.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: By 2030, this ratio is projected to become 2.7 to 1.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Put another way, each adult will need to work twice as hard to support our seniors in 2030.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And of course, we will also support seniors to stay active in the workforce if they wish.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: That is why we will redouble our efforts to support Singaporeans of all ages to stay well-educated, well-trained and well-skilled.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This Government will spare no efforts in providing our people with the avenues to fulfil their fullest potential.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We take a life-cycle approach to do this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To give every child a good start in life, we provide affordable, quality pre-school education.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I agree with Mr Don Wee on the importance of uplifting our disadvantaged children.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He had put it very well, that "a stitch in time saves nine".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will continue to help those who start off with less.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have programmes like KidSTART, UPLIFT and Learning Support Programme to help them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For our youths, they benefit from a good education system that equips them with the latest knowledge and skills.
